Sports.title: Leeds in talks with Man City over deal for Trafford
Sports.content:
Leeds United are in talks with Manchester City over a deal for goalkeeper James Trafford.

The England international is Leeds' primary goalkeeper target.

Newcastle and Aston Villa have also had an interest this summer in Trafford, but Leeds are understood to be the most advanced in their pursuit.

The 23-year-old played 17 times for City in 2025/26, following a move back to the Etihad from Burnley, keeping eight clean sheets.

He then travelled to the 2026 World Cup with England, but did not make an appearance for Thomas Tuchel's side.

Leeds have lost goalkeepers Karl Darlow and Illan Meslier this summer, with the pair joining Man Utd and Arsenal respectively.

They are understood to be hopeful about their chances of signing Trafford.

Finding a new first-choice goalkeeper is a priority for Leeds this summer after Darlow's exit and an unconvincing debut season for Lucas Perri.

Perri, who was dropped by Daniel Farke last season, and third-choice Alex Cairns are the only senior goalkeepers currently on Leeds' books.

There is the potential for Perri to depart this summer amid interest from Torino.

However, Leeds are unwilling to part with the Brazilian until they have brought in at least one goalkeeper.

In

Tarik Muharemovic - Sassuolo, £34m

Harry Wilson - Fulham, free

Out

Pascal Struijk - Brighton, £18m

Isaac Schmidt - Young Boys, undisclosed

Karl Darlow - Manchester United, free

Illan Meslier - Arsenal, free

Sports.title: ‘Don’t become the protagonist’: Andoni Iraola on the secret of Spain’s success and his role at Liverpool
Sports.content:
Over coffee in Liverpool’s plush hotel in Chicago, Andoni Iraola presents his theory for the phenomenal success of Basque and Spanish coaches. It is a theory that will shape his entire approach to life as the Liverpool head coach and his attempts to bring the connection, the joy and the belief back to Anfield. It centres on the power of the collective.

The Champions League, the Premier League, the Europa League, the FA Cup, the League Cup, the European Championship and, as of Sunday, the World Cup: all currently in the hands of Basque and Spanish coaches, even if Pep Guardiola has since taken his leave from Manchester City. Next season, four men from the small Basque region of Gipuzkoa will manage four of the Premier League’s main contenders, Iraola included, alongside Mikel Arteta, Xabi Alonso and Unai Emery. There is, Iraola believes, a simple explanation for the rise of the guys from Gipuzkoa and for Spanish dominance across a global stage.

“They ask me why a lot of Basque managers especially have arrived to this level and why Spanish teams are winning a lot of things,” Iraola explains. “I always say that a sense of collectiveness is very important. Spain has never had the best athletes. If you analyse in swimming, boxing, track and field, Spain don’t normally win medals. But in collective sports they are very good. In football, basketball, handball, hockey, normally they have good teams. We always put the team first. An example is someone like Rodri. He didn’t score or make an assist but at the end they won the World Cup and he won best player of the tournament. Team-first was always integrated in how we were raised.”

Iraola, warm and friendly despite the jetlag at the start of Liverpool’s pre-season tour of the US, then gives an immediate example of how he embodies those values. He is asked about a letter he sent to Liverpool in January 2014 when, as captain of boyhood club Athletic Club, he rejected the opportunity to sign for Brendan Rodgers’s team. By all accounts courteous and apologetic, as well as highly unusual, the letter provides a telling insight into Iraola’s character. It is an open goal of a question to a new head coach wanting to win over a new fanbase. But Iraola declines to shoot.

Following a lengthy pause, he says: “I don’t know if I want to tell this story so early in my career here. I would like to win some games first. It is a nice story but if you remember me in some months, then you can ask me again. I don’t like to do this from the beginning. I just don’t want to. It will look like I am selling myself. We need some time, and to win some games.”

Iraola’s outlook is refreshing – “Don’t become the protagonist,” he says of his role – and one that Liverpool can easily identify with. Continuing with the theme of Spain’s collectiveness, he adds: “I think there has to be something in society. It cannot only just be about football. I think things work when we are not just selfish, no? When, in the end, you prioritise the situation of the one who has less. That happens also in football. The ones that don’t play, the ones who come from the academy, the ones who earn less. You can compare it with society.”

View image in fullscreen Andoni Iraola will hope to inspire Jeremie Frimpong this season after his disappointing debut campaign at Anfield. Photograph: Nick Taylor/Liverpool FC/Getty Images

But, and it is a “but” that needs saying given what Iraola hopes to achieve, there were few signs of togetherness at Liverpool last season as Arne Slot’s reign unravelled amid acrimony in the dressing room and in the crowd. The power of the individual took over, and the power of the team appeared secondary. Mohamed Salah’s frequent attempts to undermine his former, title-winning coach was not the only example of that last season.

“I cannot change the personality of the players,” says Iraola, who will manage for the first time as Liverpool head coach on Saturday against Sunderland in Nashville. “Some players are very different to me but they are great players. I don’t want to change everyone and what they think is the best way. But I think we need to think collectively in this game. As a player you are always selfish. You always want to play, you always want to get your stats, you always want to play all the minutes, but I think there has to be an understanding that this is not going to always happen and still I have to be helpful with my teammates and with the team.

double quotation mark I always say we are assistants to the players. They are the main part Andoni Iraola

“The first thing we have to do is try to play well, but it’s not just only about playing well. Supporters have to identify with what they see on the pitch. Sometimes it’s not about just putting one ball in the top corner. A lot of the time, the ones watching the game, OK, they cannot do that but they can run, they can fight for the balls, they can press, they can fight until the last line for every situation and when they see this from the players of their team it’s easier to get behind that team. I will encourage my team to give them these things.”

Iraola never came close to signing for Liverpool 12 years ago despite the best efforts of Michael Edwards, until recently the chief executive of football for the club’s owners, Fenway Sports Group. “I never really wanted to leave Athletic Club,” their former right-back admits. “For me, Athletic Club was the place to be. The only way of leaving was to go to the MLS [with New York City FC] and try something completely different. I didn’t want to become a problem for the club.”

The 44-year-old, however, does see parallels between his boyhood club and his new one. He explains: “This is one of the biggest clubs in the world and, in some way, the comparison to Athletic Club probably isn’t fair, but in a lot of ways I see a lot of similar things. This sense of belonging, of being a little bit different. This connection, also, with players from the academy. The atmosphere of Anfield.”

At his official unveiling in Liverpool last week, Iraola said he intends to immerse himself in the city and “take some pictures” of the tourist spots. The truth is he has already done so. He visited the city a few times during his playing days with Athletic and for a very simple reason. “It had the best flight connections,” he laughs. “The best connections were Manchester and Brussels and sometimes we only had two or three days so the main thing was to go somewhere quick. I remember the first time I went to Liverpool it was already the Christmas market so it was probably around the November international break. We had no kids at the time so we are talking about a lot of years ago but it was a lovely time with my wife.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There has been no holiday this summer for Iraola and his family, now extended by two children. “I went home for one week in the half-term for the kids at the end of May,” he says. “That was once the season had ended. I have mostly been in Bournemouth but I also had some trips to Liverpool to sort the schools and the housing. This is the stuff I wanted to do before I started working officially.”

Iraola describes the process of leaving Bournemouth after three impressive years as “very, very clean” and claims he only started considering his next step once last season had ended with the club in Europe for the first time. The process of becoming Slot’s replacement “was actually quite fast”. He says: “Honestly. It was true that I was talking with some clubs [Milan, Bayer Leverkusen and Crystal Palace all made approaches]. I think it was the first or second week after the season ended. But it happened fast. They contacted me, and it didn’t take a lot [to say yes to Liverpool this time].”

View image in fullscreen Andoni Iraola answers questions in the US before Liverpool’s opening pre-season game against Sunderland on Saturday. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

It hasn’t taken long for Liverpool fans to create a song in honour of their new head coach. Sung to the tune of Christy Moore’s Viva la Quinta Brigada, written about Irish volunteers who fought against Franco’s fascist forces in the Spanish civil war, the song went viral within days of Iraola’s appointment in June. He is genuinely astonished when told, almost spluttering over a second cup of coffee.

“A new one?” Iraola asks incredulously. “For me it is a strange situation because I always understand that football is about the players. At the beginning when I arrived in England, I remember the first few games I didn’t go with the players to clap the supporters after games. Tommy and Shaun [Elphick and Cooper, Bournemouth assistants who have followed Iraola to Liverpool] said I should join in. In Spain, normally you leave it to the players; they are the ones who have played the game and we are the ones who stayed behind. In England, managers are the ones who go to the fans, so I have done it every time.

“These are the cultural things you have to learn when you arrive in a new league. But I always say we are assistants to the players. They are the main part. Our main thing is to help them and they are the only ones who can give us success. We are not as important as they are, that is pretty clear.”

The Kop may dispute that theory, but not Iraola’s take on the power of the collective if restored to full working order.

Sports.title: Arsenal sign Greece forward Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34m
Sports.content:
Arsenal have completed the £34m signing of Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge. The Greece international, 24, has signed a five-year contract with the Premier League champions and arrives as a replacement for Leandro Trossard following his switch to Besiktas.

Tzolis’ move to the Emirates Stadium – Arsenal’s third permanent transfer of the summer – arrives 48 hours after the north Londoners missed out on Morgan Rogers who signed a £117m British-record fee with Chelsea, describing his new employers as the “biggest club in London”.

Tzolis scored 43 times in 108 appearances for Club Brugge, and lined up in the Belgians’ 3-0 Champions League defeat to Mikel Arteta’s side last season. “I need some time to realise it, I think! ⁠It’s absolutely amazing to sign for such a big ​club, the champions of ‌England. I’m very ‌proud to be part of this team for ‌the next season,” said Tzolis.

Arsenal’s sporting director Andrea Berta added: “We’re delighted to have completed the signing of Christos. [He] is an extremely versatile attacking player who naturally operates on the left but is comfortable across the front line. He’s an excellent finisher with both feet, thrives in tight spaces, and possesses incredible technical ability.

“Christos has produced outstanding numbers in terms of goals and assists over the last three seasons, and he’s a player who will raise the technical level of our squad, while bringing positive energy, enthusiasm, and a strong mentality to our team. We’re confident Christos will make a significant contribution to our club, and we hope our supporters will enjoy watching him play in an Arsenal shirt. We look forward to sharing this exciting new chapter together.”

Tzolis played 14 Premier League games for Norwich during the 2021-22 campaign but did not find the back of the net. Loan periods with FC Twente and Fortuna Dusseldorf followed before he made the move to Club Brugge in 2024.

Tzolis follows Piero Hincapié – who turned his temporary deal with Arsenal into a full-time switch – and goalkeeper Illan Meslier, a free signing from Leeds, as the Gunners’ third signing. The announcement arrives as a boost of sorts for Arteta after defender William Saliba was this week ruled out for an “extensive period” with a back problem which curtailed his World Cup. The France international is set to miss the start of Arsenal’s Premier League defence.

Sports.title: Manchester United consider Camavinga and Berge as midfield overhaul continues
Sports.content:
Manchester United have identified Real Madrid’s Eduardo Camavinga and Fulham’s Sander Berge as midfield signings to further strengthen Michael Carrick’s squad.

United have already signed two midfielders this window: Andrey Santos in a £48m deal from Chelsea and Youri Tielemans for £35m from Aston Villa. But with Casemiro having departed and Manuel Ugarte ruled out for what may be a prolonged period due to knee ligament injury, the club is considering moving for another midfielder.

Camavinga is believed to favour staying at Real though the Spanish club may be open to selling the Frenchman in order to make space for Rodri. The 23-year-old Camavinga, who has three years left on his contract and was not part of France’s World Cup squad, has a €1bn release clause, but Real would listen to offers of between €50m-€60m (£42m-£51m) for the player, it is thought.

View image in fullscreen Sander Berge featured for Norway at the recent World Cup, including in the quarter-final against England. Photograph: Chris Carlson/AP

Berge, who is 28 and has previously been on United’s radar, would cost around £40m and, unlike Camavinga, has considerable playing experience in England. The Norwegian signed for Sheffield United in 2020, joined Burnley in 2023 and left for Fulham the following year. Berge played in Norway’s 2-1 World Cup quarter-final loss to England.

Sports.title: Transfer roundup: Barcelona sign Adeyemi, Monaco’s Bamba set for Newcastle
Sports.content:
Barcelona have signed German winger Karim Adeyemi from Borussia Dortmund ⁠on a deal until 2031 while Newcastle are set to make Aladji Bamba their fourth summer signing.

The La Liga club will pay around €22m (£19m) plus add-ons for the Germany international ⁠and the package includes a sell-on clause.

“FC Barcelona and Borussia Dortmund have reached an agreement for the ⁠transfer of forward Karim Adeyemi, who has signed a ​contract with the Catalans ‌until 2031,” Barcelona ‌said in a statement.

Adeyemi joined Dortmund in 2022 from ‌Austrian side Red Bull Salzburg and made 146 appearances for the Bundesliga club, scoring 36 goals in all competitions. The 24-year-old will reunited with Hansi Flick, who handed him his senior debut for the Germany ‌national team during the coach’s two-year spell in charge.

Adeyemi becomes Barcelona’s second attack-minded ⁠signing of the transfer window after the arrival ​of Anthony ​Gordon.

Gordon’s former club, Newcastle, meanwhile, are set to make Aladji Bamba their fourth summer signing. The 20-year-old Monaco midfielder flew to Tyneside on Thursday ahead of a £34m move from the Ligue 1 side.

Providing all proceeds to plan, Bamba will be the fourth player Eddie Howe has signed aged 20 or under during this close season. The France Under-20 midfielder – who made 25 senior appearances for Monaco last season – will join the former Reims goalkeeper Ewen Jaouen (aged 20), the former Hoffenheim winger Bazoumana Touré (20) and the former Ajax midfielder Sean Steur (18).

Newcastle’s new transfer policy is to sign players aged 24 or under costing – broadly – between £20m and £40m and possessing high resale potential. The idea is to help ensure a club that has recently negotiated a three-year settlement agreement with Uefa after breaching European spending rules remains on the right side of football’s squad investment regulations..

Given that he prefers to operate as a No 6, Bamba is seen as a replacement for the Italy midfielder Sandro Tonali who swapped Newcastle for Tottenham in an initial £92.5m deal.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Howe still hopes to keep Bruno Guimarães in the face of interest from Arsenal. Mikel Arteta is keen to add the Brazil midfielder to his squad and Newcastle’s captain is believed keen on moving to north London.

Arsenal though have yet to make a formal offer for Guimarães and Newcastle maintain a player who turns 29 later this year is not for sale. They seem unlikely to come to the negotiating table for an offer less than around £75m.

Sports.title: Blow for Manchester City with Rodri out for extended period due to back injury
Sports.content:
Rodri could face an extended period of time out with a back injury, which may require surgery.

The 30-year-old Manchester City midfielder returned to his finest form at the World Cup following two injury-plagued seasons. Having captained Spain to Sunday’s 1-0 final win over Argentina in New Jersey, Rodri was awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament’s best player. Yet he may now require an operation on a back issue that is set to rule him out for the start of the season.

It would be the latest setback following two injury-hit seasons which began with the rupturing of his anterior cruciate ligament in the 2–2 draw with Arsenal at the Etihad Stadium in September 2024. It ruled him out for most of the rest of that campaign before he was injured again at the Club World Cup last July. Hamstring and groin injuries followed last season, meaning Rodri started only 17 Premier League matches.

The back problem comes with the Spaniard’s future at City uncertain, his contract expiring next June. While he has a desire to play in his home country again at some point and is thought to favour a transfer to Real Madrid, they are yet to make a concrete move to sign him. Enzo Maresca, City’s new manager, hopes to keep him.

After the World Cup victory, Rodri spoke of his difficulties with injury. “For me, it’s been a very tough time,” he said. “I just want the new generations to see my example as an opportunity. When you go down, you can rise again. This is my philosophy for my entire life. Of course, sometimes things go well, things go wrong, but always the positiveness.”

Meanwhile, Leeds are in advanced discussions to sign James Trafford for a fee in the region of £50m. The 23-year-old goalkeeper rejoined City from Burnley last summer in a £27m deal believing he would be the first choice only to see that position taken by Gianluigi Donnarumma following the Italian’s arrival from Paris Saint-Germain.

Sports.title: ‘Everyone is hooked on football’: Indian league seeks to ride World Cup wave
Sports.content:
India was not at the World Cup, but the tournament drew huge interest from within the country. This has happened before but now comes with significant, and necessary, changes in the domestic game that could transform a quadrennial passion into perennial interest.

After more than a year of negative headlines regarding the Indian Super League, the country’s top tier will kick off on 4 September. “The timing couldn’t be better,” says Ravi Puskur, chief executive of the ISL’s FC Goa who last season won the Super Cup, India’s top knockout competition. “A World Cup that was not ideal in terms of viewing times has drawn strong interest and support from the Indian market. It does something a domestic league alone can’t do; it puts football at the centre of the conversation.”

Puskur and his 13 fellow club bosses in the ISL, which started in 2014, are determined to ride this wave. “Our job now is to give fans a reason to transfer that excitement to their local club,” he says.

Just starting on time would be a positive given the five-month delay to the 2025-26 season after the failure of the All India Football Federation to find a commercial partner when its 15-year masters rights agreement with Reliance had come to an end. That led to clubs suspending operations, players leaving and doubts as to whether the ISL had a future. In the end, there was a truncated 13-game campaign.

View image in fullscreen East Bengal pipped their local rivals Mohun Bagan on goal difference to win the Indian Super League, their first title for 22 years. Photograph: Hindustan Times/Getty Images

The new season is scheduled to run for eight months with a full 26 game home-and-away schedule, and that is not the only reason for optimism. In an organisational change, the 14 clubs have been given control of the commercial, marketing and sponsorship side of things, while the AIFF (which hopes to change its name to the Bharat Football Federation) keeps administrative and governance oversight. In short, the teams now have a say in their destiny off the pitch as well as on it.

“It is about starting afresh and building on this,” says Shaji Prabhakaran, the former AIFF general secretary. “The advantage is that they have resolved everything early and, at the moment, everyone is hooked on football, so finding broadcasters and investment should be easier.”

Puskur was involved in negotiating the new arrangement and is ready to make the most of it. “When you’re not spending your energy firefighting administrative uncertainty, you can focus on building squads, fan experience and commercial partnerships,” he says.

“That’s the difference this year. The old model meant clubs had very little say in how the league was packaged and sold. Now the clubs hold the broadcast and sponsorship rights directly. It puts the incentive to grow the league’s commercial value in the hands of the people who are most invested in it growing.”

It has taken 12 years to get here. In 2014, the ISL’s eight founder clubs contained famous players such as Nicolas Anelka and Alessandro Del Piero and coaches such as Peter Reid and Zico, which attracted big crowds. The stars and, to an extent, the fans have gone and this is something of a reboot. Owners are accustomed to losing money, but the hope is that the league appears to be facing in the right direction.

View image in fullscreen Big name signings such as Delhi Dynamos’ Alessandro Del Piero (right) helped attract the crowds during the Indian Super League’s inaugural season. Photograph: Hindustan Times/Getty Images

“Clubs have to think long term and look ahead four years and more,” Prabhakaran says. “They have to strengthen every aspect. It can’t just be all about the first team. They need to ask where they want to be in 10 years.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Finding the right broadcasting partner is key. “The initial value won’t be high, but the World Cup helps,” Prabhakaran says. “They need a stable broadcaster who is ready to build the property and then think of monetising in three or four years.”

Rebuilding public confidence after last season is a priority for Puskur. “Broadcasters, sponsors and fans all commit more when they trust the calendar won’t move under them.” He is also calling for real investment in youth and domestic talent to increase the domestic pool. “If ISL clubs can hold their own in the AFC [Asian Football Confederation] competitions, that changes how the whole league is perceived.”

View image in fullscreen Indian fans’ love of a sporting superstar does not stop at cricketers like Sachin Tendulkar and Virat Kohli. Photograph: Dibyangshu Sarkar/AFP/Getty Images

If it all comes together then in summers to come, India may well join the global party. “The World Cup has energised the whole population,” Prabhakaran says, “and there is an obvious question: ‘Why India is not there?’ The next question has to be: ‘What are we doing to change that?’ So we have to support the clubs and the leagues and give these millions of football discussions that are happening somewhere to go now that the World Cup is over.”

Sports.title: Don’t like the result? Don’t worry, sport no longer ends on the field of play | Jonathan Liew
Sports.content:
A funny and very small thing happened at the Formula Two race at Spa on Sunday. Noel León, of Campos Racing, carved his way through the field to finish seventh, earning himself six points in the drivers’ championship, and promptly left the circuit to go and do whatever it is Noel León likes to do after a race. Take a nap, hit the Belgian brews, congratulate himself on his palindromic name – whatever. Anyway, while he was doing that, more than three hours after the chequered flag, the FIA governing body called a meeting and decided to disqualify him.

The reason: a serious breach of appendix 5 and article 21.5 of the F2 Sporting Regulations – and assuming you don’t have those to hand, it’s the rule governing the use of headsets. During the race, a guest of León had been spotted in the Campos garage wearing what was deemed the wrong type of headset. According to the aforementioned appendix 5, only listening devices may be used by non-team personnel. This headset had a microphone, albeit upturned and unused.

Never mind that the guest had at no point attempted to communicate with the driver. Never mind the fact that León had no knowledge of any offence, no means of detecting or preventing it, and derived no advantage whatsoever from the presence of an extra unused microphone in the pit lane. How would you even cheat in this scenario, anyway? What would you even say? “Hey! Drive faster!”

We could of course devote an entire column to the pedantic weirdness of the FIA rulebook, its unshakeable fondness for petty penalties and meaningless bureaucracy. Watch any F1 race and invariably within a few laps the screen will flash up with the ominous words “FIA Stewards”, followed by some piddling infraction demanding immediate, race‑moulding punishment. (“8.5-second time penalty for Car 34 – Eating A Twix At The Wheel”).

But for the most part, at least the FIA dispenses its justice in a hurry. And in any case, the point here is a larger one. To an increasing and alarming extent, sport no longer ends on the field of play. The result is no longer the result. What happens out there is often simply a placeholder, a basis for negotiation, litigation and re-litigation: not the end of an argument but merely the start of a new one.

And this is a process that takes many forms. Debate, discourse, postmortem, pub debrief: this has always been part of the essential fabric of sport, and you would scarcely wish it otherwise. Complaining about a sporting outcome is one thing. Challenging it is another thing entirely, and a phenomenon that goes well beyond Daddy Trump and his recent invocations at the World Cup and the Open golf.

In 1990, the recently established court of arbitration for sport in Lausanne received a grand total of seven requests. As recently as the 2000s, it would hear no more than a few dozen cases a year. Now that number is close to 1,000, ranging from the minor to the seismic, from whether the Polish winger Konrad Michalak is owed unpaid wages by his former Egyptian club Zamalek, to the definition of a woman, to – at some point this year, with any luck – deciding who won the 2026 Africa Cup of Nations.

As you probably remember, the game ended in chaos. Senegal walked off in protest at refereeing decisions before returning to the pitch and winning 1-0; the Confederation of African Football later decided that they had effectively forfeited the game and awarded the cup to Morocco instead. And, of course, once you start the process of redistributing trophies and medals two months after a final whistle, why on earth would you expect Senegal to end it there? Lawyer up, gentlemen: to the death!

View image in fullscreen Bryson DeChambeau was docked two shots for a rules violation at the Open and is alleged to have said he would call Donald Trump for help over the matter. Photograph: Greig Cowie/Shutterstock

Closer to home, the Premier League’s legal battle with Manchester City has now stretched into its fourth year, with no end in sight and thus no real clarity on exactly how seriously we should take all those league titles they won under three coaches. City, as ever, fiercely deny any wrongdoing. And yet whatever the findings of the tribunal, this is basically an insane thing to happen to a sporting competition: close to half a decade in which its very history and legacy, an entire era of English football, is being argued very slowly, in a room, in secret.

Even a cursory glance at Cas’s inbox for the next few months will reveal that football is obviously the main culprit here: too big and too rich, too toxic and too tribal, too loosely and incompetently governed. At virtually every level of the game, from non‑league all the way to the World Cup, football has long been administrated along the principle that you take the money first, and work out the details later. Perhaps this is why the Lausanne dockets are replete with agent disputes, transfer disputes, competition disputes, quibbles over financial regulations and who gets to levy them.

And so when Donald Trump successfully lobbied Fifa to overturn a red card awarded to a player he had almost certainly never heard of before June 2026, it was not some shocking rupture but an act entirely on trend, for football as well as Trump himself. Don’t like the result? There is an entire apparatus constructed to indulge you: lawyers desperate for your business, administrators willing to bend an ear, armies of post-truth clones desperate to do your bidding on social media.

Perhaps all this was inevitable in a world quietly supplanting the idea of rules with the idea of brute power. Rules – in theory at least – imply fairness, the concept that we are all equal and to be treated the same. But what if – on the most fundamental level – you do not believe that we are all equal? What if your very purpose in life is to ensure that some (ie you) are treated better than others? What happens in a landscape where fairness is not an ideal, but the enemy?

And no, nobody is equating appendix 5 and article 21.5 of the FIA’s F2 Sporting Regulations with the disintegration of the rules-based world order. You might do that. I’m not going to do that. All the same, there is a kind of continuum here, one that leads all the way from the trivial to the tectonic: a portal of pedantry, a spectrum of sophistry, a continuum of choosiness. Once you start messing with sport after it has finished, even in the tiniest of ways, you can be sure the big stuff is only just around the corner.

Sports.title: How LNZ Cherkasy become a wartime success story with few modern parallels
Sports.content:
It is time for set-piece training at LNZ Cherkasy’s smart, shiny training facility. “Arsenal!” one player says with a laugh as the grappling at a corner begins, the joke spreading among others clustered in the six-yard box. That is a level everyone here must aspire to but they are edging nearer. This week a club from what used to be one of Ukraine’s football backwaters will make its European debut in a wartime success story with few modern-day parallels.

“We are making history,” the LNZ striker Mark Assinor says after the jostling has stopped and the session wound down. “But there’s been a change in mentality here and I think this is only a starting point for the club.”

On Thursday they will face the Belgian side Gent, old hands on this stage, in the second qualifying round of the Conference League. LNZ earned that right last season by finishing runners-up in Ukraine’s top flight: a phenomenal achievement given they were playing fourth-tier football as recently as 2021 and only turned professional the previous year.

One of the first waymarkers after a seemingly endless six-mile drive across the Dnipro river is a billboard reading: “Cherkasy, football centre of Ukraine” in LNZ’s striking purple tone. The country’s geographical heart sits a stone’s throw from here but the local club is now pulsing with ambition and belief. LNZ were top of the league at the halfway point in 2025-26, ultimately finishing behind the might of Shakhtar Donetsk, but something remarkable has stirred nonetheless.

“No one expected anything from us,” says Vasyl Kayuk. He is sitting in a restaurant opposite the club’s city-centre headquarters, helping polish off a post-training buffet laid on for the team. At 26, Kayuk is the youngest chief executive in Ukrainian top-flight history. “The biggest motivation and advantage is that you are young and nobody believes in you.” Along with a similarly fresh, energetic staff he is determined for LNZ to break a mould.

“The city never had anything similar to this,” Kayuk says. LNZ have existed for 20 years but, in a football scene severely hampered since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, are a rare example of a club growing at pace. Their owners, a locally based agribusiness from which the club takes its name, have sown the seeds with purposeful investment despite the turmoil that continues nationally and the aim is to build a long-term success story that acts as a beacon for Ukraine.

View image in fullscreen The LNZ Cherkasy head coach, Vitaliy Ponomaryov, at the training ground. Photograph: Anastasia Vlasova/The Guardian

“We always say that we are not sprinters, we are marathon runners,” he says. “We want to build our club and become stable.” LNZ exceeded every projection in only their third top-flight season, having finished 12th the year before. When they caused shockwaves with a 4-1 win at Shakhtar last October, Assinor among the scorers, an improbable title charge was on. A run of draws later in the campaign meant Shakhtar pulled away but foundations are being laid to ensure LNZ remain serious contenders.

A rare older face in such a youthful setup, their manager Vitaliy Ponomaryov applies the words of caution. “I don’t think that, if we celebrate this success today, it will be of use to us tomorrow,” he says, back at the training ground. “I literally told the players today that we have to forget everything, set new goals, and continue to grow.”

In some ways the 52-year-old Ponomaryov is from the Ukrainian old school: a straight-talking and no-frills coach not given to effusiveness. But he has hidden depths, including a spell officiating in top-flight games as an assistant referee during the 2000s. Since moving last year from Rukh Lviv, where he worked with Kayuk, he has created a flexible, high-functioning side comfortable playing in a mixture of styles.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“It had been difficult the previous season but he has come in and given us a winning mentality,” Assinor says. The Ghanaian was a dazzling find in 2024 after stints with obscure outfits in Poland and Slovakia, perfectly embodying a scouting setup that is not geared towards paying huge fees. “When we realised we had a chance of achieving something, everyone started to believe. He motivated everybody when he came in.”

LNZ will host the first leg against Gent in the Polish city Plock. Ukrainian sides are still required to play their European games abroad because of the precarious situation at home. It touches every part of life even at a vibrant, forward-looking club like this. In the training ground gym one of the physios, Artur Pohorilyi, describes his time as a war medic and how he survived a blast near Izyum in 2023. A club doctor, Roman Mishchenko, spends time working at a hospital for injured soldiers in Cherkasy to which LNZ also donate money. Mishchenko also works in Ukraine’s sophisticated system for amputee footballers.

A few miles along the river, in a repurposed Soviet-era sanatorium, LNZ’s academy base nurtures the stars of tomorrow. The under-16s coach, Alexei Bulgakov, worked for the now-dormant FC Mariupol before Russia attacked and took the city. He managed to escape but the cost, his home destroyed and separation from his family, was unimaginable. Bulgakov speaks vividly about a life growing up steeped in local football, describing the games between 52 teams of workers at Mariupol’s huge Ilyich steel plant.

View image in fullscreen LNZ Cherkasy has a fan shop. Photograph: Anastasia Vlasova/The Guardian

Among his current charges are a number of youngsters from illegally occupied parts of Ukraine. Some of their parents remain in those places. “We speak to each other, talk about sights and buildings in our cities, and expect that some day we will be able to return,” he says. “The club understands how hard things are for young players from these areas, and it’s very happy to give them opportunities.”

They hope for futures in a rapidly expanding LNZ setup. The training ground is new and impressive by Ukrainian standards but considered to be only 35% complete, with three more pitches, an indoor dome and new stadium planned for the site. That process may take five more years. Crowds at their ageing city-centre ground trebled last season to more than 2,000, which is no small feat in wartime. Children below 14 can attend for free and a matchgoing culture is being fostered around a city finally making its name in elite football.

“We want to make this city purple, our special colour,” Kayuk says. “This club is for our people but we also want Ukrainians to associate themselves with us, with the country’s centre. And that when they think of Cherkasy, they think of football. We want to become a real power in our league.” A tussle with Arsenal’s corner specialists still looks some way off, but Gent could be the first foreign opponents to feel the purple wave’s emerging force.

Sports.title: Chelsea set to hijack deal for World Cup star in Xabi Alonso request
Sports.content:
Chelsea set to hijack deal for World Cup star in Xabi Alonso request

Add us as preferred source

Chelsea are reportedly favourites to sign Bosnia and Herzegovina starlet Kerim Alajbegovic from Bayer Leverkusen.

The winger impressed at the 2026 World Cup as Bosnia reached the knockout stage for the first time.

2 Alajbegovic starred to help Bosnia reach the World Cup last 32 Credit: AFP

Chelsea in pole position

With his goal in his country's 3-1 group win over Qatar, the 18-year-old became the eighth-youngest World Cup scorer of all time.

And Alajbegovic appears set for a big move this summer, with the Telegraph reporting Chelsea are leading the race for his signature ahead of Juventus.

Born in Cologne, Germany, Alajbegovic began his youth career with local side 1. FC Koln.

He moved on to Leverkusen in 2021 but ultimately made his senior debut for Austria's Red Bull Salzburg.

However, he returned to Leverkusen this summer after the Bundesliga side triggered a buy-back clause.

Alajbegovic was in the youth system at Leverkusen while new Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso was managing the first team.

Alonso is thought to be keen for the Blues to bring the player to Stamford Bridge.

Alajbegovic made 44 appearances in all competitions for Salzburg last season, scoring 13 goals.

2 Alajbegovic played for Salzburg in last season's Europa League Credit: Getty

He earned his first senior international cap against San Marino last September, marking it with a goal.

And he went on to feature in all four of Bosnia's World Cup games, starting three of them.

He's been capped 14 times overall, scoring twice.

New faces keep coming at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea have already had a fairly busy summer as they begin the Alonso era.

England star Morgan Rogers is the marquee arrival so far, completing a British-record £117m switch from Aston Villa earlier this week – the third Premier League transfer of the window worth £100m or more.

Meanwhile, Alejandro Garnacho is poised to move in the other direction on loan.

Rogers follows right-back Marco Palestra, striker Emmanuel Emegha and winger Geovany Quenda to West London.

Chelsea kick off the new Premier League campaign away to local rivals Fulham on August 24.

Their first home fixture sees them take on Brighton six days later.

Sports.title: Premier League club owner leaks transfer list as fans rush to decipher targets
Sports.content:
Hull City owner Acun Ilicali has provided a cryptic update on the club's summer transfer business.

The Tigers are currently preparing for their first Premier League campaign in nine years.

3 Ilicali has 'leaked' Hull's list of transfer targets in a cryptic update for supporters Credit: PA

Sergej Jakirovic's side returned to the top-flight by beating Middlesbrough in the Championship play-off final back in May.

Hull have since made three new signings, with goalkeeper Jack Butland the first to join the club.

Oscar Zambrano sealed a return to the MKM Stadium earlier this week, with Matt Targett also joining him in East Yorkshire.

Ilicali earlier promised fans four new additions before the end of week and has now handed supporters a fresh update on social media.

Ilicali's transfer clues

The Turkish businessman shared a message along with clues over 11 potential signings who could follow Butland, Zambrano and Targett through the door.

In a post on X, he wrote: "We are reading dozens of false transfer rumours in many places.

"We are disturbed by the claims that we have been rejected and by the use of our club's name to gain attention.

"We have been working intensively for two months. I believe we will build a team that we will all be proud of.

"To prevent false speculation and to give you more information, I am leaving you with our latest transfer situation, which includes some clues."

Ilicali then added Hull's three new signings as well as the flags and a percentage for a further 11 targets.

3 Hull are set to complete the signing of midfielder Morita on a free transfer Credit: Getty

Of those teased by Ilicali, the closest to being completed is listed at 99 per cent alongside a Japan flag.

Hull are set to complete the signing of international midfielder Hidemasa Morita on a free transfer, talkSPORT understands.

The 31-year-old is available after leaving Sporting Lisbon at the end of last season.

Meanwhile, Ilicali has seemingly given the Tigers' pursuit of Marco Pasalic an 80 per cent completion rate.

talkSPORT understands their move for the Croatia and Orlando City winger is progressing.

Hull have also registered an interest in Aston Villa's Leon Bailey, who Ilicali has rated at 70 per cent complete alongside a Jamaica flag.

3 Pasalic's potential move to the Tigers from Orlando City is progressing Credit: Getty

Embolo interest

A notable absence from the cryptic list, though, is Switzerland striker Breel Embolo.

Hull are one of several clubs considering a move for the 29-year-old, talkSPORT understands.

Fellow promoted outfit Ipswich Town and MLS side Atlanta United are also interested.

Meanwhile, several clubs in Serie A are amongst those weighing up signing the £12.8million-rated Rennes forward.

Sports.title: Ella Toone already eyeing up new career and reveals dream gig after football
Sports.content:
Ella Toone already eyeing up new career and reveals dream gig after football

Ella Toone is preparing for Manchester United's upcoming season, but has told talkSPORT she wants to go on 'I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here!'.

The Lionesses star has been at Carrington as a professional player since 2018, having previously played for the club at junior level.



3 Toone recently received an MBE for the role she played in aiding the Lionesses to back-to-back European Championships Credit: Getty

The midfielder has become the Red Devils' all-time leading goal-scorer, netting 48 goals across nine seasons, as well as their record appearance maker with 213 caps for the side.

She has won two European titles with her country, becoming the only English player - man or woman - to score in the quarter-final, semi-final, and final of major international tournaments.

But Toone experienced a turbulent season last year after sustaining a hip injury in December, having scored three goals and provided five assists.



This summer, the playmaker has been celebrating after being awarded an MBE for services to football.

Additionally, she travelled to Ibiza for her hen do with several of her England teammates before getting married.



Jungle dreams

On talkSPORT, the Euros winner was asked what career path she will take when she eventually calls time on her playing days.

When asked whether she would be a coach, Toone said: "I couldn't deal with players like me moaning every day at me.



"So, no. I just want to go on 'I'm a Celeb', really. I don't know, I just enjoy being me.

"That's the programme I've watched since being a little kid. And I've just loved it. And then you watch Jill Scott go and win it..."

3 Toone is looking to stay fit ahead of Man United's next season and England's World Cup qualification matches Credit: Getty

Several former professional footballers have competed on the show, including Dennis Wise, Jimmy Bullard, and Ian Wright.



However, the only ex-player ever to win the show was former Lionesses captain Jill Scott in 2022, following the Euros victory.

Scott won with over 57 per cent of the vote having entered the jungle shortly after her retirement.

The 39-year-old has since become a regular football pundit and broadcaster across major networks, covering both men's and women's matches.

Similarly to Toone, she was also awarded an MBE in recognition of her 'outstanding contribution to sports, specifically women's sport.'



Toone was also asked whether she would also like to take up a career in punditry after she hangs up her boots.

3 Former Lioness Scott made 161 caps for England Credit: Getty Images - Getty

She told talkSPORT: "I'd give it a go. I feel like I can talk a good game. I understand the game.

"But it's obviously difficult when you're sat watching it and whatever.



"I'd like to give it a try."

Sports.title: David Moyes tipped for new job just weeks before Everton season begins
Sports.content:
David Moyes tipped for new job just weeks before Everton season begins

Alan Brazil has backed two potential candidates to become the next Scotland manager.

The national team job is currently vacant following Steve Clarke's exit this summer.

4 Scotland have been told to consider two familiar faces to succeed Clarke as manager Credit: Getty

Clarke resigned as boss following Scotland's group stage elimination from the World Cup.

Despite signing a new four-year deal ahead of the tournament, the 62-year-old ended his seven-year tenure in June.

A replacement has yet to be named by the Scottish FA, although Roberto Martinez is understood to be in the running for the role.

Brazil has now tipped both Ally McCoist and David Moyes for success if they were to be named Clarke's successor.

Brazil backing

The former Scotland striker joined Shebahn Aherne and Gabby Agbonlahor on Thursday's talkSPORT Breakfast show.

McCoist admitted on Wednesday that he would never turn down the chance to manage the national team.

As a player, the former Rangers boss scored 19 goals in 61 caps for Scotland but has been away from the dugout since leaving Ibrox in 2014.

Asked about the prospect of McCoist taking over, Brazil explained: "Ally is mad for Scotland. Rangers is his first team, but when it comes to Scotland, absolutely.

"And Ally, I think he got dealt a bad hand at Rangers, what happened, deductions, relegations and all that.

"Anyone who hears Ally on the telly, the commentaries, his idea of the game, what’s happening and how it should, how it could change in terms of substitutions and stuff, Ally is spot on.

4 McCoist has admitted he would never turn down the chance to manage Scotland Credit: PA

"He’s as good as anyone, if not the best on there, so as far as I’m concerned, why wouldn’t he (be the next Scotland manager), he couldn’t say no.

"If he said no that would be the headlines, it wouldn’t be about his tree in his garden, he’s getting pelters for that.

"If he said no to Scotland it would get even worse, so I’m with him, don’t worry."

McCoist won two promotions in three years as Rangers manager between 2011 and 2014, with both coming as champions.

Moyes for Scotland

Brazil also addressed the suggestion Moyes could replace Clarke as Scotland manager.

The Everton boss is currently preparing for the new Premier League season after a 13th place finish with the Toffees last term.

4 Everton boss Moyes would do a 'quality job' if appointed Scotland manager Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

His side begin their campaign at home to Crystal Palace on August 22.

Brazil continued: "He’s not been in a job for a while as in coaching, whereas they’re talking about David Moyes.

"David Moyes would do a quality job, make no mistake, but when you think about Scotland, the way we played and the supporters are just magnificent.

"They deserve more and it’s not the players’ fault, it’s just the players. If you look at Switzerland, look at Norway, the youngsters they bring through and how well they do, and then look at Scotland and what we do.

"I’m sorry there’s something drastically wrong with the kids in Scotland not coming through at the highest level.

"Young kids coming through and going to the top Premiership clubs, it doesn’t happen anymore. In the olden days there was always one at each club.

4 Scotland missed out on a place in the knockout stage on their World Cup return this summer Credit: Getty

"So whoever started this new revolution about coaching and academies and stuff like that in Scotland, rip it up and start again because it’s not good enough and the fans deserve better."

Despite beating Haiti in their World Cup opener, Scotland failed to reach the knockout stages in North America.

It means they have now failed to advance from the group stages at all 13 of their major tournament appearances.

This summer's finals was their first World Cup since 1998 after ending a 28-year wait to qualify.

Sports.title: World’s biggest football stadium being built to battle Spain’s Bernabéu for 2030 World Cup final hosting duties
Sports.content:
Spain and Morocco are fighting for the right to host the 2030 World Cup final.

Morocco is building the biggest football stadium on the planet in the hopes of landing the World Cup final.

The 2030 edition is being held across six countries in three continents, 100 years after the iconic tournament made its debut.



3 Stade Hassan II is an ambitious project Credit: Populous

Real Madrid's renovated Santiago Bernabéu, which cost $1.91 billion, is the favorite to land the showpiece.

But there is a growing movement calling for Morocco to be given the honor.

New footage revealed The Grand Stade Hassan II taking shape in El Mansouria -- around 25 miles north of Casablanca.



It will be able to fit 115,000 fans -- 1,000 more than North Korea's Rungrado 1st of May Stadium, which has been downgraded from the 150,000 capacity that is claimed by Kim Jong Un's dictatorship.

With a projected completion date of 2028, it will host the Moroccan national team as well as Raja CA and Wydad AC.



Populous worked on the design alongside Moroccan architects Oualalou + Choi, with a striking aluminium roof shaped like a Moussem tent to pay homage to local culture.

With a vast surrounding district featuring gardens and the capacity for 12,000 VIP and hospitality guests, it would suit FIFA to a tee.



The government is predicted to spend just $500,000 on the project, making it a bargain in a world of billion-dollar arenas.

Keen to avoid a white elephant situation, the stadium is designed to be just the starting point with a thriving sports and leisure district looking to deliver a lasting legacy.

It is a lofty goal, but Moroccan football is in a golden age on and off the field and will soon have the world's biggest football stadium to crow about, although India's Narendra Modi Stadium -- a cricket venue -- remains the largest for all sports with 132,000 fans able to pack in.

3 The stunning design has gone down well with fans



Could Donald Trump decide 2030 final host?

Spain is the long-term favorite, but Morocco's chances have been boosted by a PR push.

Morocco’s ambassador to the United States Youssef Amrani and Football Federation president, Fouzi Lekjaa are among the figureheads and Donald Trump could be an ally.

The U.S. President has a close relationship with FIFA chief Gianni Infantino and an axe to grind with Spain.

Trump, who recently endorsed Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, has been criticized by the Spanish government over his handling of Iran and Palestine.



According to Spanish news outlet Infobae, Juanma Castaño, director of El Partidazo de COPE, claimed that Trump was exerting pressure in favor of Morocco hosting the final.

There has been no confirmation from the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) and neither FIFA nor the White House has publicly commented on the claim, meaning there is no evidence to substantiate it.

3 FIFA will love the amenities on offer and the design keeps out the sun Credit: SPA

Infantino looks set to push ahead with another expansion having already gone from 32 to 48 teams.



Some believe the move could ruin the World Cup forever, but the FIFA president has adopted a clear bigger is better mentality.

"That's definitely an issue that will be examined and discussed in the relevant committees after this World Cup," Infantino told Bluewin.

"When organizing a World Cup, it's ​important to organize it for the whole world -- not just Europe and ​South America -- but effectively the entire world.

"Every nation should be ⁠allowed to dream of participating in the World Cup. You can see that ​the quality of the teams is extremely high -- and it's getting higher and ​higher, all over the world.



"If you don't give smaller countries a chance to participate in the World Cup, they'll lack the incentive to keep improving."

Sports.title: Jack Grealish tipped for European transfer one year after joining Everton
Sports.content:
Gabby Agbonlahor admits Jack Grealish moving elsewhere in Europe 'wouldn't surprise' him.

Grealish is at a career crossroads following his return to Manchester City after a season-long loan at Everton.



2 In 20 league games, Grealish created 38 chances at a rate of 2.1 per 90 Credit: Getty

The 30-year-old joined the Toffees with the hope of breaking into the England squad for the World Cup.

His stint with Everton began brightly with four assists in his first three league fixtures but ended on a sour note when he sustained a stress fracture in his foot against his old club, Aston Villa, on January 18.

Grealish subsequently underwent surgery for the injury, which ruled him out for the remainder of the season.



He's now back at City where there is a new manager to impress, as Enzo Maresca replaced Pep Guardiola following the Spaniard's decision to step down after ten years at the helm.

But if Grealish struggles to convince Maresca he still has a future at City, the 30-year-old may have to consider moving on.



Agbonlahor: 'Don't see' Grealish staying in the Premier League

Speaking on talkSPORT Breakfast, Agbonlahor, a former teammate of Grealish at Villa, couldn't see the attacking midfielder sticking around at the Etihad Stadium.

"It will be interesting to see what happens with Jack, if he's given a chance by Maresca," Agbonlahor said.



"He would have been part of that Man City squad that Maresca was at (as assistant). Or, will the manager think, 'No', and will Jack think, 'Do you know what? Maybe I want to move on'.

"I think it's still early doors, I think we have to see what happens over the next six weeks, there's still six weeks left of the transfer window...

"I don't see him staying there, I see him moving on.

2 Grealish may find himself further down the pecking order at City Credit: Getty

"It wouldn't surprise me if he moves somewhere else in Europe, I don't see him staying in the Premier League.



"I think he's still got one year left on his contract, the wages as well, will that be a problem for some clubs maybe in the Premier League?

"But don't rule out maybe going back to Everton, David Moyes loved him."

Since joining from Villa, Grealish has made 157 appearances for City, registering 17 goals and 23 assists.

In that time, Grealish has won three Premier League titles, the FA Cup, the Champions League and the Club World Cup.



However, Grealish's last season with City ended on a frustrating note as Guardiola left him out of the squad that lost the FA Cup final to Crystal Palace in favour of teenager Claudio Echeverri.

Grealish was also absent from City's matchday squad for the final game of the 2024/25 season against Fulham.

Sports.title: World Cup nation to launch formal complaint over Donald Trump intervention
Sports.content:
The Norwegian FA intends to make a formal complaint to FIFA's ethics committee over Donald Trump's intervention in Folarin Balogun's ban.

USA striker Balogun was handed a one-match ban after being sent off in his side's World Cup last-32 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina – only for the ban to be suspended after Trump called FIFA president Gianni Infantino, sparking widespread outrage.

2 Trump stepped in to get Balogun's one-match ban suspended for 12 months Credit: Getty

Trump subsequently thanked FIFA for "reversing a great injustice" in his eyes.

As such Balogun was able to feature, in the last 16 against Belgium, although the USA crashed out of their home tournament with a 4-1 defeat – after which Belgium players celebrated by mocking Trump's dance moves.

Speaking after that game, Balogun admitted the circumstances leading to his clearance to play were less than ideal.

"It was just an unfortunate situation," he said, "and I think it put a lot more pressure on us than we needed."

Subject to board backing, Norway are set to add their opposition to Trump's interference to an earlier complaint about FIFA's controversial decision to award the US president its inaugural Peace Prize – alleging it breached rules on political neutrality.

'A slippery slope'

In an interview with The Times, Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness said of the Balogun situation: "When you bend a rule like this, you’re on a slippery slope that will put the whole game at risk. It is a worry for the game when you compromise fundamental rules of the game.

"First of all, it should not have happened. It is very important now to have honest communication around it. We all know that this verdict was influenced from external forces and did not have the proper process.

"We need our leader in FIFA to say that this was an error.

"If you start to adapt in such a way towards state leaders and state politics, you will move your behaviour and the organisation’s behaviour, and also the red line of what states’ leaders should interfere with. And that happened.

"When you make controversial decisions, and when there has been an external, very powerful voice in your ear, it’s very important that you have more voices [making the decision]. And if you don’t, it’s a mistake.

2 Klaveness wants FIFA held to account over the Balogun controversy Credit: Getty

"This case was so serious and so worrying that I hope that it might contribute to bring people out a little bit and don’t fear to bring up cases. I will bring it to a board meeting and discuss with my board, and then we do it. To me, it should be in the same sphere of ethical complaint.

"To try to sweep this under the carpet now will not fly.

"Too many felt this … coaches, players, fans … that this was too close to the game."

Norway's memorable World Cup return

Norway knocked out five-time world champions Brazil to reach the quarter-finals of their first World Cup since 1998, narrowly losing 2-1 to England in extra time having taken the lead in the first half of normal time.

And Klaveness, who represented Norway at two Women's World Cups, felt the Vikings were unfortunate to lose to the Three Lions.

"I do think we played a better game," she said. "I do think we deserved to win. That said, we were perhaps lucky against the Ivory Coast [in the last 32] – they played really well against us."

Sports.title: US World Cup fans hit with brutal soccer reality after howler for Lionel Messi-less Inter Miami on MLS return
Sports.content:
Soccer fans weren't too impressed with the Fire's first goal in a defeat to Miami.

US World Cup fans hit with brutal soccer reality after howler for Lionel Messi-less Inter Miami on MLS return

Robert Lewandowski's MLS debut ended in defeat as Luis Suárez inspired Inter Miami to a 3-2 victory over Chicago Fire.

With plenty of eyeballs on the domestic product as U.S. Soccer looks to build on a hugely successful World Cup, the game didn't get off to the best start.



3 Ian Fray tries to life Rocco Ríos Novo after an own-goal Credit: Getty

Miami defender Ian Fray rolled the ball to goalkeeper Rocco Ríos Novo in the 18th minute and he somehow managed to take a wild swing with his right boot, miss completely and see the ball trickle into his own goal.

Thankfully for Fray, the effort went down as an own-goal for the goalkeeper to protect his stat sheet.

Fans quickly took to social media to share the clip and question the quality on display in MLS.



"I decided to give the MLS a shot after watching the entire World Cup. Then this happened," wrote one.

He later added: "I’m sure this is an outlier but man the quality is so far down from the World Cup it’s crazy."



"MLS delivering peak comedy as usual. That keeper looked traumatised," added another.

"Messi wasn’t crying because he lost the World Cup he was crying because he knew he had to go back to this," read one brutal joke.



"You must have forgot what the US goalie did against Belgium then," another chimed in reference to Matt Freese's whiff in the World Cup loss.

Luis Suarez steps up in Lionel Messi absence

Fortunately for MLS chiefs, the rest of the game was a great advert for the product.

Miami -- playing without Argentina stars Lionel Messi and Rodrigo de Paul, as well as new signing Casemiro -- levelled from the spot through Suárez, who made it 2-0 after half-time.

3 Suárez scored a hat-trick before the mid-season break Credit: Getty



Substitute Puso Dithejane brought Chicago level with his first MLS goal, but Preston Plambeck matched his milestone with an 87th minute winner to get off the mark for his hometown club.

Miami has won five straight in a streak that began before the six-week hiatus.

The MLS regular season runs from February 21 to November 7, but took a mid-season break to accommodate players who were called up to represent their respective nations in the World Cup, mainly the US men’s national team.

The league returned to action on July 16.

"I want to congratulate the entire squad, a group that has worked incredibly hard during this period," Herons manager Guillermo Hoyos said after the game. "We've been doing things right.



"I also want to congratulate the whole club. There are so many people working behind the scenes who make this great happiness possible. It's truly moving, because that's what football is all about: emotions, achievements, and feelings."

3 Suárez and Lewandowski are two of the biggest stars in world football Credit: Getty

Hoyos is going to give Messi and De Paul plenty to time to recover after their run to the final.

"I believe, and I've said this several times, that rest is vital," he said. "It's part of an individual's growth and development.



"They need this time, and we are completely open to giving them whatever time they require. There is no set return date.

"We trust and care for them so much, and we want them back only when they are truly ready, fully recovered in every aspect.

"It has been an incredibly grueling stretch, 50 days of intense pressure and World Cup matches.

"It's immense, and the physical and mental toll is real. They truly deserve this time off, and we'll be waiting for them to return whenever they are able and in the right condition to do so."



Lewandowski signed for the Fire on June 29 but saw his potential debut postponed over hazardous weather.

He brings plenty of pedigree from his time with Borussia Dortmund, Bayern Munich and Barcelona.

The seven-time Bundesliga Golden Boot winner's arrival is expected to see the MLS' leading scorer Hugo Cuypers join CF Monterrey of Liga MX.

Gunners get their man

Arsenal have completed the signing of winger Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34million.

The fee is a record for the Belgian Pro League.

The 24-year-old, formerly of Norwich City, scored 17 goals and added 23 assists in 36 league appearances last season.

Arsenal have completed the signing of winger Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34million

Magpies swoop for £30m star

Newcastle United have agreed a deal to sign Monaco defensive midfielder Aladji Bamba.

The 20-year-old is due on Tyneside this morning for his medical after a fee around £30million was negotiated between the clubs.

Bamba only made his breakthrough last season and has played just 18 league games but is highly regarded after his development through the France youth ranks.

Newcastle United have agreed a deal to sign Monaco defensive midfielder Aladji Bamba (left)

✈️ The 20-yr-old midfielder is due on Tyneside this morning — Craig Hope (@CraigHope_DM) July 23, 2026

Saints stand firm on Charles fee

Southampton risk pricing Shea Charles out of a move to the Premier League as they push for over £30million for the Northern Ireland international.

Fulham are the latest club to be rebuffed after they offered in the region of £24million for the 22-year-old.

The Cottagers believed they could strike a deal on the understanding Saints would accept £25m plus add-ons. However, the Championship side are demanding more.

Charles, who they bought from Manchester City in 2023, made 38 appearances last season and scored what looked to be the winning goal in the play-off semi-final against Middlesbrough only for the club to be excluded from the showpiece Wembley final as a consequence of 'Spygate', as exclusively revealed by Daily Mail Sport.

Leeds United had made the early running for Charles.

They also made three offers to Southampton which were subsequently rejected and are likely to consider other options.

Manchester City also hold a 15percent sell-on.

Saints are trying to build for the new season against the backdrop of head coach Tonda Eckert facing a suspension after he was charged with misconduct by the Football Association for his role in the Spygate scandal. He had until Tuesday to respond to the charges.

West Brom are also keen on Saints forward Cameron Archer.

Leeds in talks with City over Trafford move

Leeds United are in talks to sign England international goalkeeper James Trafford from Manchester City.

Trafford, who went to the World Cup this summer, only rejoined Manchester City from Burnley last summer but managed just four Premier League outings.

Leeds are on the hunt for a new No 1 goalkeeper after Karl Darlow left for Manchester United.

Trafford came through City's academy but, after making no first-team appearances, left for Burnley in 2023 after a series of loans.

He rejoined last summer in a £31million deal - a record sum for a British goalkeeper.

As Daily Mail Sport reported in April, Trafford was back on Newcastle United's agenda to be their number one but they were aware it as becoming increasingly difficult amid competition and valuation last week.

Leeds are acting are losing Darlow. Illan Meslier has also joined Arsenal while Torino want Lucas Perri.

They have asked about Zion Suzuki at Parma but are hopeful Trafford will join as he looks to cement his place as Jordan Pickford's main rival to the England number one jersey.

Aston Villa and Spurs have also shown interest in Trafford but he sees an opportunity at Leeds to build his future.

Leeds United are in talks to sign England international goalkeeper James Trafford (right)

Young Reds stopper leaves on loan

The 21-year-old, who made his senior international debut for Hungary last month, arrived at Anfield a year ago m.

He has been a regular for Liverpool's U21s and was also included in the senior side's matchday squad on five occasions.

Blues ramp up pursuit of Leverkusen teenager

Chelsea are stepping up their interest in Bayer Leverkusen winger Kerim Alajbegović.

As previously reported by Daily Mail Sport, the exciting Bosnia international has had interest from Leeds United, Arsenal, Aston Villa and Atalanta.

Leverkusen sold the 18-year-old to Red Bull Salzburg last year but, after an impressive season, took up their option to buy him back this summer for £7million.

However, the winger made such an impression in Austria, and on international duty with Bosnia, that a number of Premier League and Italian sides have been enquiring to see if Leverkusen are willing to make a quick profit.

His value was initially around £18m but after he scored a spectacular long-range goal in Bosnia's 3–1 group-stage win over Qatar at the World Cup, and Chelsea were alerted, his valuation is now closer to £30m.

Champions Arsenal, Aston Villa and Leeds United met his representatives for talks as have Napoli, Roma and Inter Milan from Serie A.

Atalanta were considered to be in pole position earlier this month but Chelsea and Xabi Alonso were made aware of the opportunity and are now looking to strike a deal.

They have moved Alejandro Garnacho to Aston Villa and see greater potential in Alajbegovic who was named in Bosnia's squad for the World Cup and made a big impact in Group C against Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Born in Cologne to Bosnian parents, Alajbegovic is quick, skilful and can play across the front line.

His father and agent, Semin, was also a footballer, spending his entire career in Germany's lower tiers.

Chelsea are stepping up their interest in Bayer Leverkusen winger Kerim Alajbegović

Chelsea beat off stern competition for his signature from Manchester City and AC Milan.
