World.title: Snow where you least expect it: Some of South Africa’s most unusual snowfalls
World.content:
Two KwaZulu-Natal content creators went viral during the September 2024 snow storm for taking photos in the snow while drinking their beer. Image: file

South Africa is no stranger to snow – at least in its highest mountain ranges.

Every winter, snow can fall across parts of the Drakensberg, Eastern Cape Highlands and other elevated regions. But every now and then, the weather delivers something far more unusual: snow in a major city, on a famous landmark, during spring or in a place where snow is rarely seen.

These are some of the most unusual snowfall events to hit South Africa in recent years.



Johannesburg’s 2023 snow day

Snow in Johannesburg is rare enough to become a major news event, which is exactly what happened in July 2023.

On 10 July 2023, snow fell across parts of Johannesburg and surrounding areas, delighting residents who had not experienced significant snowfall in the city for years.

The event was particularly unusual because Johannesburg is South Africa’s largest inland city and is better known for dry, sunny winters than snow-covered streets.

However, the city’s elevation, at more than 1 700 metres above sea level, means that snow is meteorologically possible when sufficiently cold air moves into the region.

The 2023 event was especially memorable because of its widespread nature, with snow reported in parts of the city and surrounding Gauteng.



For many residents, it was a rare opportunity to experience a proper snow day without leaving the province.

Snow falls on Table Mountain

It’s snowing on Table Mountain! ❄️☃️



Check out the footage taken this morning by Matt Ashwell.@tablemountainca is set to reopen on 2 September 2024. #tablemountain #snow #thingstodoincapetown #travel pic.twitter.com/0U43RpFnmj — Love Cape Town (@lovecapetown) August 28, 2024

Cape Town’s Table Mountain is one of South Africa’s most recognisable landmarks, making any snowfall on its famous flat-topped summit a particularly unusual sight.

On 28 August 2024, snow was reported on Table Mountain during a powerful winter weather system affecting the Western Cape.

While snow can occasionally fall on the mountain’s upper elevations, it is rare enough to generate widespread excitement whenever it happens.

The snowfall also coincided with snow in other high-lying parts of the Western Cape, creating striking winter scenes across the province.

For Capetonians, however, the event was a reminder that the city’s Mediterranean climate does not completely rule out snow, particularly at elevation.

Snow in spring: The September 2024 snowstorm

🌨 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝘃𝘆 𝘀𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗮𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗵 𝗔𝗳𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗮.



This is the N3, Harrismith, Ladysmith, Underberg. Cars have been stuck on the N3 since yesterday, forcing drivers to sleep inside their cars.



It is also snowing in most parts of Free State. pic.twitter.com/Q9FvfLs7Ct — The African Perspective (@theafricanptv) September 21, 2024

Snow in South Africa during winter is one thing. Snow in September, when spring has officially arrived, is another.

In September 2024, a powerful weather system brought heavy snowfall to parts of the Eastern Cape, Free State and KwaZulu-Natal.

The South African Weather Service said snow in spring is not unusual, but the scale and impact of this particular event were exceptional.

Some areas along the N3 corridor reportedly received up to 80cm of snow, causing significant disruption to one of the country’s major transport routes.

Hundreds of motorists were stranded in severe conditions, while authorities issued warnings about dangerous travel conditions.

The event was a striking reminder that South Africa’s snow season does not always end neatly with August.

Snow at a KwaZulu-Natal game reserve

One of the most surreal snowfall events in South Africa occurred in KwaZulu-Natal’s Nambiti Private Game Reserve during the September 2024 cold snap.

Images of African wildlife surrounded by snow offered a remarkable contrast: animals such as giraffes and zebras in a landscape that looked more like a European winter than a South African game reserve.

Snowfall in the higher parts of KwaZulu-Natal is not unheard of, but seeing snow-covered safari landscapes — particularly alongside iconic African wildlife — is an exceptionally unusual sight.

The images quickly attracted attention online, proving that South Africa’s weather can occasionally produce scenes that seem almost impossible.

World.title: GOOD and BAD news for PRASA and Transnet
World.content:
South African railways’ PRASA and Transnet are back in the headlines. The two state rail entities are chasing very different versions of a comeback. One is hauling coal again, to a good standard. And the other can’t get a single mainline passenger train out of the yard.

As such, Transnet freight rail is showing genuine signs of life since COVID. It railed 165 trains to Richards Bay Coal Terminal last week alone. That puts coal shipments on track for 65 million tonnes (Mt) by the end of 2026. Better locomotive availability helped. So did sharper security, which has clamped down on the dreaded cable theft and vandalism, the twin diseases that have plagued it for years.

Transnet Freight Rail now ships more than 170Mt a year. That’s up from roughly 140Mt in 2022. But it’s still nowhere near the peak of 226Mt hauled back in 2016. This was before years of underinvestment, theft and maintenance backlogs gutted the network and cost several executives their jobs.



PRASA AND TRANSNET

Coal, iron ore and general freight roughly split the annual tonnage three ways. The Department of Transport’s (DOT’s) Minister Barbara Creecy wants to see 250Mt of total rail freight by 2029. Eleven private train operating companies are gearing up to help get there, some reportedly launching this year and in 2027.

Unfortunately, cable theft remains the villain of this story. PRASA and Transnet has a solution though: A long-term answer is in-cab and radio-based signalling. It leans on radio links between trains and wayside systems instead of trackside cable. Doing so will leave thieves with far less copper worth stealing. And it should improve train safety at higher speeds, too.

GOING NOWHERE SLOWLY

A slow and steady return to form for Transnet lies in contrast to a dormant long-distance service for PRASA. Image: File

Meanwhile, PRASA mainlines are going nowhere slowly. Creecy confirmed recently there is currently no mainline long-distance passenger service running anywhere in the country. The DOT put out a Request for Information (RFI) back in August 2025, hunting for ways to relaunch three long-distance routes:

Gauteng to Musina

Gauteng to Durban

Gauteng to Mbombela

Sadly, the proposals came back and they were so expensive, flying the same routes would be cheaper. Creecy’s problem is big: How do you make a train cheaper than a plane, when the entire process relies on a state subsidy just to survive? And rhe department days it wants another R35 billion from Treasury, via the Budget Facility for Infrastructure, to fix rail lines and signalling.

PRASA AND TRANSNET TO SHARE TRIPS?

The first and best option right now is for PRASA and Transnet to run mixed trains, cross-subsidising passenger carriages with freight revenue on the same lines. The lines, it’s worth noting, belong to Transnet outright. Creecy’s says to break-even, PRASA needs to complete 300-million passenger journeys a year. 101 million trips were recorded in the 2025/26 financial year. And the ambitious target is 600 million by 2030/31, to match pre-pandemic passenger figures.

A team of UK experts is working out whether trains can run every 15 minutes instead of hourly, using the infrastructure that already exists. More frequent trains mean better economies of scale, which is exactly what a subsidy-dependent services desperately need. Creecy has given herself until the end of this term of government, 2029 at the latest, to make it work …



But what do you think of the current situation with PRASA and Transnet? Can anything beyond a taxpayer bailout save these entities? Please share your thoughts in the comments section below …

World.title: WATCH | ‘Haai, My Lord, I’m tired of this now’: Exasperated witness snaps in ‘Cat’ Matlala trial
World.content:
Former security guard at a Centurion golf estate, Bethwell Cele, is making a name for himself on social media as he proves to be an interesting but difficult witness in trial of Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala and his four co-accused

Matlala is on trial with his wife Tsakane Matlala, Musa Kekana, Tiego Floyd Mabusela and Nthabiseng Zandile Nzama.

The group is in the Johannesburg High Court to face 25 criminal counts, including 11 charges of attempted murder, conspiracy to commit murder, fraud, and money laundering. These also include an alleged attempted murder by Matlala on his ex-girlfriend, actress Tebogo Thobejane.



Cele was being questioned about his recollection of the assassination attempt on businessman Joe Sibanyoni.

His impatience became evident when he felt the questioning was repetetive and exhausting.

After raising his hand while looking at the judge, he told the interpreter: “Eish, My lord, I’m tired of this now. It’s the same thing over and over again… We’re not going anywhere…” said Cele.

While you're following the #MadlangaCommission, something hilarious just went down in the Cat Matlala trial during the witness testimony🤣🤣🤣



Andrea Johnson | IDAC | AFCON | Nota | Home Affairs | Winnie Mandela | Section 27 pic.twitter.com/riAeq5FDpH — Ya Mabala 24 (@KgoshiKgwadi) July 22, 2026

On another occasion, Cele was asked to rough sketch of the layout at the scene.

“Now the problem has started again… What do you want me to draw? I’m not an artist,” responded Cele with the help of the translator.



“…I’m not asking you to be an artist… Please do us a favour and try to do a drawing,” asked defense lawyer Nardus Grove.

“I don’t do favours, I didn’t grow up like that,” responded Cele.

World.title: City of Tshwane announces a 10-hour power outage on Saturday
World.content:
The City of Tshwane’s Energy and Electricity Business Unit will, on Saturday, 25 July, carry out planned power outage maintenance of the Koedoespoort Substation. According to the City’s Communication, Marketing and Events Department, the essential work involves testing and repairing any identified faults at the substation.

The power outage is expected to last 10 hours, from 8:00 to 18:00.

Several suburbs will be affected by the power outage

The power interruption will hit several areas supplied by the substation, including Silverton Industrial, East Lynne, Jan Niemand Park and Koedoespoort itself.



Also affected are Queenwood, Waverley, Bergtuin, Weavind Park, Transnet Works, SATS, Kilner Park and Moregloed.

The city said the maintenance operation is critical to ensuring a reliable electricity supply for residents in these areas going forward.

Residents warned to stay cautious

Despite the planned power outage, residents have been urged to treat all electricity network points as live at all times, as a safety precaution.

Anyone with queries about the interruption can contact the City of Tshwane Contact Centre on 012 358 9999, option 3.

World.title: Four people killed in minibus taxi crash near Mbombela
World.content:
Four people have died after a deadly crash on the N4 in Mpumalanga. Image: Facebook @ Mpumalanga DCSSL

Four people were killed and three others were injured in a horrific accident involving a truck and a minibus taxi in Mpumalanga on Thursday morning.



According to the Mpumalanga Department of Community Safety, a truck collided with the rear of a minibus taxi towing a trailer between Rivulets and Mbombela on the N4 Toll Road.

“According to preliminary reports, the truck driver seemingly lost control, swerved into the oncoming lane, and collided with another minibus taxi travelling from the direction of Mbombela,” said the department.

The truck was travelling from Johannesburg towards Mbombela.

MINIBUS CRASH ON THE N4

The department confirmed that three of the victims who died were passengers in a minibus taxi travelling from Mbombela.

The vehicle reportedly burst into flames after the collision, leaving the victims burned beyond recognition.



The fourth victim was found lying on the road.

MEC MACIE CONVEYS CONDOLENCES TO THE BEREAVED FAMILIES

Authorities have not yet determined which vehicle the individual was travelling in but they believe the victim may have been thrown from one of the vehicles during the collision.

The Mpumalanga MEC for Community Safety, Security and Liaison, Jackie Macie, conveyed his condolences to the families of the victims.

The department confirmed that no further injuries have been reported.

The cause of the accident remains unknown and investigations are still ongoing.

World.title: 7 South African towns that look like Europe when it snows
World.content:
Snow is never guaranteed in South Africa, but when the conditions are right, parts of the country can look remarkably different.



From the icy landscapes of the Northern Cape to the mountains of the Eastern Cape and Free State, these towns are among the best places to base yourself if you want to experience a proper South African winter.

If you’re hoping to see snow this winter, here are seven South African towns worth keeping on your radar.

1. Sutherland, Northern Cape

If there is one South African town synonymous with extreme winter weather, it is Sutherland.

Located in the Karoo, the small town is widely known for its freezing winter temperatures and regular winter snowfall. The town’s tourism association says snow occurs several times during winter, while the area’s record low reached -16.4°C on 12 July 2003.

When snow does arrive, the usually dry Karoo landscape is transformed into a white winter scene, complete with cosy accommodation and fireplaces.

Sutherland is also famous for its spectacular night skies and is home to the South African Astronomical Observatory, making it an ideal destination for combining a snowy getaway with some of the country’s best stargazing.



Best for: Stargazing, cosy winter weekends and dramatic snowy landscapes.

2. Rhodes, Eastern Cape

Beautiful snow in Rhodes Village, Eastern Cape, South Africa 🇿🇦 this morning, and it's still snowing!



📷 / Jess Machanik, Russell Grinker pic.twitter.com/sQJ7lDQshU — Africa View Facts (@AfricaViewFacts) July 8, 2024

Tucked away in the Eastern Cape Highlands, Rhodes is one of those tiny South African towns that seems to become even more picturesque when winter arrives.

The town is surrounded by rugged mountains and lies close to some of the country’s highest peaks, giving it a good chance of seeing snow during cold winter weather.

When the surrounding landscape turns white, Rhodes’ historic buildings and quiet streets take on a distinctly old-world appearance.

The town is also close to the Witteberg and Drakensberg mountain ranges, making the broader area a popular destination for those chasing winter weather.



Best for: A remote mountain escape and photographers looking for snowy scenery.

3. Barkly East, Eastern Cape

Another Eastern Cape Highlands favourite, Barkly East is surrounded by some of the province’s most spectacular mountain scenery.

The town and surrounding highlands are known for cold winters and snowfall, particularly at higher elevations. The nearby mountains can become covered in snow during major winter weather systems, creating some spectacular scenery.

Barkly East is also part of the region that attracts visitors hoping to experience the Eastern Cape’s winter landscapes, with nearby Rhodes and the surrounding mountain areas offering additional opportunities to explore.

Best for: Mountain scenery, road trips and exploring the Eastern Cape Highlands.

4. Hogsback, Eastern Cape

#KASITOUR

Let’s go play with the snow ❄️ in Hogsback Mawethu Elvis Platyi joins us. #LunchTimeShandis pic.twitter.com/nhTohoybOH  July 11, 2023

Already one of South Africa’s most atmospheric small towns, Hogsback becomes even more enchanting when snow falls.

Known for its forests, waterfalls and mountainous setting, the Eastern Cape village has long been associated with occasional winter snowfall.

Snow is not guaranteed, but when it happens, the combination of pine forests, cottages and mountain scenery can make Hogsback look like something out of a fairytale.

Even without snow, Hogsback is a popular winter escape thanks to its chilly climate and cosy accommodation, so you won’t have wasted the trip if the weather refuses to cooperate.

Best for: Fairytale scenery, forest walks and cosy cottages.

5. Clarens, Free State

Known as the “Jewel of the Free State”, Clarens is one of the country’s most popular small-town getaways, and winter can make it even more beautiful.



The town sits near the Maluti Mountains and is close to Golden Gate Highlands National Park. While snow in Clarens itself is occasional rather than guaranteed, the surrounding mountains and highlands can receive a dusting during cold winter weather.

The combination of sandstone cliffs, golden grasslands and snow-covered peaks makes this one of the country’s most photogenic winter destinations.

And, importantly, Clarens has plenty to do when the snow disappears: think restaurants, art galleries, hiking trails and cosy accommodation.

Best for: A stylish weekend getaway with the possibility of snow.

6. Underberg, KwaZulu-Natal

Snow in Underberg. Image: canva

For KwaZulu-Natal residents, Underberg is one of the most popular starting points for a snow-chasing adventure.

The town lies in the southern Drakensberg region, with the spectacular mountains providing the backdrop for winter trips into the highlands.



Snow is more likely at higher elevations than in the town itself, but the surrounding landscape can become a spectacular winter wonderland when a major cold front moves through.

Underberg is also a gateway to the famous Sani Pass, which climbs towards Lesotho. Visitors should remember that conditions can become dangerous in severe winter weather, and access to higher mountain areas can be restricted.

Best for: A Drakensberg winter road trip and snow-chasing from Durban and KwaZulu-Natal.

7. Fouriesburg, Free State

The small Free State town of Fouriesburg is another destination to consider if you’re hoping to experience snow in the eastern part of the province.

Located close to the Lesotho border and surrounded by the Maluti Mountains, the area can experience cold winter conditions and occasional snowfall.

Its location also makes it a convenient addition to a winter road trip through the eastern Free State, particularly if you’re exploring Clarens and the Golden Gate region.



Best for: A quieter alternative to the more popular Clarens and Golden Gate area.

Snow in South Africa is never guaranteed

The most important thing to remember when planning a snow trip is that snowfall is weather-dependent.

Even towns and mountain regions that regularly experience snow can have winters when the flakes are scarce. If your main goal is to actually play in the snow, it is best to watch weather forecasts closely and be prepared to travel at short notice.

For the best chance of seeing snow, keep an eye on the higher-altitude mountain regions and check local road conditions before setting off. Snow can also make mountain passes dangerous or temporarily inaccessible.

But if you get the timing right, you could find yourself standing in a snow-covered South African landscape without needing to leave the country, and that’s about as good as winter gets.

Important to note: Snowfall varies considerably from year to year. The towns listed are destinations associated with occasional or regular winter snowfall in their wider regions, but none can guarantee snow on a particular trip.

World.title: LIVESTREAM | SA Reserve Bank announces latest interest rate decision
World.content:
PRETORIA - All eyes are on the South African Reserve Bank as the Monetary Policy Committee prepares to deliver its latest interest rate decision.



Reserve Bank Governor Lesetja Kganyago will make the MPC announcement.



Inflation accelerated to 5% in June, its highest level in two years, strengthening the case for tighter monetary policy.



Some economists predict that the Reserve Bank could deliver its biggest increase in four years.

Rising inflation and ongoing tensions in the Middle East could influence a larger basis-point move.

World.title: LIVESTREAM | Andrea Johnson back for more grilling
World.content:
PRETORIA - Independent Directorate Against Corruption head Andrea Johnson is back in the hot seat at the Madlanga Commission.

Johnson began her testimony on Tuesday where she faced tough questions.

On Wednesday, she admitted that the directorate had asked MP Fadiel Adams to submit a Section 27 referral against Crime Intelligence head Dumisani Khumalo.

The admission came after Johnson initially denied that such a request had been made.

She has been accused of using her power to go after senior Crime Intelligence officials.

World.title: Four killed in Mpumalanga fiery crash
World.content:
MBOMBELA - Four people have died in a fiery collision between a truck and minibus taxi on the N4 in Mpumalanga.

Police say the truck allegedly lost control and crashed into an oncoming taxi travelling from Mbombela.

Authorities are investigating the cause of the crash.

World.title: 'He performed to move people': Seputla Sebogodi remembered
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The State Theatre Council has paid tribute to veteran actor Seputla Sebogodi, saying he leaves behind a legacy that extends far beyond his performances.

Family, friends and fans are gathering in Johannesburg to remember Sebogodi.

He died last week following complications related to diabetes.

They say Sebogodi inspired younger actors and brought honesty and dignity to every role he played.

The State Theatre Council described Sebogodi as a mentor who believed in lifting others as he climbed.

Chairperson Lenore Goss-Matjie said Sebogodi had a unique ability to make young actors feel valued, encouraging and challenging them to grow into the best versions of themselves.

READ | Veteran actor Seputla Sebogodi dies

She said Sebogodi understood that true greatness is measured not by individual success, but by the number of people inspired along the way.

"He made younger actors feel seen and heard. He encouraged them. He challenged them to become better. He understood that greatness is not measured by how brightly one shines alone, but by how many others one inspires to shine. That is true leadership," Goss-Matjie said.

She added that rather than seeking applause, Sebogodi performed to move people, bringing honesty, dignity and authenticity to every role.

"Whether audiences encountered him on the stage, on the television, or in film, they recognised something rare. They recognised truth. He never, ever performed for applause. He performed to move people. He gave every character dignity. He gave every story honesty. He gave every audience something to remember," she added.

World.title: Surrounded by militias, Sudanese fear endless cycle of war
World.content:
KHARTOUM - In Sudan's capital, young militiamen, some no older than 15, ride around in pickup trucks mounted with missiles: a familiar sight to civilians who remember how the current war began.

Three years ago, a powerful militia that had come under the auspices of the state -- the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) -- turned against the army, sparking a conflict that has killed more than 200,000 people by some estimates.

Now, with Sudan's army relying on a new coalition of militias to fight its battles, many fear it is repeating the same cycle.

"We've seen this scenario over and over. It's the same old mistakes, and it's only a matter of time before they turn on each other," said a 30-year-old Sudanese writer who, like others AFP spoke to, requested anonymity for security reasons.

Of the dozens of armed groups in army-controlled territory, technically under army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, three are the most powerful:

- The Joint Forces, a coalition of former Darfuri rebel militias

- The Sudan Shield Forces, which defected from the RSF

- And the Baraa ibn Malek Brigade, an Iran-linked Islamist force

All have inflated their ranks since the war broke out in April 2023, and possess their own artillery, anti-aircraft missiles and killer drones.

And all are "allies for now", wary civilians whispered to AFP in the army-controlled cities of Port Sudan, Khartoum and Wad Madani.

"The government's technically banned them from carrying weapons, but in the markets, on the streets, you still see them everywhere. It's frightening," said a 50-year-old father in Khartoum.

World.title: Venezuelans search for animal companions lost in the quakes
World.content:
CARACAS - Hundreds of hapless creatures are waiting to be reunited with their owners or find refuge with an adoptive family after Venezuela's devastating earthquakes struck one month ago.

Cats, dogs, turtles and even a goat were made homeless by the 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes on June 24, adding to the human misery of the disaster.

The tremors that struck within a minute of each other killed over 5,000 people, and left over 23,000 homeless in the worst-hit state of La Guaira and injured some 17,000 more.

Survivors wracked with grief over the loss of their loved ones have set about looking for their pets in animal shelters that have popped up around the coastal city of La Guaira, north of Caracas.

"When the earthquake happened, we ran out and she stayed behind. I haven't been able to find her since that day," 42-year-old Raquel Ramos told AFP as she searched for her cat Mia.

World.title: Mercedes expect Hungary challenge from Hamilton and Ferrari
World.content:
BUDAPEST - Kimi Antonelli heads to Budapest this weekend knowing he will lead the drivers' world championship into F1's summer break come what may, but fully aware that despite a 45-point lead he and Mercedes cannot relax.

His sixth win of the year, from his sixth pole position, in Belgium last Sunday lifted him beyond immediate reach and endorsed the impression that he has mastered the new hybrid era with its AI-controlled engine and power management.

An aggressive driving style has enabled him to make the best of the 50-50 battery and engine power packages, and critically a need to manage electronic recharging and power deployment.

As he races through the season and the record books, his team-mate George Russell, blessed with a smooth driving style, but 50 points behind in third place, has had to regroup and refine his approach – as rivals Ferrari have steadily closed the gap.

While Antonelli fought and won at Spa-Francorchamps, Russell retired after an opening lap collision with former team-mate Lewis Hamilton and needed much sympathy from team boss Toto Wolff to regain his composure.

Wolff promised an "arm around his shoulder" and, perhaps more usefully, insisted that the team would not switch their focus to one driver in pursuit of the title.

"We've shown at every race so far that the performance is there," he said. "But we haven't converted enough of that potential into results... We've lost points through self-inflicted issues and we know we need to improve."

He added that he did not want to see the drivers losing "time with each other. We don't want any yo-yoing and then to have a Ferrari or a Red Bull breathing down our necks and lose a victory."

This, he explained, meant Mercedes would "never take a victory away" from either driver regardless of it being "Kimi or George who was ahead."

- AFP

World.title: US teen withdraws lawsuit against Meta over social media addiction
World.content:
LOS ANGELES - A US teenager has withdrawn his lawsuit against Meta, closing out a closely watched case over social media's harms to children's mental health without a trial.

The withdrawal ends the case days before it was due to go before a Los Angeles jury on July 27 -- a trial that would have made Meta the sole defendant after YouTube, TikTok and Snap reached confidential settlements.

The plaintiff, identified by his initials R.K.C., is a 15-year-old from Florida who claims compulsive social media use contributed to anxiety, depression and suicidal thoughts for which he continues to receive treatment.

His case was selected as a bellwether to help resolve thousands of similar lawsuits across the country.

A first bellwether trial concluded in March, when a Los Angeles jury ordered Meta and Google to pay a 20-year-old woman, K.G.M., $6 million -- a historic first.

"R.K.C. came into this process wanting to hold social media companies accountable and push for changes to protect young people like himself. He did that," attorneys Emily Jeffcott and Rahul Ravipudi said in a joint statement.

"In light of the overall successful result of the litigation and his concerns about enduring a gruelling weeks-long trial, he has elected to withdraw his claims against Meta," they added.

"He's ready to close this chapter and focus on his recovery and engage in therapy as he aspires to have a normal life."

- 'Claims never held up' -

A Meta spokesperson said in a statement: "Days after settling with other social media companies, the plaintiff dropped his case against Meta, the only remaining defendant, without receiving any payment."

"The claims never held up, and this outcome makes clear that we will not back away from defending ourselves against baseless lawsuits."

Meta added that the evidence showed the plaintiff averaged just minutes a day on Facebook and Instagram and he created most accounts only after hiring a lawyer to bring this lawsuit.

YouTube reached a confidential settlement with R.K.C. in June, with TikTok and Snap following with their own settlements on July 1 and July 20 respectively.

Meta is facing a legal onslaught over accusations that its products are addictive and cause harm to young people.

Another case in New Mexico found Meta liable for misleading consumers about the safety risks its platforms pose to children. The jury ordered Meta to pay $375 million in damages.

In May, Meta, Snap, TikTok and YouTube reached confidential settlements with a Kentucky school district, averting another landmark trial in the northern California city of Oakland.

In a separate case, more than 30 US states are suing Meta over similar allegations, with a potential trial set for August in Oakland.

Another trial against Meta opened in Tennessee this week.

World.title: Guilty as charged: Obado co-accused convicted in Sharon Otieno murder
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Former Migori Governor Okoth Obado at Milimani High Court for his judgment over the alleged murder of his former lover Sharon Otieno. [Nancy Gitonga, Standard]

Former Migori Governor Zachariah Okoth Obado has been convicted of the 2018 murder of Rongo University student Sharon Otieno after the Milimani High Court found that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

In a landmark judgment delivered on Thursday, Justice Cecilia Githua found Obado and his two co-accused, former Personal Assistant Michael Oyamo and former Migori County Clerk Caspal Obiero, guilty of Sharon's murder.

The judge held that Sharon's death was unlawful and that the prosecution had established all the legal ingredients required to prove the offence of murder.

Justice Githua found that Sharon, who was seven months pregnant at the time of her death, died from multiple stab wounds and manual strangulation.

"I do not have any hesitation in finding that Sharon's death was unlawful. It was not caused by natural causes and it was not an accident," the judge ruled.

The court found that although none of the 42 prosecution witnesses directly witnessed the killing, the chain of circumstantial evidence irresistibly pointed to the guilt of the accused persons.

Justice Githua held that Obado had a strong motive to eliminate Sharon to prevent their illicit relationship and her pregnancy from becoming public.

"The first accused had a strong motive to ensure that his illicit relationship was not known by the public, thus making him a beneficiary of the death of the deceased," she ruled.

The judge rejected Obado's defence that his affair with Sharon was already known to his family and members of the public.

"It cannot be entirely true that members of the public knew about his relationship with the deceased," Justice Githua observed.

The court heard that Sharon had informed her mother that Obado was responsible for her pregnancy and that the former governor had offered her Sh30,000 to terminate it.

However, Sharon declined after being advised by her mother to keep the baby.

Evidence further showed that Obado repeatedly pleaded with Sharon to stop posting photographs of places they had visited together and later distanced himself by refusing to take her calls despite initially providing financial support. The late Sharon Otieno. Autopsy results showed she was stabbed eight times, raped and strangled.

Justice Githua said the support was not genuine, noting that Obado later withdrew emotionally after Sharon insisted on keeping the pregnancy.

The prosecution called 42 witnesses and produced 81 exhibits during the lengthy trial.

Among the key witnesses was a protected journalist who testified that Sharon had sought his help to publicise her story in a bid to compel Obado to acknowledge responsibility for her pregnancy.

The court also relied on evidence from the government pathologist, who testified that Sharon suffered seven deep stab wounds, including one that penetrated her uterus and fatally injured her 28-week-old unborn baby.

The post-mortem further established that she was manually strangled.

Justice Githua also considered evidence showing attempts by the second accused, Michael Oyamo, to create a false alibi using forged medical documents after reporting that he had been abducted.

The court concluded that the prosecution had firmly established the chain of circumstantial evidence linking the three accused to Sharon's killing, leading to their conviction.

Sentencing is expected after mitigation.

World.title: Gachagua: Why Ruto will not steal the 2027 General Election
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

DCP leader Righathi Gachagua during a live interview with KTN at his Karen home, Nairobi. [Kanyiri Wahito, Standard]

Democracy for Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has claimed that President William Ruto will not be able to manipulate the outcome of the 2027 General Election, arguing that Kenyans have become more vigilant in protecting their votes.

Speaking during a live interview with KTN from his Karen residence, the former Deputy President said the recent Ol Kalou by-election had provided opposition supporters with a blueprint on safeguarding the electoral process.

"Voting is not enough; you vote and protect the vote. We now have a template from the Ol Kalou by-election," Gachagua said.

He urged Kenyans to remain vigilant during the next General Election, saying the alleged intimidation witnessed in Ol Kalou had failed to influence voters.

"They tried intimidating the people of Ol Kalou, but they did not succeed. We are celebrating what happened, and people from across the country are calling to benchmark on how it worked," he said.

Gachagua also questioned the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC)'s ability to conduct a free and fair election, accusing the electoral body of failing to condemn alleged voter suppression and bribery during the Ol Kalou by-election.

"IEBC has not even condemned the wrongs that happened during the by-election in Ol Kalou. We lost two people who were actually protecting our votes," he alleged.

The DCP leader further renewed his criticism of President Ruto, accusing him of betraying voters from the Mt Kenya region despite earlier warnings.

According to Gachagua, the outcome of the Ol Kalou by-election should serve as a warning to the Kenya Kwanza administration ahead of the 2027 General Election.

He maintained that the by-election demonstrated that Kenyans could no longer be intimidated by the State and described the result as a preview of what to expect in the next national polls.

Gachagua also revisited the Mbeere North by-election, alleging that DCP lost because of widespread voter bribery, intimidation of elderly voters and failure by the party to adequately protect its votes.

"We lost the Mbeere North by-election because we didn't protect our votes properly. There was also massive voter bribery, and those who participated were allegedly given the balance of their bribe after showing a photo of whom they had voted for," he claimed.

The former Deputy President further argued that DCP would have secured an even larger victory in Ol Kalou were it not for what he described as voter suppression and police intimidation.



More to follow...

World.title: Charles Owino appointed as Government Spokesperson
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The former Police Spokesperson has been appointed the new Government Spokesperson, taking over from Mwaura.

President William Ruto has promoted Government Spokesperson Isaac Mwaura in a fresh round of changes within the Executive, while also making nominations to key constitutional commissions and statutory bodies.

In an Executive Order issued on Tuesday, Chief of Staff and Head of Public Service Felix Koskei said the Public Service Commission had approved promotions and redeployments affecting senior government officials.

Under the changes, Mwaura was promoted and redesignated as the Head of the Office of Diversity, Inclusion and Disability Rights in the Executive Office of the President.

Charles Owino Wahong’o was redeployed from the Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy to the Executive Office of the President, where he will serve as Acting Head of Government Communications.

The former Police Spokesperson has been appointed the new Government Spokesperson, taking over from Mwaura.

At the same time, Ruto also nominated new office holders to key constitutional commissions and approved changes within the senior ranks of the Executive in a fresh round of appointments aimed at filling vacancies and strengthening government institutions.

Among the nominees is Dr. Duncan Ojwang Oburu, who has been picked to serve as the Chairperson of the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA).

Ruto also nominated Ms. Antonina Lentoijoni and former Kenya National Union of Teachers (KNUT) Secretary-General Wilson Sossion as members of the Teachers Service Commission (TSC).

Ms. Flora Mutua was nominated as a member of the Public Service Commission (PSC).

In the nominations, Ruto also named seven individuals to serve on the Intergovernmental Relations Technical Committee (IGRTC), subject to ratification by the National and County Government Co-ordinating Summit in accordance with the Intergovernmental Relations Act.

The nominees are Wilson Kuria Thuita (Murang'a), Silvya C. Apaa (Busia), Ahmed Kanyara Bishar (Wajir), Pascalyne Ntang'enoi Kimiriri (Laikipia), Ken Riaga (Migori), Evalyn Chepkirui Aruasa (Nakuru) and Mary Nanjala Kilobi (Nairobi).

World.title: Why public servants have less than a month to update pension records
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Public servants given until August 14 to update pension records [File]

Government has directed all public servants to update their records with the Public Service Superannuation Fund (PSSF) by August 14, 2026, in the latest step towards modernising pension administration.

In a circular signed by Principal Secretary for Public Service and Human Capital Development Dr Jane Imbunya, all PSSF members are expected to update their personal information and beneficiary details through the PSSF Member Self-Service Portal or the PSSF Mobile Application.

The circular was addressed to Ministries, State Departments, Constitutional Commissions, Independent Offices, County Public Service Boards and County Governments.

The exercise is expected to streamline pension administration and accelerate the processing of retirement benefits supported by a new Pension Administration System (PAS), a digital platform developed by PSSF to deliver faster, more transparent and more efficient pension services.

The registration exercise targets 529,635 members drawn from across the public service, including 332,950 teachers under the Teachers Service Commission (TSC), 120,084 officers in the disciplined services, 60,322 employees in Ministries, Departments, Constitutional Commissions and Agencies (MDCAs), and 16,279 county government employees.

PSSF Chief Executive Jonah Aiyabei said updating member records is critical to the success of the pension reforms and the delivery of efficient retirement services.

“By updating their records, public servants will enable quicker processing of retirement benefits, reduce administrative delays, improve data integrity, allow members to access pension services seamlessly through digital channels and ensure that the right benefits reach the right beneficiaries at the right time,” he said.

Under the new system, members can access their pension statements in real time, monitor contributions, view projected retirement benefits, update beneficiary nominations and personal details and initiate and track pension claims remotely.

The platform also features a Sponsor Portal that enables employer institutions to submit payroll information, contribution schedules and member data electronically, significantly improving efficiency and accountability in pension administration.

Dr Aiyabei said the Pension Administration System marks a significant milestone in the government’s efforts to digitise pension administration and restore dignity to retirees through faster, more accessible and transparent services.

“It will provide our members with real-time access to their pension information, enable seamless engagement with the Fund and support a fully digital, paperless pension administration process. Ultimately, our goal is to restore dignity in old age by ensuring every public servant receives timely and efficient pension services,” he said.

World.title: Inside Kenya's Ebola defences as seven Americans enter quarantine
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

A doctor provides care to a patient with Ebola virus disease at the Rwampara Ebola Treatment Centre (ETC) in Bunia, Ituri, July 13, 2026. [AFP]

Seven American humanitarian workers are spending 21 days under medical observation in Kenya not because they are ill, but because they could become ill.

A Reuters report published today confirms they are seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team (DART) staff from the Christian humanitarian organisation Samaritan's Purse . Franklin Graham, the organisation's President and CEO, confirmed this, saying:

“Samaritan's Purse has seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team staff members there. None of them have any symptoms, but they are being quarantined by the Kenyan government for 21 days."

The aid workers, all returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where they were involved in responding to the world's largest recorded outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, have no symptoms and have not tested positive for the virus.

Yet under new US public health rules, they cannot travel home immediately. Instead, they are completing a precautionary quarantine on Kenyan soil.

Their arrival has reignited debate over Kenya's role in regional outbreak preparedness and raised a question that extends far beyond the fate of the seven Americans:

If Ebola crossed Kenya's borders tomorrow, is the country ready?

The answer, infectious disease experts say, lies not in panic but in years of quiet preparation that most Kenyans have never seen.

That preparedness became evident during a recent visit by The Standard to Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH), where access to one of the hospital's high-security isolation areas was restricted.

Hospital officials informed the reporting team that patients with Mpox were being managed in the unit and, for safety reasons, journalists were not allowed to enter or film inside.

The brief encounter offered a glimpse into the strict infection prevention measures that underpin Kenya's readiness for dangerous infectious diseases.

According to an infectious disease physician at the Kenyatta National Hospital and head of the isolation ward, preparedness is far more than having an isolation room.

"One thing we should never do as Kenyans is panic," he says. "Panic only makes the situation worse. Instead, we should ask ourselves one question: Are we prepared?"

His answer is unequivocal. "As a government and as health institutions, we are in preparedness mode."

Dr Nyukuri explains that preparedness begins long before the first patient arrives at a hospital.

It means evaluating whether enough trained personnel are available, whether laboratories have the necessary testing reagents, whether protective equipment is adequate, and whether health workers understand every step required to safely manage a suspected Ebola patient.

"Here at Kenyatta National Hospital, we have conducted extensive training for healthcare workers," he says. "We have carried out readiness assessments, simulated patient scenarios and practised every stage of care from the moment a suspected patient arrives, through admission, isolation and treatment."

The simulations, he explains, are designed to ensure that no decision is being made for the first time during a real emergency. "When we eventually encounter a suspected case, it should not be something new to us." Dr Duncan Nyukuri, an Infectious Diseases specialist, during an interview with The Standard on July 16, 2026 at Kenyatta National Hospital. [Benard Orwongo, Standard]

Preparedness also extends beyond hospitals. Health surveillance teams remain stationed at airports and land border crossings, screening travellers arriving from affected regions while rapid response teams stand ready to investigate suspected infections.

"So far, Kenya has done a good job," Dr Nyukuri says. "We have not recorded a confirmed case despite the increasing numbers in the DRC. We pray that remains the case. But if we receive one patient, we are prepared."

How Ebola jumps from animals to people

Although Ebola is often associated with outbreaks, the virus begins its journey quietly in nature.

Dr Nyukuri explains that fruit bats are believed to be the natural reservoir of the virus. "They carry the virus without becoming sick themselves," he says.

Problems arise when increasing human activity brings people into closer contact with wildlife.

Mining, logging, hunting, charcoal burning, expanding settlements and encroachment into forests all increase the likelihood of viruses crossing from animals into humans.

"We call these zoonotic diseases," Dr Nyukuri explains. "Once the virus infects a human being, it can then spread from person to person through contact with infected body fluids, leading to outbreaks within families and communities."

You see, Ebola is a family; many people speak about Ebola as though it were a single virus.

In reality, scientists recognise five different species.

The best known is the Zaire strain, responsible for the devastating West African epidemic between 2014 and 2016.

"It is highly infectious and highly deadly," says Dr Nyukuri. "But because we have studied it extensively, we now have licensed vaccines and effective treatment options."

The Sudan strain, which has repeatedly caused outbreaks in Uganda, is the second most significant.

The current emergency, however, involves the Bundibugyo strain, first identified in Uganda's Bundibugyo District.

"This is the third recorded outbreak caused by Bundibugyo," Dr Nyukuri explains. "We have not studied it nearly as much as the Zaire strain."

There is currently no licensed vaccine specifically targeting Bundibugyo Ebola.

Instead, researchers are evaluating experimental vaccines while clinical trials in eastern DRC are testing promising treatments, including the monoclonal antibody MBP134 and the antiviral drug remdesivir.

"That is why this outbreak concerns many of us," he says. "We still have limited tools compared to what exists for the Zaire strain."

While Kenya has not recorded a confirmed case linked to the current outbreak, neighbouring countries remain on high alert.

Uganda on Thursday declared its last Ebola patient and has begun the mandatory 42-day countdown required before the country can officially be declared Ebola-free.

In contrast, eastern DRC continues battling sustained transmission, placing enormous pressure on treatment centres and frontline health workers.

It is against that backdrop that Kenya has found itself playing an increasingly important role in regional preparedness.

Their presence has nevertheless fuelled public debate over Kenya's preparedness infrastructure and the country's place in global health security.

Earlier this week, two American humanitarian workers who contracted Ebola while working in eastern DRC were medically evacuated to Germany for specialised treatment after receiving initial care in Bunia. Their evacuation underscores an important distinction: Kenya is currently serving as a precautionary observation site for exposed but healthy personnel, while confirmed Ebola patients requiring advanced clinical care have been transferred to Germany.

For Dr Nyukuri, the conversation should remain grounded in science rather than fear.

Preparedness, he says, is not measured only by isolation wards or specialised equipment, but by the ability of an entire health system to detect threats early, respond quickly and protect both patients and healthcare workers.

"My prayer is that Kenya never records a case," he says. "But preparedness means planning for the day you hope never comes."

As seven healthy humanitarian workers quietly complete their quarantine in Kenya, that preparation is no longer an abstract exercise.

It is being tested in real time. The development has also drawn attention to the contrasting roles played by East African countries during the current outbreak.

Uganda, widely regarded as one of Africa's most experienced countries in responding to Ebola, recently brought its own outbreak under control and has now entered the 42-day countdown required to be declared Ebola-free. Over the years, the country has built a reputation for rapidly detecting cases, tracing contacts and isolating patients, earning praise from the World Health Organization for repeatedly containing outbreaks before they spread widely.

Yet despite that experience, Uganda did not become a destination for foreign humanitarian workers requiring precautionary quarantine or post-exposure observation.

Instead, that role has fallen to Kenya, where seven American aid workers are now completing a mandatory 21-day quarantine after working in Ebola-affected areas of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

The contrast raises broader questions about how countries are selected to support international outbreak responses. While Uganda has demonstrated its capacity to treat Ebola patients within its own borders, Kenya's involvement appears to reflect a different function—serving as a precautionary observation site for exposed personnel rather than a treatment centre for confirmed cases.

Health experts caution against interpreting the distinction as a measure of either country's clinical capability. Instead, they say such decisions are often influenced by a combination of bilateral agreements, operational logistics, evacuation arrangements and the specific objectives of international public health partners.

World.title: MPs push for urgent resolution of higher education funding crisis
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

HELB Chief Executive Officer Geoffrey Monari before the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Education on July 16, 2026. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

The National Assembly Departmental Committee on Education has called for urgent and coordinated action to address persistent funding challenges affecting Kenya's higher education sector.

The MPs proposed a joint engagement involving Parliament, the National Treasury and the Ministry of Education to streamline implementation of the Higher Education Funding Model.

The committee, chaired by Vice Chairperson Eve Obara, made the recommendation after holding separate meetings with officials from the State Department for Higher Education, the Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) and the Universities Fund during a review of the 2025/2026 Budget Implementation Status.

Appearing before the committee, Higher Education Principal Secretary Dr. Beatrice Inyangala said the Higher Education Funding Model is operational but continues to face implementation challenges due to inadequate alignment between the funding framework and budget allocations.

"The funding model is functional. However, the main challenge lies in budget alignment," Dr. Inyangala told Members.

The funding model was introduced to allocate financial support to university students based on their level of need, while ensuring sustainable financing for public universities.

However, implementation has generated debate over affordability, funding adequacy and delays in disbursement of resources to institutions.

MPs observed that the mismatch between policy and budgetary allocations has undermined effective financing of universities and agreed that a joint meeting involving the National Treasury, the Ministry of Education and Parliament would help harmonise the funding framework.

The committee also sought explanations over the growing stock of pending bills owed by public universities.

Dr. Inyangala informed Members that most of the outstanding obligations were inherited over several years, with universities continuing efforts to clear the debts despite increasing interest charges.

According to the State Department for Higher Education, public universities had accumulated pending bills amounting to Sh100.3 billion as of January 2026.

The ministry said institutions are prioritising settlement of pending obligations, suspending stalled development projects and exploring alternative revenue streams to prevent further accumulation of debt.

During a separate session, Members questioned HELB officials on how the board allocates student loans when available funding cannot meet demand from all eligible applicants.

Led by Chief Executive Officer Geoffrey Monari, HELB officials were asked to explain the criteria used in determining beneficiaries during periods of constrained resources.

Legislators emphasised that the allocation process should be fair, transparent and predictable to protect deserving students from being unfairly excluded.

World.title: High court suspends President Ruto's executive order placing IPOA under Interior Ministry
World.content:
The High Court has temporarily suspended the implementation of president William Ruto's Executive Order No. 2 of 2023 that placed the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA) under the Ministry of Interior and National Administration, pending the hearing and determination of a constitutional petition challenging the directive.



Justice David Mburu of the High Court in Milimani law court issued the conservatory orders in a case filed by Jonathan Obwogi under Maalim and associates advocates against the Attorney General, the Cabinet Secretary for Interior and National Administration, and the Independent Policing Oversight Authority.



The court ruled that the contested section of the Executive Order would remain suspended until the constitutional petition is fully heard and determined.



The decision does not amount to a final declaration on the legality of the Executive Order. Instead, the court restored the legal position that existed before the order was issued to safeguard the constitutional issues raised in the petition from further prejudice.



Under Section 4 of the IPOA Act, the authority is required to operate independently and is not subject to the direction or control of any person, office or institution in the performance of its functions. The law further requires all government agencies to assist and protect IPOA's independence, prohibits interference with its decision making and operations, and obligates Parliament to ensure it receives adequate funding.



The conservatory orders mean that the Ministry of Interior cannot, for now, supervise, administer, direct or exercise authority over IPOA based on Executive Order No. 2 of 2023.



The court's decision, however, does not affect IPOA's day-to-day operations. The authority will continue carrying out its statutory mandate, including investigating complaints against police officers, probing deaths and serious injuries arising from police action, and undertaking all responsibilities assigned to it under the IPOA Act.



In the petition, the applicant also sought to compel IPOA's Chairperson, or another authorised officer, to disclose through an affidavit whether the authority had implemented the Executive Order, the extent to which it had operated under the Ministry of Interior, and any operational changes that may have resulted. The petitioner argued that such information would help establish whether the authority's statutory independence had been compromised.



The High Court observed that the question of whether Executive Order No. 2 of 2023 is constitutional will only be determined after hearing submissions from all parties.



The matter is scheduled for a mention on September 21, 2026, when the court is expected to issue further directions.

World.title: “Not a single drop of oil”: Iran issues stark warning to US over infrastructure threats
World.content:
The Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters stated in a press release on Wednesday, that US President Donald Trump has resumed threatening Iran with strikes on its infrastructure.

“The Strait of Hormuz remains closed, and if any vessel is permitted passage, it will proceed solely along the designated route and under the previously announced protocols,” the headquarters’ leadership said in the statement.

The statement added that if the United States carries out its threats, the Iranian Armed Forces will not allow “even a single drop of oil to be exported,” warning that oil, gas, electricity, and economic infrastructure throughout the region will become targets for attacks.

It further stressed that repeated threats from the US and its military will only broaden the scope of the war across the region, and potentially beyond.

Trump had previously declared that “if Iran fires a missile, shell, drone, or any other weapon at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz at any time, the United States will bomb and destroy a bridge or power station—including those located in or near the capital, Tehran.

World.title: Reviving a legend: Farrah El Dibany to star in new musical bringing Dalida’s life story to the stage
World.content:
A new Egyptian-French musical play commemorating the 40th anniversary of the legendary singer Dalida’s passing, was officially announced during a press conference at the residence of the French Ambassador in Cairo. The launch featured French Ambassador Éric Chevallier, Egyptian mezzo-soprano Farrah El Dibany, film director Khairy Beshara, and writer Waleed Khairy.

The project is an Egyptian-French collaboration staged as part of the “Mediterranean Season 2026,” an initiative aimed at fostering cultural and artistic exchange among regional nations while highlighting the shared creativity and cultural diversity of Mediterranean peoples.

Scheduled to serve as the grand finale of the season, the production will premiere at the Bibliotheca Alexandrina on October 31, followed by performances in Cairo in November.

During the press conference, French Ambassador Éric Chevallier underscored the vital significance of Egyptian-French cultural cooperation, noting that the production represents a major step in reviving Dalida’s legacy through a joint musical theater venture.

For her part, Farrah El Dibany shared that portraying Dalida had been a childhood dream. She explained that she pitched the concept to director Khairy Beshara, who collaborated with writer Waleed Khairy to develop the idea into a full-fledged theatrical project.

Beshara stated that the work aims to present different facets of Dalida’s personality beyond her familiar stage persona, while writer Waleed Khairy explained that his script focuses on humanizing the artist by highlighting lesser-known aspects of her life. The production is produced by Ahmed Fawzi.

The play chronicles Dalida’s artistic and personal journey, emphasizing her deep connection to Egypt and the profound impact of her Egyptian upbringing on her artistic identity. It also features a fresh musical vision arranged by French-Armenian composer André Manoukian.

The show falls under the umbrella of the “Mediterranean Season 2026,” an initiative launched in 2023 by French President Emmanuel Macron and organized with the support of the French Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Culture.

Running from May 15 to October 31, 2026, across France and several Mediterranean nations—including Egypt, Lebanon, Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco—the initiative seeks to strengthen cultural ties and support creative endeavors throughout the region.

World.title: Flight cancellations and airspace closures expected as US raises worldwide security alert
World.content:
The US Department of State has issued a security alert advising American citizens worldwide to exercise heightened caution amid escalating tensions in the Middle East and a increasingly complex security environment, warning of potential unexpected developments and further escalation.

The Department emphasized that US citizens currently in the Middle East should maintain a high state of vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, temporary airspace closures, and travel disruptions. It noted that several airlines have postponed the resumption of previously scheduled flights, while others have canceled specific routes altogether.

Additionally, the State Department urged citizens outside the Middle East to reconsider traveling to or transiting through the region, advising travelers to continuously monitor the operational status of airports and airlines.

The advisory pointed out that US diplomatic facilities—including some located outside the Middle East—have been targeted, warning that Iran and its aligned proxy groups may target additional U.S. interests abroad or sites affiliated with the United States and American citizens globally, including commercial enterprises and other institutions.

World.title: When will the Barcelona vs. Al Ahly Joan Gamper Trophy match take place?
World.content:
The management of Spanish giants FC Barcelona has decided to face Egypt’s Al Ahly SC in a historic friendly match as part of the upcoming edition of the annual Joan Gamper Trophy.

According to a report published by the Spanish newspaper Mundo Deportivo, Al Ahly will be Barcelona’s opponent in the exhibition match. The report highlighted that Barcelona will take on a team boasting a massive fanbase across Egypt, Africa, and the Arab world. Additionally, Moroccan journalist Ashraf Ben Ayad, who is close to the Catalan club, confirmed that the Egyptian powerhouse will serve as Barcelona’s opponent in the upcoming edition of the tournament, which is held annually as a warm-up for the new season.

The highly anticipated fixture between Al Ahly and the Catalan club is scheduled for August 19, marking Barcelona’s season opener at the Camp Nou.

The match aligns with Barcelona’s strategy to strengthen ties with prominent Arab clubs while capitalizing on the Red Giants’ massive popularity and commercial pull throughout the Middle East.

World.title: Peak heatwave hits Egypt: EMA warns of worst 24 hours with soaring heat and humidity
World.content:
Egypt’s Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA) has issued a weather update for Cairo and the governorates, warning that a severe heatwave across most parts of the country is reaching its peak.

Extremely hot and humid conditions are expected during the day in most regions, with hot and humid weather along the northern coast. Moderately warm and humid conditions will prevail overnight and into the early morning.

In its statement, the authority detailed that expected high temperatures will hit 40°C in Greater Cairo, reaching 43°C in Upper Egypt, 41°C in Northern Upper Egypt, 39°C in the Nile Delta, 35°C along the northwestern coast, and 33°C along the northeastern coast.

The EMA added that elevated humidity levels will intensify the feel-like temperature, driving the heat index up to 42°C in Greater Cairo, 44°C in Southern Upper Egypt, and 43°C in Northern Upper Egypt, marking what is expected to be the most intense 24-hour stretch of this heatwave.

Weather maps indicate the formation of morning fog between 4:00 AM and 8:00 AM across parts of northern Egypt extending to Greater Cairo, the Canal Cities, Central Sinai, and Northern Upper Egypt, which may be dense at times on select roadways.

The report also noted intermittent wind activity across most areas, offering slight evening relief in open spaces. However, active winds along parts of the Mediterranean coastline—including El Saloum, Matrouh, El Alamein, Alexandria, and Baltim—are expected to produce wave heights ranging between 1.5 and 2.25 meters.

Furthermore, the authority pointed to a minor chance of low-lying cloud formation over scattered areas of the northern coast, the Nile Delta, Greater Cairo, and the Canal Cities, which could lead to light, non-disruptive drizzle in isolated spots.

The EMA urged the public to avoid direct sunlight during peak hours and stay well-hydrated by drinking plenty of water and fluids, with a special emphasis on the elderly, children, individuals with chronic illness, and outdoor workers.

World.title: Prolonged blackouts and soaring heat leave several Egyptian governorates in darkness
World.content:
Several villages and towns across the governorates of Qalyubia, the Red Sea, Port Said, Sharqia, and Minya are experiencing a major crisis due to prolonged power outages lasting for hours at irregular intervals.

The blackouts, which occurred without prior warning to residents, have sparked widespread anger and resentment—particularly amid soaring temperatures, rising humidity, and the intense summer heat of July. Meanwhile, officials from electricity supply companies attributed the power instability during this period to extreme temperatures and increased strain on the grid.

Residents called for the immediate intervention of governors and members of parliament to swiftly contain the crisis and transparently announce its causes and mitigation plans. They emphasized that frequent electricity and water cuts have caused them significant financial losses, damaging numerous household appliances and repeatedly disrupting water pumping stations.

The recurring power cuts continued to impact a large number of neighborhoods, towns, and villages across the governorates.

Residents stated that the issue is no longer limited to “emergency breakdowns,” but has become an almost daily occurrence without official statements clarifying the reasons for the outages or estimated times for service restoration. This has heightened anxiety and disruption among families—especially those caring for the elderly, children, or patients who rely on stable living conditions and powered medical equipment.

They added that prolonged blackouts during peak hours turn their homes into unbearable heat traps, particularly given the high humidity.

The impact has also extended to the commercial sector; owners of grocery stores, supermarkets, restaurants, and cafes confirmed that repeated outages cause direct financial losses due to failing refrigerators and coolers, the risk of spoiled food items, and the disruption of electronic payment systems and internet service.

World.title: Egypt supports any pathway leading to a complete Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon
World.content:
Egyptian Ambassador to Lebanon Alaa Moussa reaffirmed Cairo’s steadfast support for any path leading to a complete Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory, emphasizing Egypt’s active efforts to end Israeli attacks and enable the Lebanese state to assert full control over its lands.

Moussa made the statements on Wednesday following a meeting with Lebanese Speaker of Parliament Nabih Berri at Ain El-Tineh. He noted that discussions focused on stopping Israeli assaults, empowering state authority, and assessing regional developments impacting Lebanon.

The ambassador stated that he briefed Berri on “the latest developments and Cairo’s ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions and facilitate a return to the negotiating table regarding the situation between the United States and Iran.”

He added that Speaker Berri reiterated several critical priorities, namely “an immediate and complete halt to Israeli attacks on Lebanon, full withdrawal from all Lebanese territories, the return of displaced persons, and the launch of reconstruction efforts.”

“Egypt’s position remains firm and unambiguous: we support any pathway that ultimately leads to a full Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon, the return of our displaced brothers and sisters to their towns and villages, and the commencement of rebuilding under a clear timetable,” Moussa said, underscoring Cairo’s full backing for initiatives aimed at achieving these goals.

Highlighting recent progress, the ambassador pointed out that operations began in designated “pilot zones” the previous day. He expressed hope that this step would expand to other areas to pave the way for a complete Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese soil, stressing that success hinges on the commitment of all parties and providing the necessary support and resources to the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF).

Moussa further emphasized the importance of empowering the Lebanese army to fulfill its mandate, stating that Egypt supports hosting an international conference to back the LAF. He noted that Cairo had hosted a preparatory conference for this purpose earlier this year and expressed optimism that remaining obstacles to holding the main conference would be resolved.

He concluded by noting that he updated the Lebanese Parliament Speaker on Cairo’s latest diplomatic moves to defuse regional tensions, including efforts aimed at reviving negotiations between Washington and Tehran.

World.title: Huthi blockade threat raises risk of dual energy chokepoint crisis, Kpler says
World.content:
A threat by the Iranian backed Houthis to blockade Saudi-linked shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has raised the prospect of the Middle East’s two key energy chokepoints coming under pressure at the same time, shipping analytics firm Kpler warned Tuesday.

A “simultaneous and prolonged disruption of Bab el-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz could affect maritime routes carrying approximately one-quarter of global oil supply,” the firm said in a written analysis.

The firm said Bab el-Mandeb – which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean – remains open, but traffic is already running far below pre-crisis levels while conditions in Hormuz have “deteriorated sharply.”

According to Kpler, crossings through Bab el-Mandeb averaged about 41 vessels a day between July 15 and July 20, “43% below the 2023 peak of 72/day.”

Saudi crude loadings through the strait fell 34% in two weeks, dropping from 29.58 million barrels in the week of June 29 to 19.50 million barrels in the week of July 13, the analysis said.

Kpler said the Houthi threat is especially significant because Saudi Arabia has increasingly used the Red Sea route as a fallback for exports after disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.

Kpler examined several possible scenarios, ranging from limited self-diversion by cautious operators to a full blockade. Under “selective targeting,” it said, “compliant commercial traffic could fall 40–50% within weeks, pushing crossings toward 20–25/day.” Under a full blockade, Bab el-Mandeb “could follow Hormuz and fall below 15 vessels/day within days,” the analysis said.

In a separate note published Tuesday, Kpler said two tankers carrying Saudi crude reversed course in the Red Sea after the Houthi declaration.

World.title: First Quantum rejects Global Witness claims of covert UPND funding
World.content:
Global Witness report accusing FQM of covertly funding UPND meets scepticism as company denies claims

A report published by London-based investigative organisation Global Witness alleging that First Quantum Minerals ran a long-running covert influence campaign in Zambia, including offering as much as US$50 million toward President Hakainde Hichilema‘s political party, has drawn sharp pushback from Zambian commentators and a categorical denial from the mining company itself, even as legal experts argue the claims deserve independent scrutiny.

The 36-page report, titled “How a Canadian mining giant infiltrated Zambia’s democracy,” alleges that First Quantum Minerals and associated individuals provided financial support to the United Party for National Development across several election cycles, making it, in the organisation’s telling, the party’s most prominent funder ahead of the 2026 general election. Global Witness says it interviewed government insiders, businesspeople close to the President, current and former FQM employees, political actors, diplomats and civil society representatives, and supported its findings with public records and documents.

The organisation states explicitly, however, that it has no evidence FQM engaged in corruption and does not allege that any of the described conduct was illegal. Editorial columns published in both News Diggers and Times of Zambia seized on that admission, arguing the report’s central claims rest largely on unnamed insiders and one named individual, former diplomat Emmanuel Mwamba, without producing bank transfers, receipts or other verifiable transaction records to substantiate its most serious allegation, that FQM promised a US$50 million cash donation.

“The report is shouting ‘evidence’ in the headline but whispers ‘sources said’ in the body,” one of the columns argued, questioning why Global Witness, an organisation funded partly by Norway, a major oil and gas producing state, chose to publish the findings mere weeks before Zambians go to the polls. The commentary also noted that the report acknowledges fiscal reforms coincided with major new investment, increased copper production, and roughly US$902 million paid to government in 2025, figures the columns argue undercut the narrative of a captured state.

First Quantum Minerals categorically rejects the report’s claims. The company says it has never paid or authorised bribes, never engaged in illicit party funding, never funded UPND and never promised to finance its 2026 campaign, describing the allegations as based on unsubstantiated speculation from anonymous individuals rather than verifiable facts.

Not every Zambian commentator dismissed the report outright. In a “Legally Speaking” column, constitutional law academic Prof Cephas Lumina wrote that the allegations, while unproven, are “too serious to dismiss” and require independent investigation in both Zambia and Canada, where FQM is incorporated. He argued that Canadian authorities, including the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and relevant securities regulators, should examine whether any funds, benefits or disclosures connected to the alleged conduct breached Canadian law, adding that Canada’s foreign bribery legislation can apply to qualifying conduct by Canadian companies abroad even though the allegations themselves do not prove an offence occurred.

Lumina used the controversy to highlight what he described as a deeper structural problem: nearly five years into its term, the UPND government has still not enacted the campaign finance regime required under Article 60(4) of the Constitution, which mandates legislation establishing a Political Parties’ Fund, party accounts, funding disclosure and spending limits. He called for reviving and strengthening the Draft Political Parties Bill of 2017, which had proposed a Political Parties Board and Registrar along with mandatory annual reporting and audited accounts, arguing that without such a framework “the country cannot readily determine who financed a governing party, how much was contributed and through which intermediaries.”

The report also touches on Zambia’s mining tax regime, estimating that changes to the mineral royalty structure and deductibility rules saved FQM subsidiaries approximately US$771 million between 2022 and 2025, and saved mining companies collectively more than US$1 billion over a similar period. Lumina argued this raises separate but related questions about fair taxation, suggesting government should publish the value of major mining incentives, their intended benefits and whether commitments attached to them were met, and consider a windfall tax given the recent rise in copper prices.

UPND spokespersons have previously stated that President Hichilema’s campaign is financed locally. Lumina argued that if this remains the party’s position, it should publish a donor register and independently audited campaign accounts to allow citizens to evaluate the allegations against verifiable evidence rather than competing claims.

Neither the Zambian government nor First Quantum Minerals had issued a formal joint response addressing all elements of the report by the time of publication, though FQM’s rejection of the core funding allegation has been widely reported. Civil society organisations in both Zambia and Canada are calling for mandatory disclosure of political donations, parliamentary scrutiny of mining agreements, and tighter rules governing movement between government and mining company personnel.

The controversy arrives at a politically sensitive moment, with the allegations surfacing weeks before an election in which UPND is seeking a second term and mining policy, including tax treatment of major operators such as FQM, has featured prominently in campaign debate.
