For Colombian men, turning 18 comes with an obligation few in wealthier countries still face: military service.

In 2026, that duty reaches the generation born in 2008 — the newest class called to define their place in a system Colombia is still debating.

How Colombia Military Service Works

Colombia requires military service of its young men. Those aged 18 to 24 must “define their military situation,” and the class of 2008 reaches that age this year.

For most, service lasts 12 months; for those who did not finish high school, it can run up to 18. In return, conscripts get a monthly payment close to the minimum wage, plus board, kit and health care.

The framework is Law 1861 of 2017, which overhauled an older, often abused system, tightened the rules and set clearer compensation.

Failing to sort out one’s military status can block a young man from a diploma, a formal job or leaving the country, making the requirement hard to ignore.

In practice, many young men resolve their status by obtaining a “military card,” a document long required for jobs and study.

Who Is Exempt

Not everyone serves. The law exempts men who are married or have children, and those who are the main financial support for parents or siblings.

Members of indigenous communities living in their own territories are exempt, as are clergy of recognised religious institutions.

The old system was notorious for letting the well-off buy or dodge their way out. Reforms have curbed that, but the burden still falls hardest on poorer young men with fewer ways to defer.

Conscientious objection is recognised in principle, though rights groups say the process to claim it can be slow and inconsistent.

The Peace Alternative

The bigger change is the option not to bear arms. Under the outgoing government of Gustavo Petro, Colombia created a “Social Service for Peace.”

Formalised by decree in 2024, it lets young people spend 12 months on civilian work — environmental, social or community projects — instead of the barracks, with similar benefits.

It reflects Petro’s belief that a country trying to end its conflicts should not force its youth into uniform. How fully the option is funded will decide whether it is a real choice or a paper one.

The peace-service idea grew out of Petro’s wider “total peace” agenda, an attempt to reduce the state’s reliance on force.

A Draft in a Divided Moment

The timing is charged. The class of 2008 comes of age just as Colombia prepares to swap Petro for president-elect Abelardo De la Espriella, a hardliner who has vowed to crush armed groups.

Where Petro softened conscription with a peace alternative, De la Espriella’s security-first agenda points toward a bigger, more active military.

Colombia’s armed forces have leaned on conscripts for decades of counter-insurgency, so any shift in the draft touches the heart of its security. What service looks like for this generation may depend on which vision prevails.

For the incoming government, a well-staffed military is central to its promise to retake territory from armed groups.

Why It Matters

For Colombian families, the draft is a personal reality: a year that can mean discipline and a wage, or, for some, danger in a country still at war in parts of its territory.

Even as violence has ebbed in the cities, it persists in rural zones like Cauca and Catatumbo, where young soldiers are often deployed.

Conscription has long been criticised for falling on the poor while the well-off avoid it; reforms have eased but not erased that gap. For the class of 2008, adulthood begins at a hinge moment in Colombia’s long struggle between the gun and the negotiating table.

How the class of 2008 is treated — drafted, offered peace work, or something in between — will be an early sign of the direction Colombia’s new government takes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who has to do military service in Colombia?

Military service is compulsory for Colombian men aged 18 to 24. The generation born in 2008 reaches 18 in 2026 and must now define their military situation under Law 1861 of 2017.

How long does Colombian military service last, and is it paid?

It lasts 12 months for high-school graduates and up to 18 months for those without a diploma. Conscripts receive a monthly stipend close to the minimum wage, plus food, housing, uniforms and medical care.

Is there an alternative to carrying a weapon?

Yes. Since 2024, Colombia offers a “Social Service for Peace,” a 12-month civilian alternative to compulsory military service with similar benefits, created under President Gustavo Petro.

World.title: Colombia’s President-Elect De la Espriella’s 30-Day Ultimatum
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Politics

Key Facts —The man. Abelardo De la Espriella, a combative right-wing lawyer, is Colombia’s president-elect, due to take office in 2026. —The ultimatum. He has told illegal armed groups they will have roughly one month to surrender to justice once he takes power. —The setting. He plans to be inaugurated at a military base, the Cantón José Hilario López in Popayán, in the conflict-ridden Cauca region. —The doctrine. His program promises to end peace talks, restore territorial control and wage a “Plan Colombia II,” including destroying 330,000 hectares of coca. —The stakes. Cauca is a stronghold of dissident guerrillas loyal to “Iván Mordisco,” making it a symbol of the security crisis he vows to confront.

Colombia is about to swap a president who sought “total peace” for one who promises the opposite. De la Espriella, the hardline lawyer elected to lead the country, is signalling that his first target is the armed groups of Cauca.

A Colombian Army helicopter. President-elect Abelardo De la Espriella has promised a security-first agenda centred on Cauca. (Photo: National Police of Colombia / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0)

For four years, Colombia’s government chased peace with the armed groups that haunt its countryside. The man about to replace it has a very different plan.

Abelardo De la Espriella, the country’s new president-elect, is promising force where his predecessor promised dialogue — starting in the embattled region of Cauca.

Who Is De la Espriella

De la Espriella is a flamboyant, hard-charging lawyer who built a career representing high-profile clients and cultivating a combative public image.

He won Colombia’s 2026 presidential election on a law-and-order platform, casting himself as the antithesis of the outgoing left-wing government of Gustavo Petro.

His rise reflects a wider swing to the right in parts of Latin America, and a public exhausted by insecurity and stalled peace efforts.

He campaigned as an outsider willing to say what mainstream politicians would not, a style that resonated in a country weary of insecurity.

What De la Espriella Is Proposing

His security program is unusually blunt. He has said armed groups will have about a month, once he is in office, to lay down their weapons and submit to justice.

He vows to end peace dialogues with those groups, restore state control over lost territory, and reassert the government’s monopoly on force.

The centrepiece is what he calls a “Plan Colombia II,” echoing the US-backed anti-drug campaign of the 2000s, with a target of eradicating 330,000 hectares of coca.

That would be a vast undertaking. Colombia remains the world’s largest cocaine producer, and past eradication drives have often seen crops simply move rather than disappear.

The one-month deadline is as much political theatre as policy, meant to signal resolve to the voters who backed him for exactly this.

Colombia’s armed landscape is fragmented — guerrilla dissidents, the ELN and criminal bands all vie for coca routes — so any single deadline collides with a tangled reality.

Why Cauca, and Why the Army Base

The choice of venue is a message. De la Espriella plans to be sworn in not in Bogotá but at the Cantón José Hilario López, a military base in Popayán, the capital of Cauca.

Cauca is one of Colombia’s most violent regions, where dissidents of the guerrilla commander known as “Iván Mordisco” hold sway over rural territory and coca economies.

Taking the oath there frames his presidency around confronting that threat from day one. For families in Cauca, caught between armed groups and the state, the promises land amid a daily insecurity no ceremony can quickly fix.

Cauca has seen assassinations of social leaders and clashes that displace whole communities, making it a byword for Colombia’s unfinished war.

The Risks and the Critics

Not everyone believes force is the answer. Critics — including figures on the left such as senator Iván Cepeda — argue that a purely military approach has failed before and can deepen the very violence it targets.

Analysts note that ending peace talks abruptly could push wavering fighters back to war, and that ultimatums are easier to declare than to enforce across Colombia’s rugged terrain.

History offers warnings: the original Plan Colombia weakened the FARC but did not end the drug trade, and heavy-handed operations drew accusations of civilian harm.

The outgoing government’s “total peace” talks had already frayed, and violence in several regions had climbed, giving De la Espriella his opening.

What It Means for Foreigners

For investors and residents, the shift signals a harder, more confrontational security policy after years of negotiation.

A crackdown could improve safety in some areas but also risk renewed fighting, displacement and human-rights scrutiny — the tensions that have long dogged Colombia’s conflict.

Human-rights groups will watch closely how any offensive is conducted, mindful of past abuses in Colombia’s long war, and much will depend on whether force is paired with courts, jobs and services that can hold territory once it is retaken.

The first test will come quickly, since De la Espriella has tied his own credibility to that one-month clock; for businesses, a calmer countryside could open mining, farming and tourism, while a return to open conflict would do the opposite.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Abelardo De la Espriella?

He is a right-wing Colombian lawyer who won the 2026 presidential election on a hardline security platform, positioning himself against the outgoing government of Gustavo Petro.

What is his plan for Colombia’s armed groups?

He has said illegal armed groups will have about a month to surrender once he takes office, and promises to end peace talks, restore territorial control and launch a “Plan Colombia II” against drug trafficking.

Why does Cauca matter?

Cauca is one of Colombia’s most violent regions, a stronghold of dissidents loyal to “Iván Mordisco.” De la Espriella plans to be inaugurated at a military base there to signal his focus on the security crisis.

Sources: National Police of Colombia.

World.title: Brazil Navy Ex-Chief Gets 24 Years for Coup Plot
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Defense

Key Facts —The conviction. In September 2025, Brazil’s Supreme Court sentenced former navy commander Admiral Almir Garnier Santos to 24 years in prison, for what prosecutors called a plot to overturn the 2022 election. —The charges. The court found him guilty of five crimes, among them attempted coup d’état and belonging to an armed criminal organization. —The distinction. He is the only one of the three armed-forces chiefs convicted; the army and air force chiefs refused, a refusal prosecutors credit for the plot never advancing. —The dissent. Justice Luiz Fux voted to acquit him of the coup charges, and his 2026 appeal is built around that dissent. —The contested court. The verdict came from a five-justice panel whose rapporteur, Alexandre de Moraes, was himself named a target of the alleged plot — part of a long dispute over the court’s impartiality and reach.

On 8 January 2023, supporters of the defeated Jair Bolsonaro stormed Brazil’s Congress, presidential palace and Supreme Court in Brasília. More than two years later, the only armed-forces commander convicted over the alleged plot is the former navy chief, Admiral Almir Garnier Santos.

What the Court Found

In September 2025, the Supreme Court’s First Panel convicted Garnier and sentenced him to 24 years. It found him guilty of five crimes, including attempted coup d’état and membership of an armed criminal organization.

Prosecutors placed him, alongside Bolsonaro, in what they called the plot’s “crucial nucleus.” Bolsonaro was convicted in the same cases and sentenced to 27 years.

Much of the case rested on the plea-bargain testimony of Mauro Cid, Bolsonaro’s former aide. Cid told the court that Bolsonaro personally edited a draft decree meant to annul the 2022 result.

Bolsonaro’s defense spent the trial trying to discredit that testimony. Garnier, for his part, denies any wrongdoing.

The Detail the Wires Often Skip: The Forces Did Not Go Along

Brazil has three armed forces, each with its own commander. According to trial testimony, the army and air force chiefs resisted the plan; only Garnier, at the navy, did not.

Prosecutors argued that this refusal is a large part of why the coup never got off the ground. In their own account, the institution held even as one commander broke.

That distinction shapes the story. This was one service chief offering his force, not the armed forces as a whole moving against an elected government.

A Conviction From a Court on Trial Itself

What sets the Brazilian coup cases apart is that the court handing down the verdicts is itself under sustained challenge. Critics — the defense, much of the political right, and voices beyond it — say the prosecutions were shaped by a tribunal that had gathered extraordinary power.

Several threads feed that argument. The case was decided by a five-member panel rather than the full court.

Its rapporteur, Justice Alexandre de Moraes, was himself named among the alleged targets of the plot. Bolsonaro’s lawyers argued that this dual role was incompatible with impartiality.

The defense also alleged mishandling of evidence and questioned the reliability of Cid’s plea deal. And one justice, Luiz Fux, broke with his colleagues to vote for acquittal on the coup charges.

Supporters of the prosecutions reject all of this. They say the evidence was overwhelming, and that holding a former president and a service chief to account is exactly what an independent court is for.

An International Dispute, Not Just a Brazilian One

The controversy has spread well beyond Brasília. In 2025 the United States revoked visas for Justice Moraes and other Brazilian officials and moved to sanction them.

Washington has otherwise reserved such measures for figures like Venezuela‘s judges, an explicit and pointed comparison. It also tied trade tariffs to Bolsonaro’s treatment.

Brasília rejected the pressure as foreign interference. The opposition, in turn, has courted it, at one rally unfurling U.S. flags and signs reading “SOS Trump.”

None of this settles whether the convictions are sound. It does mean the Garnier verdict lands inside a live argument, with one side seeing a democracy defending itself and the other a court expanding its power over political opponents.

The Defense, the Appeals, and What Comes Next

Garnier’s case is not over. In 2026 his lawyers filed a further appeal, a device used to reopen a conviction when a judge has dissented — their opening being Fux’s vote.

Separately, the admiral is contesting the loss of his military rank before the armed forces’ own court. Higher panels of the Supreme Court will decide whether the 24-year term stands.

The case has already sent a signal through the barracks that backing a coup now carries a personal price. For its critics, it sends a competing signal about how much power Brazil’s judges have gathered.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Almir Garnier Santos?

He is a retired admiral who commanded Brazil’s navy under President Jair Bolsonaro. In September 2025 the Supreme Court sentenced him to 24 years in prison for taking part in the alleged plot to overturn the 2022 election.

Why is the navy chief the only commander convicted?

According to testimony presented at trial, of the three armed-forces commanders only Garnier agreed to put his force at the plot’s disposal; the army and air force chiefs refused. He is the only service chief convicted.

Why is the court itself controversial?

Critics, including the defense and the U.S. government, question the impartiality and reach of the Supreme Court and of Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Supporters call the prosecutions legitimate accountability; both readings are part of the story.

Is the case final?

No. Garnier denies wrongdoing and, in 2026, his defense filed a further appeal citing the dissent of Justice Luiz Fux; higher panels of the Supreme Court will decide whether the conviction stands.

World.title: US Court Orders Argentina to Pay $391M for Airline Seizure
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Business

Key Facts —The ruling. A US appeals court in Washington confirmed that Argentina must pay more than US$390.9 million, plus interest, over the 2008 nationalization of Aerolíneas Argentinas. —The claimant. The money is owed to the Titan Consortium, an investment fund that held shares in the flag carrier when it was expropriated. —The origin. The case dates to 2008, when the Kirchner government re-nationalized Aerolíneas and Austral; an ICSID tribunal ordered about US$321 million in 2017. —The twist. The bill lands even as Aerolíneas has turned a profit — US$112.7 million operating income in 2025 — after years of heavy state support. —The response. Milei’s government says it still has legal tools, and continues to aim at eventually privatizing the airline.

A decision made nearly two decades ago has just come due. A US court has confirmed that Argentina must pay more than US$390 million over the 2008 nationalization of Aerolíneas Argentinas — a costly ghost arriving as the airline finally finds its feet.

An Aerolíneas Argentinas jet. A US court has confirmed a US$390.9 million judgment over the airline’s 2008 nationalization. (Photo: BriYYZ / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0)

Argentina’s flag carrier, Aerolíneas Argentinas, has spent years as a symbol of state largesse, soaking up billions in public money. Lately it had started to look like a turnaround story.

Then a US court handed it a bill from the past.

What the Ruling on Aerolíneas Argentinas Says

On 21 July 2026, a US appeals court in Washington upheld a judgment ordering Argentina to pay the Titan Consortium more than US$390.9 million, plus interest.

Titan was an investor in Aerolíneas Argentinas and its sister carrier Austral when the government took them over. The court agreed the state owed compensation for that seizure.

The ruling came from the appeals court for the District of Columbia, a venue where sovereign states are often pursued over unpaid awards.

The award has been growing for years as interest accrues, turning the original arbitration figure into a still larger sum.

For Argentina, it is another foreign-court defeat in a long line of disputes stemming from past nationalizations and defaults.

A Case Rooted in 2008

The story begins in 2008, when the government of Cristina Fernández de Kirchner re-nationalized Aerolíneas Argentinas, then in private hands, framing it as rescuing a strategic company.

Nationalizing the airline was popular at home at the time, presented as saving jobs and a national symbol. Abroad, it deepened Argentina’s reputation as a risky place to invest.

The takeover was part of a wider wave of nationalizations in that era, from an oil company to private pension funds, that unsettled foreign investors.

Foreign shareholders disputed the terms. In 2017, an arbitration tribunal at the World Bank’s ICSID ordered Argentina to pay roughly US$321 million, plus interest and costs, for the expropriated stakes.

The latest US ruling confirms and enforces that line of decisions, pushing the total past US$390 million.

The Irony of the Timing

The judgment arrives at an awkward moment — because Aerolíneas is, for once, doing well. In 2025 it posted an operating profit of about US$112.7 million, roughly double the year before.

That followed its first surplus without a Treasury bailout in 2024, after the state had poured billions into the carrier over the years; one tally puts past support at some US$8 billion.

The turnaround has been driven by cost cuts, route changes and an end to the automatic bailouts that once masked the airline’s losses.

Aerolíneas has also trimmed staff and renegotiated contracts, moves that sparked strikes but helped close the gap between revenue and costs.

So a company just weaned off subsidies is now attached to a nine-figure legacy bill for a decision taken long before its recovery.

Milei, Privatization and What Comes Next

The airline sits at the heart of President Javier Milei’s drive to shrink the state. His government has long said it wants to clean up Aerolíneas and, eventually, sell it — a step that needs congressional approval.

After the ruling, officials insisted they still have legal tools, suggesting further appeals rather than immediate payment.

Selling a flag carrier is politically explosive in Argentina, where Aerolíneas is a source of both pride and patronage, so any privatization faces a hard fight in Congress.

How Argentina handles the bill also matters for its credibility with investors, already strained by a history of contesting foreign judgments.

Buenos Aires can appeal further, including to the US Supreme Court, so the money may not change hands soon.

Why Foreigners Should Care

The case is a reminder that Argentina’s past reaches into its present. Nationalizations and defaults leave legal tails that surface years later, often in foreign courts.

Argentina has spent years, and considerable money, contesting awards from ICSID and other tribunals, with mixed results. Each unpaid or contested judgment feeds a cycle in which investors demand higher returns to offset the risk that Argentina will not pay.

For Aerolíneas itself, the ruling complicates a privatization the government hopes to pitch as a clean break from a costly past.

An unresolved judgment also hangs over any sale, since a buyer would want the liability settled or ring-fenced first.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the US court rule about Aerolíneas Argentinas?

A US appeals court in Washington confirmed, in July 2026, that Argentina must pay more than US$390.9 million, plus interest, to the Titan Consortium over the 2008 nationalization of Aerolíneas Argentinas and Austral.

Why does Argentina owe this money?

In 2008 the government re-nationalized the airline, and foreign shareholders challenged the terms. An ICSID tribunal ordered about US$321 million in 2017; the US ruling enforces and updates that judgment.

Is Aerolíneas Argentinas losing money?

No longer. It posted an operating profit of about US$112.7 million in 2025, roughly double the prior year, after its first surplus without a Treasury bailout in 2024 — even as this legacy bill comes due.

Sources: US appeals court in Washington; Titan Consortium; ICSID tribunal.

World.title: Argentina’s Fiscal Innocence Plan Aims to Tap US$170 Billion
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Markets

Key Facts —The plan. Argentina’s economy minister, Luis Caputo, unveiled “Fiscal Innocence II,” a bill to coax dollars held outside the banking system back into the economy. —The prize. Caputo estimates Argentines keep about US$170 billion in cash outside the system — more than four times the dollars held in banks. —The pitch. Savers could deposit and use those dollars without explaining where they came from or facing tax penalties. —The change. The relaunch scraps the income and wealth caps that limited the first version, widening who can take part. —Why redo it. An earlier version, passed in December 2025, drew weak take-up and complaints from accountants, prompting the overhaul.

Argentina is sitting on a fortune it cannot see. With fiscal innocence, the government is making its boldest attempt yet to lure an estimated US$170 billion out from under the country’s mattresses and into the economy.

US$100 bills. Argentina’s plan targets an estimated US$170 billion held outside the banking system. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons, public domain)

Argentines are famous savers in one very specific way: they keep their money in dollars, in cash, out of the banks.

Now the government wants that money back in the open — and it is offering an amnesty to make it happen.

How Fiscal Innocence Works

The idea, championed by Economy Minister Luis Caputo, is disarmingly simple: let Argentines bank and spend their hidden dollars without questions.

Under the scheme, a saver can move cash into the financial system without explaining its origin or exposing themselves to tax penalties.

“Keeping dollars under the mattress is a very bad deal,” Caputo argued, urging savers to put idle money to work.

The scheme leans on ARCA, the tax and customs enforcement agency, to administer who qualifies and how the funds are declared.

Alongside the amnesty, the package also touches the income tax, part of a wider effort to make declaring money less costly.

Why Argentines Hoard Dollars

The habit is a rational response to history. Decades of inflation, devaluations, defaults and frozen bank accounts taught Argentines to trust cash — preferably US dollars — over their own banks.

The result is one of the world’s largest pools of informal savings. Caputo puts it at roughly US$170 billion, more than four times the dollars formally deposited in the system.

For many families, dollars in a safe or a drawer are not tax evasion but a form of self-defence against a currency that has repeatedly collapsed.

What Changed in “Version II”

This is a relaunch, not a new idea. An earlier “fiscal innocence” law passed in December 2025 but attracted far fewer participants than hoped.

Accountants complained the rules were confusing, and take-up was low. So the government spent weeks reworking the scheme with the tax agency and specialists.

The headline change: the caps on income and wealth that limited who could join have been removed, opening the regime to far more people.

Officials hope simpler rules and no caps will finally tempt savers who watched the first version and stayed away.

The low uptake was a warning. Argentines have been burned by past amnesties and confiscations, and trust is not restored by decree.

The Bet Behind It

For Milei’s government, the logic is growth. If even a fraction of that US$170 billion enters the banking system, it could fund credit, consumption and investment in a cash-starved economy.

Success would also help rebuild reserves and steady the peso, long-standing weaknesses of the Argentine economy.

It fits the administration’s broader promise, too: shrink the state’s reach, lower taxes and treat citizens’ money as their own.

Argentina’s banks are unusually small relative to the economy, so even a modest inflow of dollars could reshape how much credit is available.

The Money-Laundering Question

Not everyone is comfortable. Critics warn that letting money into the system with fewer controls and no questions about its origin risks laundering illicit funds.

The government counters that the target is ordinary savings, not crime, and that the dollars are already inside the country regardless.

Argentina has faced international scrutiny over money-laundering rules before, and any loosening invites questions from watchdogs abroad. Where the line falls — between freeing honest savings and shielding dirty money — is the tension Congress will test.

What It Means for Foreigners

For investors, a successful amnesty could deepen Argentina’s thin financial system and signal that Milei’s market-friendly reforms are taking hold.

For residents, it is a practical question: whether to trust a government promise after so many broken ones.

The scale of the prize — US$170 billion, in a country whose economy is worth several hundred billion — is why the government keeps trying, and why the world is watching.

Milei has staked much of his credibility on stabilising the economy, and coaxing out the mattress dollars is now part of that gamble.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Argentina’s “fiscal innocence” plan?

It is a scheme, relaunched by Economy Minister Luis Caputo in July 2026, that lets Argentines bring dollars held outside the banking system into it without explaining their origin or facing tax penalties.

How much money is involved?

Caputo estimates Argentines hold about US$170 billion in cash outside the financial system — more than four times the dollars formally deposited in banks.

What changed in the second version?

The relaunch removes the income and wealth caps that limited the original December 2025 law, widening who can take part, after the first version drew weak participation.

World.title: Chile Electricity Law Makes Utilities Pay for Blackouts
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Energy

Key Facts —The law. Chile’s Congress cleared a new electricity tariff-protection law on 22 July 2026, sending it to be enacted. —The key change. When the power fails, distributors — not customers — must pay the compensation owed for outages, reversing an earlier arrangement. —The scandal. Under a 2024 tariff calculation, 21 of Chile’s 26 distribution companies had passed the cost of those compensations on to users. —The backdrop. The law lands amid winter storms that have again cut power to homes, and a lingering saga over errors in electricity bills. —The aim. It also seeks to lower regulated tariffs, tidy up the tariff-setting process and improve the reliability of supply.

For years, Chileans who lost power in a blackout were, in effect, paying for their own compensation. A new Chile electricity law just cleared by Congress puts that bill back where many think it belongs: on the companies.

Santiago, Chile. A new law will stop customers footing the bill for the compensation they are owed when the power fails. (Photo: 3BRBS / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0)

Chile has long sold itself as Latin America’s orderly market economy, and nowhere more than in electricity, where private companies run much of the grid.

So a new law that makes those companies pay when the lights go out is more than a technical fix. It is a signal that patience with the utilities has run out.

What the Chile Electricity Law Does

On 22 July 2026, Chile’s Chamber of Deputies ratified the Senate’s changes to a “tariff-protection” bill, clearing its final hurdle to becoming law.

Its headline provision is simple but pointed. When distributors cut off or fail to deliver service, the compensation owed to customers must be funded by the companies themselves — not passed on to users.

The law also aims to lower regulated tariffs, regularise the often-messy process of setting distribution and transmission charges, and improve the security and quality of supply.

Because it protects regulated tariffs, it reaches almost every household, which buys power at prices the state sets rather than on an open market.

The measure passed with broad support, a sign of how politically toxic the status quo had become.

Why Chileans Were So Angry

The anger has deep roots. In the 2024 calculation of the “distribution added value,” the cost of mandatory outage compensations was quietly shifted from the power companies to their customers.

According to Chilean reporting, 21 of the country’s 26 distribution firms applied that arrangement — meaning users were, in practice, financing the very refunds they were owed when the lights went out.

Layered on top was a separate saga over errors in electricity bills, which left many Chileans feeling overcharged and mistrustful of the whole system.

For a country that prides itself on orderly institutions, the sense that the rules had been tilted against consumers struck a nerve.

Compensation for a blackout is meant to punish the company that failed; having customers pay for it, critics said, inverted the whole point.

The Storms That Keep the Lights Off

The reform arrives as Chile is once again battered by winter storms. A frontal system has knocked out power to homes, with utilities and the regulator fielding a flood of outage reports.

Chile has been here before. Past storms and a near-total blackout have left large parts of the country dark for hours or days, fuelling public fury at the distributors.

Winter in central and southern Chile regularly brings fierce frontal systems, and the grid’s ability to withstand them has become a recurring test of the utilities.

Utilities such as Enel have been fined before for slow restoration after storms, but fines alone did little to change behaviour.

What It Means for Consumers and Companies

For households, the promise is twofold: potentially lower regulated tariffs, and no longer bankrolling their own compensation.

For the distributors — including large operators such as Enel and CGE — it is a direct hit, adding the cost of outages to their own books and raising the price of poor reliability.

The bet is that making companies pay will push them to invest in a grid that fails less often.

How much tariffs actually fall will depend on the detailed tariff processes the law also promises to clean up.

The Bigger Picture

The tariff fights and blackouts have tested Chile’s market model, feeding a wider debate about whether privatised utilities serve consumers well enough.

President Gabriel Boric’s government has leaned into consumer protection, and the electricity fight fits a broader push to be seen defending ordinary Chileans’ pockets.

The debate echoes across Latin America, where governments from Colombia to Argentina wrestle with how to price power fairly.

Separately, Congress has moved to regularise a roughly US$900 million debt with the distributors, part of the tangle of unfinished business in Chile’s power sector.

What Foreigners Should Watch

For investors, the law signals a tougher stance toward utilities and a government willing to shift costs back onto companies after years of consumer complaints.

For residents, it is a concrete change: the next time the power goes out, the compensation should not quietly reappear on a future bill.

Whether it delivers cheaper, steadier electricity — or simply moves costs around the system — is what the coming winters will reveal.

Chile’s experience is being watched around the region, where privatised power grids face the same tension between profit and reliability.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Chile’s new electricity law do?

Cleared by Congress on 22 July 2026, it stops customers from financing the compensation they are owed for power cuts — shifting that cost to distributors — and aims to lower regulated tariffs and improve supply reliability.

Why were Chileans paying for their own blackout compensation?

In the 2024 “distribution added value” calculation, the cost of mandatory outage compensations was passed from the power companies to users; Chilean reporting says 21 of the 26 distribution firms applied it.

How does this connect to Chile’s storms?

The law passed as winter storms again cut power across parts of Chile, reviving public anger over blackouts and sharpening the question of who should pay when supply fails.

Sources: Chile's Congress; Chile's Chamber of Deputies.

World.title: Brazil’s INSS Backlog Hits 2.6 Million Claims
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Politics

Key Facts —The backlog. About 2.6 million Brazilians are waiting for the INSS, the national social-security institute, to decide their benefit claims — up from 2.4 million in mid-2025. —The setback. A programme that paid staff bonuses to clear cases faster, the PGB, was suspended in October 2025 after its R$200 million (about US$39 million) budget ran out early. —The fix. Since January 2026 a new National Queue lets any authorised official anywhere in the country handle any claim, prioritising the longest waits. —The focus. Disability and the BPC welfare benefit for the poor and elderly make up about 80% of the pending demand. —The backdrop. The queue swelled as the INSS tightened checks after a 2025 fraud scandal over unauthorised deductions from retirees.

Behind a dry bureaucratic number lies a very human wait. Brazil’s INSS backlog has climbed to roughly 2.6 million people, each stuck in a queue for the retirement, disability or welfare payment they have claimed.

A Previdência Social (INSS) office in Brazil. The benefits backlog has swelled to about 2.6 million people. (Photo: Senado Federal / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0)

Every month, tens of millions of Brazilians depend on a single institution for their income: the INSS, the national social-security institute.

Right now, about 2.6 million of them are stuck waiting for it to say yes or no.

What the INSS Is

The INSS — Instituto Nacional do Seguro Social — pays Brazil’s retirements, pensions, disability aid and welfare benefits. It is one of the largest such systems in the world.

Its scale is staggering. More than 35 million benefits are paid every month, most worth around a single minimum wage, moving tens of billions of reais to retirees and the poor.

It is often described as the machine that supports half of Brazil — a reminder of how central the state is to household survival in an unequal country.

For millions, an INSS payment is not a top-up but their entire income. A delay is not an inconvenience; it can mean going without.

Its reach touches almost every family, directly or through an elderly relative, which is why any wobble at the INSS reverberates through the whole country.

Why the INSS Backlog Grew

The queue has risen for months, from about 2.4 million claims in mid-2025 to some 2.6 million later in the year.

One trigger was the suspension, in October 2025, of the Benefits Management Programme, which paid officials a bonus for each extra case they analysed. Its R$200 million (about US$39 million) budget was exhausted before the year ended.

With the bonus gone, the pace of decisions slowed, and the pile of pending claims grew.

The bonus had been a pragmatic patch: pay overworked staff to take on extra cases. When the funding vanished, so did the incentive to clear the pile.

Changes to the law and reported system failures added friction, with beneficiaries describing glitches and long waits after the rules shifted.

The Fraud Scandal in the Background

The backlog cannot be separated from the scandal that rocked the INSS in 2025, when investigators found unauthorised deductions siphoned from millions of retirees’ benefits.

The fallout brought leadership changes, criminal probes — one touching a son of President Lula — and a drive to tighten controls.

Tighter checks guard against fraud but also slow processing, part of why claims now take longer to clear.

For many retirees, the discovery that money had been quietly skimmed from their pensions shook trust in the very system meant to protect them.

The National Queue Fix

Since January 2026, the government has tried a new approach: a single National Queue. Instead of a claim being tied to the office where it was filed, any authorised official anywhere can pick it up.

The idea is to balance the load, so a backlog in one overwhelmed city can be worked on by staff in another.

Priority goes to those who have waited longest and to disability and BPC claims, which the agency says account for roughly 80% of demand.

It is a managerial fix rather than a spending splurge, betting that better organisation can do what extra money did before.

Officials say the redistribution has begun to move the oldest cases, though independent proof of faster decisions will take months to appear.

Will It Work?

Lawmakers have also moved to revive a bonus scheme, with the lower house approving a measure meant to “zero out” a queue of nearly two million cases.

Whether these fixes stick depends on money and staffing — the very things that ran short in 2025.

Clearing a backlog this size is less a single reform than a grind, and past promises to end the wait have often fallen short.

Brazil has announced “end of the queue” plans before, only for the backlog to swell again once attention moved on.

Why It Matters

For Brazilians, the queue is a daily anxiety: people who have stopped working and are owed a pension can wait months with no income.

For the government, it is a political liability in an election year, and a fiscal one, since every delayed claim eventually becomes a lump-sum payment.

For a country that spends a large share of its budget on pensions, how efficiently the INSS runs is a question that reaches far beyond the people in the queue.

For foreigners living in Brazil, the same system governs disability and some welfare benefits, making its speed a practical concern as well as a political one.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big is Brazil’s INSS backlog?

About 2.6 million benefit claims were waiting for a decision by late 2025, up from around 2.4 million in the middle of the year.

Why did the INSS backlog grow?

A programme that paid staff bonuses to clear cases faster was suspended in October 2025 after its budget ran out, slowing decisions. Tighter checks following a 2025 fraud scandal also lengthened processing.

What is the INSS doing about it?

Since January 2026 it has used a National Queue that lets any authorised official handle any claim, prioritising the longest waits and disability and BPC benefits. Lawmakers have also moved to revive staff bonuses.

Sources: INSS.

World.title: Startup Summit 2026 Returns to Brazil’s Tech Island
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Dates and location. August 26–28, 2026, in Florianópolis, Santa Catarina. —Expected attendance. More than 10,000 in-person participants and over 200 speakers. —Organizers. Sebrae Startups, the entrepreneurship arm of Brazil’s micro and small business support service, together with the Santa Catarina technology association ACATE. —Main themes. Artificial intelligence, SaaS, venture capital, deeptech, HealthTech, EnergyTech, and internationalization. —Ticket access. Passes are sold through the official event website, with early-bird tiers typically released months in advance.

The Startup Summit 2026, Sebrae’s flagship gathering for startups, innovation, and entrepreneurship, will take place in Florianópolis from August 26 to 28, bringing more than 10,000 people to the southern Brazilian island city.
