World.title: Schools under scrutiny
World.content:
Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown addressing the region’s One Back-to-School Conference held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover, on Tuesday.Anthony Lewis

POINT, Hanover — The Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown has sounded the alarm over what he alleges are numerous accounting breaches in primary schools within Kingston and St Andrew.

“The breaches are too many. Here is what is happening now, colleagues. We are getting documents from the Integrity Commission (IC) for principals to be investigated… Accountability is stepping up,” he said.

Brown made the revelation, Tuesday, during the second of a three-day back-to-school conference for Region One that was held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover.

“Stakeholders in the communities are writing to the ministry. They talk about what they observe in schools. They go to a school and they get no receipt for the money they pay. They call you and ask if they should get a receipt and what it should look like,” he told an audience of educators.

The regional director said primary schools are the main offenders.

“Do you know where we tend to find the bulk of the breaches now? The primary schools. It’s a serious problem,” said Brown.

While he conceded that there may be administrative issues such as inadequate staff that impact how money is handled, he said there can be no excuse for some of the behaviour seen.

“Some simple things. Why would you keep money in excess of a million dollars locked up in a room for two, three weeks, months, and so forth? The bursar not being there caused that? So what I’m saying: I know you need those people, and we are working on that, but don’t do things to set up yourselves in the process,” added the senior officer.

Brown used the opportunity to explain proper administrative procedures when handling school funds.

“I beg you, lodge the money in a reasonable time frame. Money must be lodged intact. Can somebody please explain what the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit) Act means when it says ‘money must be lodged intact’? ‘[It means as soon] as collected,” he emphasised.

He explained that if five $100-notes are collected, that exact configuration must be deposited into the account.

“Don’t use it to make any change for anybody who wants to pay somebody something. That is what they mean [by] to lodge the money intact. If you are guilty, don’t say anything. Just sit like nothing is wrong but pray a prayer in your heart. I’m giving you 30 seconds to ask God to forgive you,” stated Brown to an outburst of laughter.

“You saved the money, but the law says treat it a particular way,” added the senior officer.

During his address Brown also expressed gratitude to the Ministry of Education for providing the region with additional professionals to conduct audits of schools within the region.

“We want to publicly say thanks to the members of the central ministry team, our CEO, [and] the permanent secretary. We spoke and they have given us a large number of people to build out the finance unit in the region. I have about five or six additional staff members now so we can do more audits. Clap the central team for that,” he said magnanimously.

World.title: Danger in John’s Hall
World.content:
A bedhead and concrete block are among items used to alert commuters to danger on the John’s Hall road in St James..

MONTEGO BAY, St James — An old bedhead and the top of a broken table used to cobble together a crude guard rail serve as warning that there is danger on the road between John’s Hall and Spring Mount in southern St James. One section appears on the verge of collapse, much like a nearby house whose foundation was eroded by Hurricane Melissa, last October, and commuters are worried.

“I’m afraid but mi just have to drive on it, can’t do better,” a shopkeeper who identified herself as Sancia told the

Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

“If little rain fall it gone, because underneath it, it’s deteriorating,” she explained.

The gaping cavern in a section of the Spring Mount Road is just a few kilometres up the hill, impassable as residents eagerly await word from the Government on when it will be repaired. Now, they have added the danger at John’s Hall to their list of urgent issues.

When contacted, community relations officer for the National Works Agency (NWA), Western Region, Janel Ricketts said they are aware of this latest development at John’s Hall. Though none were seen by the Observer, she said signs are in place to help guide motorists.

“This too, like Spring Mount, is on the radar of the NWA but in terms of an update, I don’t have that right now,” she told the Observer.

For shopkeeper Sancia and others who use the road, help cannot come soon enough as the alternative route is longer and more costly. What was once a straight route from John’s Hall to Montego Bay has now become a meandering journey to Sunderland, around Blackshop, and through Patosi.

“And the hottest part is we dropping out right at the square down there and we don’t reach Montego Bay as yet. It’s going to be more money, more gas, more everything,” Sancia lamented.

She also highlighted challenges being faced by students in that area of the community.

“Children that live here now that have to go Maldon are paying double or triple fare because they have to take taxi from here go to Montego Bay and a next taxi go and vice versa,” Sancia explained.

“It bad for everybody: Parents, children, business owners,” she added.

A roadside vendor in John’s Hall who chose not to provide his name spoke of the downturn in business he has seen as commuters from southern St James have had to find new routes.

“It rough because the road block up that side so people can’t come down. They would stop and buy drinks, food stuff, shop stuff; that’s not happening again,” he said.

He also pointed to the impact it has had on other areas of life that used to generate income, such as sporting competitions.

“Football was a thing where the different communities partake in and now them can’t come,” he said.

“Spring Mount people a bawl now because nobody can’t come down. We just want to see the road fix, the two place; because without it we don’t have any real livelihood, nobody can’t come, nobody can’t go,” he said.

A motorist who gave his name as Richard said travelling to the area has been a financial challenge and, like area residents, he is also worried about the increasing deterioration at John’s Hall.

“With this breakaway now, we would have to find a next way to go in town, it’s really pressuring. I hope they do something fast, whether it’s construction to start the new road or they find something better that we can travel on. But do something better,” Richard appealed.

World.title: Germany rebukes Trump over South Africa’s G20 ban
World.content:
The U.S. president announced in a social media post last November that South Africa would not be invited to the next G20 meeting.

During his speech, Wadephul also emphasized his interest in fostering closer relations with South Africa, despite disagreements on key geopolitical questions like Russia's war in Ukraine, the Gaza conflict or China. As a BRICS member, South Africa holds traditionally close relations to Moscow and Beijing.

"In some disputed matters we can agree to disagree", he said. "And at the same time keep on working together. What matters is that we are committed to the same international principles."

Wadephul also argued that Russia "continues to pose an existential security threat to us," which was made evident by Russia's Iskander ballistic missiles in Kaliningrad, which "would take only a matter of minutes to reach Berlin."

On China, he said that both countries should work more closely together as they were both "too dependent on supply chains coming from one country. We’re too dependent on one country as being the most important market."

World.title: France’s far left faces accusations of antisemitism from Olympics DJ
World.content:
On Saturday, Butch was forced to interrupt a show in the southeastern town of Grenoble amid heckling and reports that objects had been thrown at the stage.

“I was extremely scared, so much so. And the shock was such that I couldn’t move for days,” Butch said on Thursday. “And now there are new calls to boycott that have been made by the France Unbowed [locally].”

Critics, including former prime minister and presidential hopeful Gabriel Attal, have accused the far left of targeting Butch because she is Jewish. France Unbowed and Mélenchon, who has been gaining ground against centrist candidates in recent polls ahead of next year’s presidential election, have previously faced accusations of antisemitism.

Ahead of Butch’s show in Grenoble, local branches of France Unbowed and pro-Palestinian activists called for a boycott and protest, accusing her of supporting Israel. In a leaflet, they said she had “censored Palestinian voices” by signing a petition backing controversial French draft legislation against antisemitism in 2024. The bill was later dropped.

France Unbowed has been on the defensive over the incident. Mathilde Panot, the leader of its parliamentary group, said Wednesday that the leaflet targeting Butch was “bad.”

World.title: Russia chokes Ukraine’s lifeline Black Sea export corridor
World.content:
The attacks forced shipping giant Maersk to stop operations at the Chornomorsk Fishing Port in the Odesa region this week, redirecting cargo to Romania’s Constanta Port. Ukraine says it would still provide security, but the vessel owners decided to halt traffic due to heightened security threats.

“Previously, there had also been many hits on ships, but most of them concerned ships already docked in ports,” Andrii Klymenko, head of the Black Sea and Baltic Strategic Research Monitoring Group, told POLITICO. Vessel owners have halted operations, wanting to see how the situation unfolds and what new solution Ukraine can find, Klymenko added.

Russia's actions prompted Ukraine to request an urgent U.N. Security Council meeting for July 27, urging all states to immediately demand that Moscow stop its attacks on freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.

The attacks intensified after Ukraine conducted a series of successful strikes against Russian shadow fleet oil tankers in the Azov and Black Seas, forcing Russia to halt exports earlier this month.

But it would be wrong to say that’s a response, because Russia never paused the attacks on Ukraine’s ports and cargo, Klymenko said. “This narrative would only help Russia to force a maritime ceasefire on us, which would benefit only the Kremlin, as it has to sell oil,” the expert added.

Ukraine’s Navy spokesman Dmytro Pletenchuk said there is a big difference, as while Russia shells vessels operating in a completely legal way, Ukraine targets cargo vessels breaking maritime law by illegally transporting sanctioned oil or entering ports of Ukraine’s occupied territories.

“The war in the sea never stopped. We have already been in a similar situation. Yes, pressure increased, and yes, shipping companies see risks and reduce operations. But we will keep working to restore maximum capacity of our maritime corridor," Pletenchuk added.

Russia’s blockade of Ukrainian ports in 2022 strangled vital agricultural exports and helped drive global food prices more than 60 percent higher by March. But after Ukraine’s navy established a protected maritime corridor in the Black Sea, the country exported more than 168.9 million tons of cargo through it, including over 100 million tons of grain, much of it bound for countries in the Global South, despite repeated Russian attacks on Odesa’s ports.

World.title: Donald Trump’s envoy threatens tariffs if Burnham hits Big Tech with new taxes
World.content:
Warren Stephens attends bilateral talks with Donald Trump and Keir Starmer in Turnberry, Scotland on July 28, 2025. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Warren Stephens also warns UK social media ban is “a little draconian from a freedom of speech point of view.”

LONDON — Donald Trump’s ambassador to the U.K., Warren Stephens, has warned Britain could face further tariffs, if new Prime Minister Andy Burnham raises taxes on American tech giants.

“If we go down further taxation on primarily American companies, that could certainly [elicit a tariff response],” Stephens told Sky News on Thursday morning.

The warning comes as Burnham announces his plans to slash business rates bills for pubs, clubs and live music venues by shifting the tax burden elsewhere.

World.title: EU fines Google €890M for breaching Big Tech rulebook
World.content:
The larger fine covers Google’s self-preferencing in search, where the European Commission found Google gives its own shopping, hotel, transport and sports results better placement than it gives competitors. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

Brussels orders U.S. search giant to overhaul how it ranks rivals in search results and how it polices its app store — or face further penalties.

BRUSSELS — The EU fined Google €890 million on Thursday and ordered the U.S. internet giant to overhaul how it ranks rivals in search results and how it polices its app store, as it concluded two investigations into whether the company had breached the bloc’s flagship Big Tech law.

Google becomes the third company to face significant fines under the EU’s three-year-old Digital Markets Act, a rulebook meant to fast-track investigations into dominant tech platforms that has been denounced by Washington as discriminatory because most of the companies covered by it are American.

“Google has fallen short of effective compliance with the Digital Markets Act, and today we have taken decisive yet balanced enforcement action sanctioning these breaches,” said Teresa Ribera, the European Commission’s executive vice-president for competition policy. “The best products should succeed because they’re better, not because they’re owned by the company running the search engine.”

World.title: US ambassador shrugs off Ed Miliband’s jibes at ‘idiot’ Trump
World.content:
Pushed on whether Miliband could work effectively with his White House counterparts, Stephens said only: “People were people. People’s view of President Trump in 2016 is probably a lot different than it is … now.”

While Miliband was “wrong then,” Stephens acknowledged he had also made remarks “where you come back a few years later and say, Yeah, why did I say that? I don’t think that’s really right.”

Miliband was previously quizzed about his combative comments following the U.S. president’s second election victory in 2024. He has described his prior statements as “irrelevant,” adding: “I genuinely don’t think that Donald Trump is reading my tweets. I don’t have such a high opinion of myself.”

The foreign secretary’s predecessor-but-one, David Lammy, also had a history of posting critical tweets about Trump before taking on the top diplomacy job. But he was able to point to a friendship with U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

World.title: Le parquet de Paris ouvre une enquête sur le site “libertin” Wyylde
World.content:
La plateforme Wyylde est au cœur d’une vaste enquête de justice sur l’affaire dite des viols “libertins”, relatée par Le Monde dans une série d’articles. Dix-neuf hommes ont été mis en examen pour viols avec tortures et acte de barbarie dans cette procédure, qui a pour figure-clef “Christophe B.”. Pendant plusieurs années, ce dernier a utilisé Wyylde pour trouver des hommes prêts à avoir des relations sexuelles avec ses compagnes.

Christophe B. a également utilisé Wyylde pour diffuser en direct des vidéos de ces actes sexuels, visionnables par les inscrits sur le site.

“Libertinage” grand public

Actif dans plusieurs pays européens, dont la France, l’Allemagne, l’Italie, le Portugal ou l’Espagne, le site Wyylde revendique sept millions d’inscrits et quelque 700 000 visites par jour. Il dépend de la société Koala Interactive, immatriculée à Levallois-Perret en région parisienne, et qui compte plusieurs dizaines d’employés en France.

Cette entreprise opère depuis plusieurs années sur le marché des sites de rencontre “pour adultes”. Après avoir lancé dans les années 2000 le site Netechangisme, Koala Interactive et son fondateur, le développeur Kais Ahmed, ont lancé Wyylde.

Si une partie de la plateforme est gratuite, son modèle repose sur un abonnement payant qui donne accès à une messagerie, des tchats, des partages de photos et de vidéos ou encore des diffusions en direct. Wyylde revendique une communauté “respectueuse, ouverte et libre”.

Sur le site, consulté par POLITICO, on trouve cependant plusieurs dizaines de lives simultanés de vidéos d'exhibitionnisme ou de relations sexuelles en direct.

Wyylde s’était fait remarquer à l’automne 2024 avec une campagne de communication dans le métro parisien et dans les réseaux de transports de plusieurs métropoles françaises. Sur ses affiches, Wyylde promettait alors aux potentiels utilisateurs de venir “vivre ce que l’on ne peut pas montrer ici”.



Cette campagne a été lancée en parallèle du procès dit “de Mazan”, qui a vu comparaître plus de cinquante hommes accusés du viol de Gisèle Pélicot. Son époux, Dominique Pélicot, orchestrateur des abus, avait recruté ces hommes en passant par un autre forum en ligne, coco.gg.

Le site Coco constitue lui-même un précédent dans la manière dont la justice appréhende ces plateformes qui hébergent des contenus potentiellement illicites. Après l’ouverture d’une information judiciaire pour “fourniture d’une plateforme en ligne pour permettre une transaction illicite en bande organisée”, le site a été fermé par la justice en 2024. Son fondateur, Isaac Steidl, a été ensuite inculpé en janvier 2025 à Paris, notamment pour complicité de détention et diffusion d’images pédopornographiques.

World.title: Forget Slack and Teams — your next work chat could come with AI co-workers
World.content:
Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey's fintech company Block has released Buzz, an open-source workplace platform that treats AI agents as full members of a team, not a browser tab you quietly close when a colleague walks by.

 

The platform launched on Tuesday and is available now at buzz.xyz. It combines channels, threads, direct messages, voice, media sharing, code repositories and automated workflows, giving it a similar shape to Slack.

The key difference is how it handles artificial intelligence.

Agents in Buzz get their own cryptographic identities and permissions, letting them post, review code, run automations and take part in conversations alongside human colleagues.

"Every company is going to need a place where humans and agents work together," said Bradley Axen, Block's head of AI capabilities, in the company's announcement.

"The question is whether that place is proprietary or open. We built Buzz because we believe it should be open."

Buzz runs on Nostr, a decentralised protocol that gives every participant, whether human or AI, a cryptographic keypair that belongs to them rather than to the platform.

Block says this means an agent's identity and history are portable and can travel across other Nostr-compatible systems, rather than being tied to one vendor's account system.

The platform is model-agnostic. Teams can plug in agents built on Claude Code, Codex or Block's own goose framework, or bring their own.

Matt Ross, head of investor relations at Block, said he had watched several agents collaborate on a project in real time, producing work that was then instantly available for his team to build on further.

"This is going to completely transform how we work," he said in a post on X.

Block is offering Buzz under an Apache 2.0 licence, meaning developers can inspect, modify and self-host the code freely.

Teams that want to avoid running their own infrastructure can instead 

Block says it open-sourced Buzz because most AI tools right now lock companies into one company's platform and rules, while Buzz will let businesses own their AI setup and modify it accordingly.

World.title: Social media: Florence opens Italy's first centre for digital addiction
World.content:
On Tuesday in Florence, an agreement was signed for the launch of the project "Discover - Out of the shell", the first specialised centre in Italy dedicated to social media addiction and the conscious use of digital technology.

 

The initiative, promoted by ASL Toscana centro, the City of Florence and the Retesviluppo cooperative, is Italy's first attempt to tackle the phenomenon of addiction to the digital world, which mainly affects young people and has social and cultural repercussions.

"Digital technologies are part of young people's everyday lives and represent an extraordinary opportunity. Precisely for this reason we have a duty to support them in making increasingly conscious use of these tools, helping them to find a balance between the time spent online and the time devoted to relationships, sport, culture and shared experiences," explains Councillor for Youth Policies Letizia Perini, one of the main promoters of the centre.

Rules and restrictions in Europe

The debate on the issue is extensive worldwide and in recent days, various solutions have been adopted in Europe. The first country to adopt strict legislation against the platforms was Australia, which requires providers to verify users' age. The measure applies not only to social networks such as Instagram, TikTok or Facebook, but also to several types of online services.

Following Australia's lead, France on Tuesday became the first European country to introduce a ban on social media for under-15s, which will come into force as early as September.

Similar initiatives are spreading across Europe, after the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, backed the introduction of measures to protect minors online, drawing on data that highlight the risks for younger people.

On 15 July_,_ the United Kingdom announced plans to introduce a night-time social media curfew for 16 and 17-year-olds, although the measure has been criticised as ineffective.

Other European countries, including Greece, Slovenia, Sweden and Spain, are planning restrictions on social media use by under-16s and under-14s.

Italy focuses on prevention

Italy has not yet introduced solutions similar to those adopted in other EU countries. The Discover project, which will be operational after the summer, instead seeks to act in terms of preventing the abuse and misuse of screens and platforms, while at the same time promoting mindful use.

"We will not simply be imposing bans, but an innovative approach based on two pillars: guided disconnection and the promotion of conscious use of technology, to turn young people from passive consumers into active protagonists of their time. The Discover Centre aims to be a hub open to the local community, to analyse the phenomenon, launch interventions and practical workshops and train the educational community, rebuilding the social fabric that digital isolation risks fraying," says ReteSviluppo President Ester Macrì.

The centre will welcome young people aged between 10 and 25 and will be run by Retesviluppo, which has a decade of experience in schools, with a team of employees, collaborators and volunteers. The services on offer will include guidance programmes, a listening desk and workshop activities, focusing both on media education and on enhancing social interaction through board games, manual activities and group work.

Discover is intended as an educational space, open also to parents and external educators, but in the case of complex situations such as social withdrawal, isolation or psychological distress, the ASL can intervene by coordinating specialist services in the area.

"It was a much-needed centre that was missing from our area and that commits all of us, the signatory bodies, to keeping the sharing of strategies and projects alive. A key added value is the possibility of integrating prevention activities with constant links to the competent services. All this is done from a perspective of empowerment, far removed from logics of prohibition or simple bans," stresses the Director of ASL Toscana centro Valerio Mari.

World.title: ECB holds rates at 2.25% as the reignited Iran war keeps a second hike in play
World.content:
The European Central Bank kept interest rates unchanged on Thursday, holding steady as it waits to see how much of a lingering energy shock from the Middle East conflict will feed through into eurozone inflation.

 

The ECB's governing council held the deposit facility rate at 2.25%, with the main refinancing rate staying at 2.4% and the marginal lending facility at 2.65%.

Monetary policy for the eurozone is set through these three key interest rates, with the deposit facility rate serving as the main benchmark.

"The outlook for energy prices, while highly volatile, currently stands close to the baseline of the June Eurosystem staff projections and well above the levels recorded prior to the conflict in the Middle East," the central bank's statement read.

"Uncertainty remains high and the full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to play out. The Governing Council is therefore closely monitoring the intensity and duration of the shock, as well as its indirect and second-round effects," it added.

The decision follows confirmation last week that eurozone inflation eased to 2.8% in June from May's 3.2%, the first decline this year, with core price growth slowing to 2.4%.

The pause comes just six weeks after the ECB raised rates for the first time in nearly three years, responding to a war-driven energy shock that had pushed inflation to its highest since September 2023.

ECB President Christine Lagarde has been careful to keep the door open.

At the central bank's Sintra forum, Lagarde insisted June's move was not an "insurance hike" but a response to a genuine inflation problem, with projections showing a return to the 2% target only in late 2027, and only if monetary policy tightened further.

Lagarde also refused to pre-commit to a path, saying "forward guidance is not currently in the cards."

July is not a forecasting round and economists at ING, for example, had argued the bank would prefer to wait for September's fresh projections, when they see a second hike as the more realistic outcome.

The complication is that the shock behind June's hike is back.

Oil neared $120 a barrel in March before sliding to around $72 after an interim peace agreement at the end of June, but the truce has frayed badly this month, with the US and Iran exchanging fresh strikes, attacks on tankers and renewed sanctions pushing Brent back above $90 a barrel.

A prolonged rise in energy prices would feed through to household bills and headline inflation in the second half of the year, precisely the second-round effects central bankers currently fear.

The ECB and its peers

As the chart shows, Frankfurt tightened from previously being far below its peers.

The Federal Reserve's target range sits at 3.50% to 3.75% and the Bank of England's rate at 3.75%, while the Swiss National Bank is parked at zero.

Both of the ECB's larger counterparts decide again next week.

The Fed announces next Wednesday, with futures markets assigning roughly an 89% probability to a hold, according to CME's FedWatch tool, after June's unanimous decision and projections signalling no cuts this year.

The Bank of England follows the next day, on 30 July, with new forecasts in tow and economists overwhelmingly expect a hold at 3.75%, although a Reuters poll found nearly 40% see at least one hike before year-end, after two policymakers voted for an increase to 4% in June.

For now, the ECB is the only major Western central bank to have actually raised rates in this cycle.

World.title: Venice Film Festival backs auteurs: Herzog, Kore-eda, McDonagh and Moretti's return
World.content:
The 83rd Venice International Film Festival, running from 2 to 12 September on the Lido, will showcase major auteurs, international stars and a strong Italian presence.

 

Artistic director Alberto Barbera presented the official programme at a press conference in Rome, stressing that cinema continues to prove itself “a living organism, capable of constantly regenerating”, despite the fall in cinema audiences.

This year around 4,500 films were viewed, up from 4,200 last year, a sign of an ever more vibrant global production. According to Barbera, the programme reflects the major issues of our time – war, the climate crisis, migration, social and family tensions – told through the language of cinema.

Danny Boyle – making his Venice debut – will open the Festival with “Ink” on the evening of 2 September.

Five Italian films competing for the Golden Lion

Italy will take centre stage with five films in competition, entrusted to some of the most important names in national cinema.

The most eagerly awaited return is that of Nanni Moretti, back in the running for the Golden Lion after 37 years with “Succederà questa notte”. Strict secrecy still surrounds the film, but the first teaser has already piqued the interest of fans: the lead is Louis Garrel, alongside Jasmine Trinca, Hippolyte Girardot and Angela Finocchiaro. The images show Garrel in a basketball scene that clearly evokes the celebrated Michele Apicella from Bianca, one of the many nods to Moretti’s own cinema.

Also competing are Edoardo De Angelis with “Il fuoco che ti porti dentro”, starring Vanessa Scalera, Andrea Pallaoro with “The Echo Chamber”, Paolo Strippoli with “L’Estranea” and Marco Bechis with “Ritorno a Buenos Aires”. The five titles range from more established auteur cinema to the new voices of Italian directing, confirming the Festival’s ambition to champion productions capable of portraying the present through different styles and cinematic languages.

The most hotly anticipated from around the world

The international competition brings together some of the most acclaimed directors on the global scene.

Florian Zeller, Oscar winner for The Father, comes to Venice with “Bunker”, a psychological thriller starring Penelope Cruz and Javier Bardem.

There is great anticipation too for Martin McDonagh, the filmmaker behind The Banshees of Inisherin and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, who presents “Wild Horse Nine” with Sam Rockwell, his favourite leading man.

Among the most eagerly awaited titles is “Primetime” by Lance Oppenheim, with Robert Pattinson, while Casey Affleck directs “Company”, starring veteran actor Nick Nolte.

German master Werner Herzog returns with “Bucking Fastard”, entrusting the leading roles to sisters Kate and Rooney Mara, while Japanese director Hirokazu Kore-eda, who won the Palme d’Or in 2018 with Shoplifters, brings “Look Back” to the Lido.

Rounding out the international panorama is the new work by Japanese cult director Shinya Tsukamoto, “Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People?”, once again underlining the Festival’s vocation for sparking dialogue between major auteur cinema from every corner of the globe.

One of the most heavily represented industries is France, with four films in competition: Stéphane Brizé presents “Un bon petit soldat”, starring Alba Rohrwacher and Vincent Lindon; Cédric Kahn directs “15/18 (A Place to Heal)”; as mentioned, Florian Zeller returns behind the camera with “Bunker”; while Nicolas Pariser brings “Un peu avant minuit” to the Lido.

There is a debut in the main competition for Iranian director Ali Asgari, already acclaimed in the Orizzonti section with Divine Comedy, who this year is vying for the Golden Lion with A Bit of Light.

The only woman in competition is Danish director of Egyptian origin May el-Toukhy, contesting with her second feature, Woman Unknown.

Completing the line-up of international auteurs is Russian filmmaker Ilya Khrzhanovskiy, who continues his ambitious cinematic project dedicated to Soviet physicist Lev Landau with the new chapter in the Dau saga, developed over more than twenty years.

Out of competition: Amelio, Martone, Guadagnino and a documentary on Renzo Rosso

The out-of-competition programme is also rich, particularly in the Venice Open section.

Among the Italian titles stands out “Nessun Dolore” by Gianni Amelio, starring Alessandro Borghi, Valeria Golino and Valerio Mastandrea.

Another hugely anticipated film is “Scherzetto” by Mario Martone, based on Domenico Starnone’s novel of the same name, with Toni Servillo in the lead role of Daniele Mallarico. The film follows the relationship between an elderly widowed illustrator and his lively five-year-old grandson, in a story that moves between irony, memory and reflections on the passing of time. The cast also includes Serena Rossi, Leonardo Lidi, Lorenzo Perrotta and Gianluca Di Gennaro.

Among the special events, a highlight is “Joie de vivre”, Luca Guadagnino’s monumental documentary dedicated to Bernardo Bertolucci. The work, which runs for around seven hours, offers a journey through the filmography of the director from Parma, blending analysis, first-hand accounts and reflections on modern cinema. Barbera has described it as “an experience you simply cannot tear your eyes away from”.

There is also curiosity about “Be Brave”, a documentary by Francesco Carrozzini dedicated to entrepreneur Renzo Rosso, the founder of Diesel. It is the first Italian feature-length documentary to be made entirely using artificial intelligence as a creative tool, while still preserving the director’s full artistic control.

Golden Lions for Lifetime Achievement and a short film on Marilyn Monroe

One of the most prestigious moments of the 2026 edition will be the presentation of the Golden Lions for Lifetime Achievement to George Clooney and Ellen Burstyn.

Burstyn has starred in film masterpieces such as The Exorcist (1973), Alice Doesn’t Live Here Any More (1974), which earned her an Oscar, and Requiem for a Dream (2000). She will receive the honour ahead of the screening of “Flash Impact”, a short film directed by jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal and dedicated to the myth of Marilyn Monroe, marking the centenary of the actress’s birth. The film features Ellen Burstyn and Dakota Johnson, each offering a different interpretation of Marilyn’s figure.

Barbera: “Cinema continues to tell the story of our times”

Presenting the line-up, Alberto Barbera, director of the Venice International Film Festival, rejected gloomy predictions about the future of the seventh art.

“For sceptics, it would be enough to step into a cinema where Christopher Nolan’s Odissea is being shown to realise that cinema is anything but moribund,” the artistic director said.

According to Barbera, cinema remains the privileged place for interpreting contemporary life: not mere reporting, but a medium capable of transforming present-day events into universal stories. With this spirit, the 83rd Venice Film Festival is preparing to turn the spotlight on the Lido, once again confirming its status as one of the world’s leading events devoted to auteur cinema.

World.title: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs linked to “low” but real risk of hair loss, study finds
World.content:
Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, mainly used to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity, are associated with a significantly higher risk of hair loss than other diabetes medications, according to a new study published in The BMJ.

 

While rare, some people taking semaglutide and tirzepatide have reported hair loss. The new study confirms the low risk of hair loss, with authors arguing that this can help make better informed decisions.

Importantly, the most observed cases of hair loss linked to GPL-1 were reversible, as hair follicles remained intact, the authors said.

“Although the absolute risk of clinically recorded alopecia associated with GLP-1 receptor agonist use is low, the observed association may still influence patients’ satisfaction, adherence, and decisions to start or continue therapy,” authors wrote.

The researchers analysed electronic records of patients on medication for type 2 diabetes, including GLP-1 and two other alternative diabetes drugs: SGLT-2 inhibitors and DPP-4 inhibitors. Compared with SGLT-2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists were linked to a 37% higher risk of alopecia; compared with DPP-4 inhibitors, the risk was 68% higher.

GLP-1 medications were initially developed to treat type 2 diabetes, but their use has expanded to several other indications, including weight loss, cardiovascular risk reduction and obstructive sleep apnoea.

They work by mimicking glucagon-like peptide-1, a hormone produced in the gut after eating. They activate receptors in the pancreas to stimulate insulin secretion, and in the brain to help regulate appetite.

The authors point out that rapid weight loss and reduced calorie intake are well-established triggers of hair shedding.

Hormonal changes may also play a role, they noted, although further studies are needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms. Caloric restriction can further contribute to physiological stress and deficiencies in micronutrients such as iron, zinc and biotin, which may disrupt the hair growth cycle.

While hair loss does not typically result in physical harm, it may have significant psychosocial consequences, affecting self-esteem, quality of life, and treatment adherence, the authors added.

The authors conclude that further research is needed to clarify the mechanistic links between GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy, weight loss and hair loss, and to identify the patients who may be at greatest risk.

World.title: Fact check: No evidence links Norway fire to alleged Israeli settlement import ban
World.content:
Norway has been reeling from a huge fire that broke out in a townhouse in the southern city of Drammen last week and spread through the surrounding area and into nearby forests.

 

More than 100 homes were destroyed, and hundreds of people were forced to evacuate following the start of the blaze on 17 June.

The Associated Press reported that Norway's Directorate for Civil Protection described it as the "largest fire of its kind in modern times".

Since then, posts circulating online have attempted to link the blaze to a decision allegedly taken by the Norwegian government.

They claim the fire started just two days after Norway voted to ban trade and investment linked to illegal Israeli settlements.

But this is misleading. As things stand, Norway has not voted to ban imports from Israeli settlements, and there is no public evidence indicating that the fire was the result of a criminal act.

No ban on imports from Israeli settlements

The Norwegian government last addressed the issue of Israeli settlement trade on 19 June, when the Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced a public consultation on a proposal for a new bill banning trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories.

The government said the proposal was intended to address what it described as a settlement policy that "undermines the prospects for a two-state solution in which both Israelis and Palestinians can live in peace and freedom."

"The Israeli settlements in Palestine are in breach of international law," Norway’s Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said. "They contribute to displacement, extreme violence and a situation that makes a peaceful solution impossible."

“We intend to prohibit trade with the unlawful settlements," Eide added. "By proposing legally binding prohibitions, the government makes it clear that Norwegian citizens and Norwegian companies must not profit from or support activities that help sustain Israel’s unlawful settlement activity in Palestine."

Norway's Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide addresses a media conference at EU headquarters in Brussels, Monday, April 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Geert Vanden Wijngaert) AP Photo

Under the proposal, Norway would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as exports to those settlements.

It would also prohibit the purchase of real estate in the settlements, the provision of services related to the construction, renovation, purchase or sale of property there, and the acquisition of businesses headquartered or producing goods in the settlements.

However, the proposal is not yet law and has not yet been adopted by the Norwegian parliament.

It has been put out for public consultation, allowing affected companies, organisations, experts and other interested parties to submit comments. The consultation is open until 19 September 2026.

The only measures Norway has taken so far in relation to Israeli settlements are sanctions and other measures targeting violent Israeli settlers in the West Bank, announced on 9 June alongside Canada, France and the UK.

No evidence of criminal activity

The cause of the fire remains under investigation, with police saying they had identified a possible point of origin without disclosing further details.

"The investigation is exploring several possible causes of the fire," police said.

Smoke rises over terraced houses on fire in the Krokstadelva village in Drammen, Norway, Friday. July 17, 2026. (Thomas Fure/NTB Scanpix via AP) AP Photo

They added that they had no concrete suspicion of criminal activity at this stage.

However, police also explained that, as part of a fire investigation, anyone who was present at the scene or had a connection to the affected area may be considered a suspect as investigators establish what happened.

"One person is currently considered a suspect and has been questioned," police said.

Reports state that, following questioning, the authorities now believe that negligence is the most likely cause of the fire.

On 23 July, the municipality of Drammen announced that firefighters were ending their operation in the affected area of Krokstadelva. No one has been reported missing.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: WAFCON 2026: What you need to know
World.content:
Several months after it was supposed to start and with more teams than first planned, WAFCON 2026 is finally set to begin. The hosts want a maiden title while a tournament outsider have one of its best players.

What is WAFCON?

The Women's Africa Cup of Nations is the continental tournament to find the best women's international team in Africa. It has existed in some form since 1991 but the current competition's history really starts in 1998, since when it has generally been held every two years.

Holders Nigeria have won a record 10 titles with only Equatorial Guinea (2012 as hosts) and South Africa (2022) having broken their domination of the tournament.

Originally planned as a 12-team tournament, the African football federation (CAF) added four more teams after qualification. Those four sides had all lost out in the second phase of qualifying but were then reinstated despite CAF earlier denying such changes were afoot. It was a sign of things to come.

Where and when is WAFCON 2026 being played?

For a third successive tournament, WAFCON is to be hosted by Morocco. Specifically, games are to be played in Rabat and Casablanca with a a third city, Fez, dropped from the initial lineup when the fixtures were announced.

Building the game from the ground up To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since pulling out of hosting the men's AFCON in 2015, Morocco has become the favored African destination for both CAF and global football's governors FIFA. The North African country, which also hosted the men's AFCON last year, is to cohost the 2030 men's World Cup and has been chosen, or been the sole bidder, for a number of continental and international youth tournaments.

The tournament opener, between Algeria and Senegal, is on July 26, with Morocco opening against Kenya later that day. The final is scheduled for August 16 in Rabat.

Why is WAFCON being played straight after the men's World Cup?

It wasn't supposed to be. After weeks of rumor, denial and a South African offer to step in as hosts, CAF announced just 12 days before the tournament was due to start in March that it would be postponed. CAF, rather vaguely, cited "unforeseen circumstances" as the reason for the delay.

"It is a combination of factors, and it is not a decision taken lightly," Luxolo September, CAF's head of communications, told DW at the time.

"There is a question of the host nation, Morocco, requesting a postponement for a number of reasons. There has been a lot of interaction between Morocco, FIFA and CAF regarding the date. This is not a nice position for us. We have taken no joy from this. We would have loved to play in this window. It is a window we had requested."

Many teams, fans and players were frustrated by the short notice, with preparations made and money shelled out far in advance. It was not the first time though. Two years earlier, the tournament had been postponed by a year because the tournament clashed with the Olympics in Paris — a key date in the women's football calendar.

As well as coming hot on the heels of the men's World Cup, WAFCON 26 will now finish as the season starts in many countries. Germany's women's season for example, kicks off with the first round of the DFB Cup on same weekend as the WAFCON final.

Who are the favorites at WAFCON 26?

Hosts Morocco will want to match their men's side, who won their AFCON tournament in controversial circumstances earlier this year, their maiden title, having lost the previous two finals.

Nigeria wins women's Africa Football Cup of Nations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Perennial champions Nigeria will once again enter as favorites while the 2022 winners, South Africa, will also fancy their chances. Below that are a host of teams who could cause a few surprises, including Ivory Coast, Egypt and debutants Cape Verde, whose men's side became one of the stories of the World Cup.

Who are the players to watch at WAFCON 26?

Apart from Zambia's Barbra Banda and Racheal Kundananji,Nigeria's Rasheedat Ajibade may be the most highly regarded talent. Named player of the tournament in 2024, Ajibade is a leader for her team, as well as its sharpest attacking threat. At the other end of the pitch, Nigeria will rely on Chiamaka Nnadozie, regarded as the continent's best goalkeeper.

Hosts Morocco will look to Ghizlaine Chebbak. The top scorer at the last two tournaments, 35-year-old Chebbak may not have too many better chances to win a first major international honor.

Elsewhere, Tabitha Chawinga, of French champions Lyon, will carry the hopes of debutants Malawi, the lowest FIFA-ranked side in the competition. Chawinga's international career has been interrupted by her club commitments but she has an exceptional 25 goals in her 11 caps to date. Her sister, Temwa, is also in the Malawi squad and plays her club football for the Kansas City Current of the NWSL, the top league in the United States. There, she won the 2025 Golden Boot as top goal scorer with 15 goals in 23 games.

World.title: Nigeria: Armed 'bandits' kill more than 20 in Zamfara state
World.content:
Armed gangs, known locally as "bandits," are a constant threat in northwestern and central Nigeria. They typically raid villages, steal livestock and kidnap residents for ransom.

More than 20 people were killed after gunmen attacked several villages in Talata Mafara in Nigeria's northern Zamfara state on Wednesday.

Nasiru Lauwali, a local councilor representing the Sauna district, told AFP that 21 people had been killed.

Meanwhile, Sauna district secretary Alhaji Shehu Garba said 23 people had been killed across five villages.

Three others wounded by gunfire were transferred to a hospital in neighboring Sokoto state.

Bandits remain a threat in Nigeria

Local residents told SaharaReporters that the raid began at around 2 p.m. on Wednesday and went "unhindered" for around three hours. Some residents accused local security forces of not intervening.

The attackers also rustled a large number of livestock, according to the news outlet.

Armed gangs, known locally as "bandits," are a constant threat in northwestern and central Nigeria. They typically raid villages, steal livestock and kidnap residents for ransom.

The bandit raids are separate from the ongoing jihadi insurgency in the northeast of the country led by militant group Boko Haram.

'Nigeria is much, much more complex' than Trump suggests To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Violence in Nigeria has been in the spotlight after US President Donald Trump made unfounded claims of Christians being persecuted in the West African country.

However, the bandits who raid villages are largely motivated by financial gain and typically do not espouse an ideology, while jihadi militants have attacked both Muslims and Christians indiscriminately.

World.title: Germany seeks energy and trading partners in Africa
World.content:
Germany is keen to boost its economy. On his third trip to Africa, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is visiting Nigeria and South Africa to promote greater cooperation.

In a tent in the Nigerian metropolis of Lagos, two worlds collide: Three fashionable influencers sit on cushioned stools across from Germany's 63-year-old Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul. For half an hour, the senior politician meets youth from Africa's creative scene.

These young people are among the stars of Nigeria's creative industry — in a country with a population of around 240 million and a median age of just under 18. Wadephul wants to understand what moves the younger generation. What issues are on their minds? How do they view Germany? And what do they expect from a collaboration?

After a brief hesitation, they reply: Germany and Europe listen to their music, view their art, and want to collaborate with them. But anyone who wants to travel to the German capital for Fashion Week or the Berlinale film festival can hardly get a visa, says a young man in the audience.

A conversation gets underway; everyone enjoys the exchange and subsequently uploads upbeat videos to social media platforms — to the influencers' channels as well as those of the Federal Foreign Office. This is how German diplomacy seeks a direct line of communication with Africa's younger generation.

Nigeria as a valuable energy supplier

There is good reason for the Foreign Minister to be promoting Germany in Nigeria. "The country is an economic powerhouse and, as Africa's largest domestic market, also a key destination for German exports," he says. Nigeria is sub-Saharan Africa's second-largest economy and already imports machinery, chemicals, and food products "Made in Germany."

However, Nigeria's raw materials account for the largest share of the trade balance. They have become even more important since the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. "In June, 25% of jet fuel shipments to Europe came from Nigeria. But we can do significantly more," emphasizes Wadephul.

Vital infrastructure support

Wadephul is accompanied by a business delegation on his third trip to Africa. The group includes major corporations like Siemens as well as small and medium-sized enterprises. One of these is VIDA , a Munich-based AI company that is finalizing a multi-million-euro contract with the Nigerian government. The focus is on AI-driven infrastructure planning.

"Our solutions help identify and evaluate new locations. AI allows us to determine much more quickly the economic potential of a site, as well as the local conditions regarding security, climate trends, and other key factors," explains VIDA founder Tobias Engelmeier. His company is already implementing projects in 20 African countries.

German support for infrastructure development is in demand in many places. Since the European Union launched a €290 million ($330 mio) package as part of its Global Gateway strategy, hopes have been rising — both in Africa and among European companies — for faster progress in expanding transport, energy, and utility networks. The Nigerian government is also actively lobbying for German investment to modernize its power supply.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and President of the ECOWAS Commission Omar Touray attended the Nigerian-German business roundtable Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

Underestimated economic and political significance

Yet Germany has long underestimated Nigeria's economic and political importance. Given the potential of what is Germany's second-most important trading partner in sub-Saharan Africa, the presence of around 100 German companies is comparatively small. Siemens is involved in expanding the power grid, while Bayer is planning pharmaceutical production facilities together with regional partners. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are also increasingly entering the market, though many complain about a lack of transparency in market and decision-making structures.

"It is a challenging market with high operating costs. That is why local partners who understand the diverse structures across the 36 states are essential," says Sabine Dal'Omo, Managing Director of Siemens Sub-Saharan Africa and Chairwoman of the German-African Business Association.

Renewable energy provider Enertrag is among the companies taking a wait-and-see approach. "For us, Nigeria holds great potential — there is strong domestic demand and favorable conditions for exporting green energy. However, the overall framework remains too uncertain for us to commit to a long-term investment," says board member Anne Bendzulla.

Instead, Enertrag has been successfully investing in South Africa for several years. There, the company states it is prepared to invest around €850 million in wind energy.

Missing out by arriving late

The security situation in Nigeria is a matter of concern for German business. Consequently, the Federal Government is making additional funds available for cooperation with Nigeria's police authorities.

He urges the German business community not to hesitate too long. "Anyone not present in Africa today risks missing out on crucial opportunities," Wadephul told reporters. The country, with its young population, possesses immense potential and abundant resources, he added. "It would be grossly negligent of us to overlook that."

On the final day of his third trip to Africa, Johann Wadephul is visiting South Africa — by far Germany's most important economic partner on the continent. Around 600 German companies have already invested there.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Czechia: Army helicopter crashes, killing at least one
World.content:
A Czech army helicopter carrying five troops crashed in eastern Czech Republic, the military said.

A Czech army "Venom" helicopter carrying five troops crashed on Wednesday, the country's military said on X.

"A Venom ​helicopter crashed at the 22nd Helicopter Air Force Base in ⁠Namest ​nad Oslavou," ​the army said. "There were five

soldiers ​on board. The ‌integrated emergency system is responding at the scene."

The regional rescue service reported that one person died in the crash, while three others were injured and transported to the hospital.

The crash occurred at the Air Force base Namest nad Oslavou, 180 kilometers (112 miles) ‌southeast of Prague.

The Czech Army has not yet released additional information about the circumstances surrounding the crash.

The UH-1Y Venom, produced by Bell Textron, is a multipurpose helicopter. It is powered by two T700-GE-401C engines produced by General Electric.

World.title: Lenacapavir will slow HIV infections if there's enough of it and it reaches at-risk groups
World.content:
Lenacapavir is one injection, twice a year. It's a big improvement for people in high-risk groups, currently taking a pill a day against HIV infection. But its long-term impact depends on its reaching those very people.

For a healthy young woman in South Africa, the greatest risk of HIV may come from someone she wants to trust, but can't.

She may not know her partner's HIV status, may not always be able to insist they use a condom, and may have little control over whether he has other partners.

There is an option: Daily Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) pills keep antiretroviral drugs in the body at high enough levels to stop HIV before it can establish any infection.

But PrEP only works if she keeps taking the medication.

Miss too many doses and drug levels can fall too low to provide sufficient protection.

She may forget, resent having to take a daily pill, or fear that a partner or relative will find the medication, causing stigma. She may also experience side effects from PrEP or struggle to obtain new supplies.

Zimbabwe takes a big shot toward an HIV-free future To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How can lenacapavir help?

Taking medication consistently — known as adherence — is a challenge for people with conditions like hypertension and diabetes. With PrEP, however, the difficulty is even greater.

"You're asking people who are healthy, who don't have any illness, to take a tablet every day," said Salim Abdool Karim, director and co-founder of the Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa. "That's a high bar."

"Repeated studies, including our own, show that patients who start taking PrEP, by month three, about half of them have given it up. By the end of the year, you're left with only a handful that are still taking PrEP," Abdool Karim told DW.

Lenacapavir sharply reduces that daily burden: It requires just one injection every six months.

"That's infinitely easier to do than to remember to take a tablet every day," he said. "For those who receive the injection every six months without fail, it works superbly because adherence is effectively complete."

But lenacapavir is still too expensive in some regions and access is low.

How does lenacapavir last so long in the body?

Most established PrEP drugs block enzymes that allow the virus to reproduce and spread —it uses the enzymes to copy its own genetic material and insert it into a human cell's DNA.

Lenacapavir works completely differently. It is the first PrEP drug to target the capsid, a cone-shaped shell that surrounds the viral genetic material. But the capsid is also essential to the virus' replication process — and therefore a promising target.

Lenacapavir attacks the capsid of HIV, shown in green because they are vital for the virus' ability to replicate and spread in the body Image: Cavallini James/BSIP/picture alliance

"[Lenacapavir] is the most potent molecule we know of against HIV," Wesley Sundquist, a University of Utah biochemist and leading expert on the HIV capsid, told DW.

Sundquist said lenacapavir remains effective over long periods and that it is potent even at low concentrations.

"It sets up a little depot that slowly dissolves," said Sundquist.

Which groups would benefit from lenacapavir (if they can get it)?

Abdool Karim pointed to three groups where HIV incidence remains stubbornly high and greater PrEP uptake is urgently needed:

Adolescent girls and young women in parts of Africa

Younger gay men in the West

Vulnerable gay communities in Eastern Europe and Central Asia

In South Africa, a rollout for people at risk began in June 2026, backed by a July 2025 agreement between the drug's developer, Gilead, and a public-private financing organization called the Global Fund.

Gilead agreed to supply lenacapavir at no profit to up to 2 million people over three years.

Earlier, in October 2024, Gilead also agreed to allow the production of cheaper, generic versions of the drug in 120 resource-limited countries, where HIV infection rates are high.

But some countries still lack access to the drug.

Latin American countries excluded from lenacapavir deals

Melissa Scharwey of Doctors Without Borders said some Latin American countries, including Brazil, Mexico, Peru and Argentina, have been excluded from recent rollouts of lenacapavir, despite their having participated in its clinical trials.

Even within eligible countries, vulnerable groups may still be missed, Scharwey told DW.

"There's by far not enough of it," said Scharwey, calling on Gilead to increase supply and sell directly to MSF at an affordable price of around $40 per shot.

The decisive question in driving down HIV, according to University of Washington epidemiologist Monisha Sharma, is whether the drug reaches the people and places where HIV is spreading most rapidly.

"In our modeling of South Africa, Zimbabwe, and western Kenya, providing lenacapavir to approximately 2–4% of the adult population, with targeted uptake among people at greatest risk, averted approximately 12–18% of new infections over ten years," Sharma told DW.

Is injectable HIV medication really a 'silver bullet'? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Lenacapavir 'unlikely to eliminate HIV on its own'

"Lenacapavir could substantially accelerate progress toward lowering incidence, but it is unlikely to eliminate HIV transmission on its own," said Sharma.

"This impact is highly dependent on affordable lenacapavir drug prices, efficient distribution channels, and targeted uptake among people with the highest HIV risk," she added.

That final condition is what gives Abdool Karim his greatest concern. Lenacapavir can largely solve the adherence problem for people who receive it. It cannot solve the harder problem confronting HIV specialists: identifying and reaching those in greatest danger.

"The problem is that those at highest risk need to come forward to take the medication. And often those at the highest risk don't see themselves at risk. That's why they're at risk," said Abdool Karim. "If we cannot reach those at highest risk, then we're not going to make a dent in this epidemic in the manner in which we were hoping."

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

World.title: US citizens are ramping up pressure on data centers
World.content:
Rapid data center construction across the US, fueled by AI, comes with serious threats to the environment, public health and energy supply. Local opposition has blocked or delayed dozens of projects.

When construction on a major Amazon data center in the small rural county of Frederick, Maryland, got underway, community activist Elizabeth Bauer found her peace with it.



But when it expanded by about 1,000 acres beyond its original plans to dig into green space and farmland without addressing the community's concerns, she took a stand.

Together with other locals she is protesting the proximity of the construction site to residential areas, which she says is causing dust and pollution that is exacerbating asthma among the population.

Protesters in Frederick demand that farmland is used for farming, not to host data centers Image: Elizabeth Bauer

"I'm okay with data centers in the right place. I'm not okay with them taking prime farmland," Bauer said.

Protest against data centers is getting louder

Bipartisan backlash against data centers has gotten louder in the US, with nationwide demonstrations calling on politicians to take action.

The US District of Columbia, Maryland, and Virginia region has been a flashpoint. Virgina alone has currently around 640 data centers listed.

These conflicts are not only related to the construction phase, but longer-term impacts. Data centers require vast amounts of energy to operate — as much electricity as 100,000 households, according to the Enviornmental Protetion Agency.

But those under construction could consume 20 times as much, largely due to the increased demand for data storage and processing capabilities needed to support AI development and use.





Overall, data centers account for 4.4% of US power, but a study by investment banking firm Goldman Sachs projects an increase of up to 8.5% by the end of 2027.

Data centers devour power and water

The battle in Frederick reflects the tensions across the US, which is already home to 4,600 data centers — around 1,000 more than the next 10 countries combined.

Almost 40% of citizens live within a five-mile radius of at least one, and that number is likely to rise given that more than 1,500 more sites are under construction. Nowhere in the world is the concentration higher than in North Virginia.





This is all happening against a backdrop of discontent, with a recent Gallup poll suggesting that 71% of the population opposes data center development in their communities.

Data centers can use up to five million gallons of water each day (as much as a city of 50,000). Yet, it is not uncommon for them to be built in areas under water stress. According to the US drought monitor, Frederick County is experiencing a severe drought.



Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard's School of Public health, said tech companies also regularly disregard this concern.

"They're not looking at the water issues at all," she told DW. "They prioritize where they can get the land cheaper, where they can get the local politician to give the approval faster."

Higher fuel bills and air pollution

States with high concentrations of data centers have seen a 267% increase in electricity prices over the last five years.

Residents at a town hall meeting, here in Kenmore, New York, protesting against data center plans Image: Craig Ruttle/Sipa USA/picture alliance

"Electric utilities are building massive amounts of new transmission lines to serve data centers," said Hannah Wiseman, a professor in environmental law at Penn State University. "But the costs of those transmission lines are being socialized among the rate payers."

There are also concerns that data centers could overburden the grid meaning they have to resort to backup diesel generators. In the case of the Frederick community, the planned center would have 99 diesel generators, which comes with health risks.

"Exposure to fine particulate matter, even at a low level, [means] increased risk of birth defect, respiratory, cardiovascular, neurocognitive and early deaths," said Harvard's Dominici, adding that they also threaten local wildlife and minimize plant growth and yield.

How are data centers regulated?

Despite negative effects on communities, Wiseman said that the locations of data centers are mostly overseen at the municipality level, and that many states offer data center developers a regulatory environment that allows rapid development, regardless of proximity to people or nature.

"Lots of local governments have chosen not to issue land use regulation, in which case a data center developer can pretty much do whatever they want."

At a federal level, US President Donald Trump cut red tape for developing data centers as part of his 2025 executive order "Removing Barriers to American Leadership in AI."

Many tech companies have insisted that localities sign non-disclosure agreements to limit communities' understanding of the scale of the projects and consequences of widespread resource consumption.

So instead of inviting resident input, they are working directly with municipality officials to draw up their plans.

Data centers and the global water crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Wiseman also noted that tech and development companies are increasingly collaborating with state governments in establishing zoning and power consumption standards.

"They've been involved in all the state regulatory proceedings to create special electricity rates for data centers," she said. "It appears that tech companies are getting more involved now in the many state legislative proposals to preempt local control."

How tech companies respond to the pushback

Though tech companies argue that data centers invigorate local economies, a University of Michigan study found that they generate temporary construction jobs to local communities, but not long-term tech positions.

There are some suggestions that these companies are looking to build trust with local communities. In March, Microsoft stopped using NDAs with local governments for data center development, saying they wanted to build more trust with their neighbors. And Meta says it is piloting and deploying low-carbon concrete in data center construction.

Why people are throwing AI data centers into the ocean To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dominici says she sees "a win-win future path" that combines technological advancement with community benefit. "I would love to see nonpartisan scientific evaluation of all the impact, and the data center can act based on minimizing this impact as much as possible."

Putting the brakes on, at least temporarily

And protests in local communities seem to have paid off. Just last week, New York became the first US state to halt construction of new large-scale data centers for up to a year. Moratoriums have also been proposed in other states, and some counties and municipalities have issued their own temporary bans.

In Frederick, Bauer and fellow activists continue to push back against the data center going up in their back yard. They've collected enough signatures to propose the ordinance be subject to a referendum in the county elections, though any idea of that happening was quashed by Maryland's supreme court.

The county has responded to this blowback by issuing a temporary pause on new data center construction, yet Bauer feels the democratic process failed Frederick residents.

"The average citizen has no chance," she said. "This whole effort was not to fight data centers, it was to give people a voice."

Despite challenges, Bauer still sees hope. She said there are county council candidates in the upcoming Frederick election that oppose expansion.

"If the new council comes in, they can overturn this map completely," she said. "We're disappointed, but we are not giving up."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker, Sarah Steffen

World.title: Thailand: 5 soldiers killed in attack on security checkpoint
World.content:
The attackers stole three AK-47 rifles, three bullet proof vests and three mobile phones from the soldiers. A low-level conflict has been simmering in Thailand's southern provinces for two decades.

Five Thai soldiers were killed in an attack on a military checkpoint in Narathiwat province in the country's restive south.

At least six civilians were also injured in the attack, including a 10-year-boy, local officials said.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Thursday called the attack a "brazen act of terrorism" that posed "a serious threat to national security."

What do we know about the attack?

The incident took place on Wednesday when around 10 people opened fire at the security checkpoint and threw pipe bombs at soldiers from the Thai Rangers auxiliary force, before fleeing the scene.

Thailand's Internal Security Operations Command said the attackers stole three AK-47 rifles, three bullet proof vests and three mobile phones from the soldiers.

Their vehicle was later found abandoned and set on fire 21 kilometers (13 miles) away from the scene.

A low-level conflict has simmered since 2004 in Thailand's southernmost provinces, with rebels in the Muslim-majority area fighting for greater autonomy in Buddhist-majority Thailand.

More than 7,000 people have been killed in the conflict. Government spokesperson Ratchada Thanadirek said the past few months in particular had seen a series of violent incidents carried out by a "terrorist network seeking to instill fear among the public and target state officials."

World.title: EU fines Google €890 million over competition rules
World.content:
The European Commission said it found that Google had preferenced its search engine and app store in ways that unfairly harmed competition.

The European Union has imposed fines of €890 million ($1.015 billion) on US tech giant Google for violating EU digital regulations.

The European Commission said it found that Google had preferenced its ubiquitious search engine and its Play app store in ways that unfairly harmed competition.

What did the EU say about the fine?

"We found that Google harms businesses offering similar services, such as shopping or sports, by not granting them the same level of prominence on Google Search," Digital Commissioner Henna Virkkunen said.

"We also found that Google has restricted app developers from offering cheaper offers to customers in the Google Play app store," she said.

The commission stressed that Google could face further fines if it does not take steps to comply with regulations.

"The best products should succeed because they’re better, not because they’re owned by the company running the search engine," Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera said. "European consumers have a right to be told by app developers where to sign up to the best offers, even when the app store owner does not get a cut."

The EU has described Google and its parent company Alphabet as a "gatekeeper" alongside other major US firms — namely Amazon, Apple, Meta and Microsft — and China's ByteDance, saying that the companies control access for consumers.

Top Google executive Kent Walker criticized the fine, describing it as "product degradation driven by a small group of self-serving complainants."

He said that the penalty would "strip away real-time search features Europeans love — like instant pricing and direct availability for hotels, flights, and restaurants — and dismantle safety protections on Google Play."

Brussels aims to curb Big Tech under anti-trust and safety regulations Image: Virginia Mayo/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

What is the EU's policy on Big Tech and competition?

The European Union has been working to rein in Big Tech companies in the face of larget market shares held by major US and Chinese firms.

The European Commission already imposed a €4.3 billion penalty on Google in 2018, accusing the company of abusing Android system's market dominance by requiring phone makers to pre-install Google Search and the Google Chrome web browser. The firm lost its appeal against the fine in February.

The EU has also fined tech firms under safety regulations, with Chinese retailer Ali Express being hit with a €550 million fine earlier this month after the bloc had found shortcomings in the firm's efforts to curb illegal, unsafe and counterfeit goods.

On July 10, the EU threatened social media giant Meta with a heavy fine unless it changes "addictive design" used on the platforms Facebook and Instagram.
