World.title: Ridon asks: Was OVP dragging Senate into procurement issue over meals?
World.content:
Rep. Terry Ridon —Screengrab from a House of Representatives YouTube video

MANILA, Philippines — Another question brought by Vice President Sara Duterte’s request for the Senate to shoulder the meals of her lawyers for the impeachment trial is whether this matter would have led to a procurement issue for the legislative body, Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said on Thursday.

Ridon in an online press briefing said that the Office of the Vice President (OVP) will cause a procurement case had the Senate granted its request to shoulder the defense panel’s meals, because Duterte requested for their own caterer which the Senate should pay for.

“The way I look at it, it seems that the OVP is basically opening up the Senate for a procurement case,” Ridon, speaking Filipino, told reporters after he and other members of the prosecution panel were asked about Duterte’s letter dated July 7.

Article continues after this 

“Because they want to hire their own caterer, but the one who would pay it is a different entity. So I think it’s the Senate who should decide on what would be their decision regarding this matter,” he added.

Under Section 15 of Republic Act No. 12009 or the New Government Procurement Act, having another office to do procurement is only allowed if the procuring entity — in this case, the OVP — “does not have the capability or proficiency to undertake a particular procurement.”

However, procuring agents generally refer to government agencies whose primary role is procurement, like the Procurement Service of the Department of Budget and Management.

“As part of strategic procurement planning, the HoPE (head of procuring entity) may authorize the engagement of a government procurement agency, which shall undertake the functions of the BAC (Bids and Awards Committee), if the Procuring Entity does not have the capability or proficiency to undertake a particular procurement,” R.A. No. 12009 stated.

“Provided, that the Procuring Entity cannot delegate the issuance of the notice of award and the award of contract to the procurement agent and there shall be no transfer of funds to the procurement agent, except for the payment of service fee, if applicable,” the same section added.

Article continues after this 

On Wednesday, copies of Duterte’s letter were released to the media, showing her request for food and beverage from OVP’s accredited caterers due to “legitimate security concerns.”

According to the letter, Duterte requested that all food and beverages for her team and witnesses be served only in their designated holding room for their safety, and that the Senate shoulder the costs for these arrangements.

Article continues after this 

“As these arrangements are required solely in connection with these proceedings, the OVP respectfully requests that the Senate shoulder the reasonable costs of food and beverage and catering services for the defense team, support staff, and witnesses,” Duterte said in the letter.

READ: Sara Duterte asks Senate to foot bill for exclusive catering at trial

But Ridon said this request is “very interesting” as the Senate, sitting as an impeachment court for Duterte’s trial, has no obligation to shoulder the meals of either the defense panel or the House of Representatives’ prosecution team.

“The request is very interesting, because it is true that the Senate Impeachment Court has no obligation to pay the food of anyone, whether it is the prosecution or the defense. The truth is that these sides have their own offices, the defense and the prosecution,” he said.

“So the defense, the OVP has its general budget, the House has its own general for the impeachment proceedings. So I cannot understand why — it looked like a demand from the OVP, from the Vice President herself — they are asking the Senate to actually pay for the food expenses of the defense panel,” he added.

Ridon is not the first House lawmaker to comment on Duterte’s request. On Wednesday, hours after news outlets reported on the letter, House Deputy Speaker Janette Garin said that this request comes off as improper and funny at the same time, since the OVP is an office which has been allocated funds for such purposes.

Garin also said she has not heard of such a setup in a regular courtroom proceeding.

READ: Garin: VP Duterte requesting Senate to cover meal cost ‘improper, funny’

Aside from this, Garin said that the reason behind Duterte’s request may be offensive to the Senate, as there was an assumption that the meals from the Senate may be bad for them.

This is not the first time that Duterte’s requests for a caterer became an issue. Early into the impeachment trial, Duterte grabbed headlines not only because of the proceedings, but because OVP inquired about the possibility of bringing its own equipment, including a refrigerator and coffee maker, to the holding area assigned to the defense panel.

The request was made by OVP chief-of-staff and Undersecretary Zuleika Lopez, while the information about the request was provided by Senate Secretary and impeachment clerk of court Renato Bantug Jr.

World.title: Analyst: Visayas, Mindanao voters’ loyalty drove 2028 top bets’ survey lead
World.content:
From left, Vice President Sara Duterte, former President Rodrigo Duterte and Senator Christopher “Bong” Go (File photos)

MANILA, Philippines — A political science professor attributed the lead in a recent survey of top bets for the 2028 presidential, vice presidential and senatorial elections to the “loyalty” of some ethnic groups in Visayas and Mindanao.

It also pertains to the people’s connection to former President Rodrigo Duterte.

The results of a survey by polling firm Pulse Asia published on Wednesday showed Duterte’s daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, in the lead for the presidential race polling at 49 percent.

Article continues after this 

The same poll showed the former president’s aide-turned-senator – Christopher “Bong” Go – topping the vice presidential race at 27 percent; and vocal Duterte supporter Sen. Robin Padilla leading the senatorial race at 48.4 percent.

In an interview with the Inquirer on Thursday, University of the Philippines (UP) Diliman – Department of Political Science professor Jean Encinas-Franco pointed to Duterte’s hold on Visayas and Mindanao voters.

The Pulse Asia survey showed Duterte polling at 53 percent among Visayas voters and 87 percent among Mindanao voters, compared to 39 percent among National Capital Region (NCR) voters, and 31 percent among voters in Luzon outside Metro Manila.

“That tells you that there is somehow what we call the ethnolinguistic loyalty that Sara Duterte captures among the Visayans and those that are from Mindanao. I think it’s a big factor,” Franco explained.

READ: Sara Duterte, Bong Go top bets for president, VP in 2028, survey says

Article continues after this 

Rodrigo Duterte effect

The UP political science professor also pointed to Vice President Duterte’s fallout with President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. after their UniTeam alliance succeeded in the 2022 elections.

“UniTeam was powerful because they both have a legacy of strongman rule through former Presidents Ferdinand Marcos Sr. and Rodrigo Duterte. So, they both borrowed it from their fathers,” Franco said.

Article continues after this 

“But, when Marcos became president, people discovered that he was unlike his father. Then, their tandem fell apart. So, people who thought Marcos would be like his father would be more supportive of Sara Duterte,” she observed.

“Perhaps, in their minds, Sara Duterte has been consistent with what they expected of a politician, given that their narrative, the discourse in which they appreciate Sara Duterte, is still very much affected by how they look at Rodrigo Duterte,” she said.

Franco also attributed Go and Padilla’s leads in the surveys for the vice presidential and senatorial race to their association to the former president.

“It’s not so much because it is Bong Go. It is because of what Bong Go represents,” she said.

As for Padilla, she explained, “He’s very vocal about his support of the Dutertes, and also his support of the Dutertes is very much aligned with his celebrity appeal – action star, speaking like a regular guy.”

READ: ‘Broken from start’, UniTeam sees complete collapse

Vice President Duterte’s impeachment

Vice President Duterte is currently the subject of an impeachment trial in which she is accused of misusing public funds, amassing unexplained wealth, bribing Department of Education officials and threatening Marcos’ life.

Has the impeachment proceedings affected Duterte’s polling?

“It doesn’t reveal much about the impact of the impeachment trial, so that may be one explanation,” Franco said.

While the Duterte impeachment trial began last July 6, the Pulse Asia survey was conducted from June 28 to July 3 and July 6.

But, with only nine of the estimated 92 days in the impeachment trial passing so far, will the proceedings have any effect on Duterte’s lead?

“It’s difficult to speculate given the high numbers of VP Sara currently,” Franco replied.

“But, my sense is that, somehow, her popularity will be affected, especially when revelations about her bank records and the confidential funds will once again be revealed in the impeachment trial,” she said.

The political science professor also drew a stark comparison between Duterte’s impeachment trial and that of former President Joseph “Erap” Estrada due to the prevalence of social media now.

So, people can actually participate while the trial is ongoing even if they are not in the trial itself, even if they are not present in the plenary halls of the Senate.

“At the end of the day, if the prosecution presents the case against VP Sara as somehow reneging on her promise to better the lives of the Filipino people, somehow going against the strongman appeal, it’s very potent,” Franco pointed out.

“In the past, people, kind of, withdrew their support against politicians—not so much that they are corrupt—but if they see that this corruption led to a lifestyle that is very far from their own lifestyle,” she recalled. /apl

World.title: Kazakhstan Temporarily Reduces Oil Production Amid CPC Export Suspension
World.content:
15841

ASTANA — Kazakhstan has temporarily reduced oil production following the suspension of loading operations at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) marine terminal in the Black Sea, the Energy Ministry said on July 23.

Loading operations at the CPC marine terminal have been temporarily suspended to ensure the safety of vessels, crews and the environment in the Black Sea. All production and technical facilities of the consortium remain fully operational and are ready to resume crude oil shipments as soon as conditions normalize.

“Due to restrictions on oil intake into the pipeline system, oil-producing companies have made a controlled adjustment to daily production levels to prevent storage facilities from reaching capacity. The temporary reduction in oil output is a technological measure aimed at maintaining stable production processes,” reads the ministry’s statement.

The ministry said it is in contact with CPC management, major shippers, shipowners and relevant government agencies. Consultations are ongoing to ensure safe navigation and facilitate the prompt resumption of stable exports of Kazakh oil to global markets.

Reuters reported earlier that Kazakhstan’s oil production had declined following the closure of a Black Sea terminal serving as the country’s main export route for crude oil, which was recently targeted by drone attacks. According to industry sources cited by Reuters, the decline has been notably sharp at the Chevron-led Tengiz field, Kazakhstan’s largest oilfield.

Kazakhstan condemned the drone attacks on civilian vessels transporting oil through the CPC infrastructure on July 17 and 19, describing them as threats to international energy security.

World.title: Kazakhstan Allocates Over $22 Million for KazSat-3R Communications Satellite
World.content:
61722

ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s government has allocated 10.4 billion tenge (US$22.3 million) to begin developing the KazSat-3R communications satellite, which will replace the existing KazSat-3 spacecraft and ensure the uninterrupted operation of the country’s national satellite communications system.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov signed the corresponding resolution as part of the implementation of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s directive to strengthen Kazakhstan’s digital infrastructure and expand access to modern telecommunications services, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on July 23.

KazSat-3R will replace the current KazSat-3 satellite, whose planned operational life expires in 2029. The new spacecraft is intended to ensure continuity of national satellite communications services while supporting the long-term development of Kazakhstan’s telecommunications sector.

The project is expected to enhance the reliability of satellite communications and television broadcasting networks, expand internet access in sparsely populated and remote areas, strengthen information security and reinforce the country’s technological sovereignty.

The KazSat satellite system currently provides television broadcasting, data transmission, mobile communications and internet services. It is used by 19 domestic telecommunications operators and government agencies, serving more than two million television subscribers.

The satellite project forms part of broader efforts to modernize Kazakhstan’s digital infrastructure. Over the past two years, high-speed internet coverage has reached 99% of the population, including more than 4,500 rural settlements. Other initiatives include expanding fiber-optic networks in rural areas, implementing the Last Mile project, rolling out 5G, extending mobile coverage along highways and deploying modern satellite technologies.

More than 90% of public services are now available online, while the launch of national supercomputing capacity and the unified QazTech digital platform is intended to support the development of artificial intelligence and the digital economy.

According to the government, KazSat-3R, together with new Earth observation satellite projects, will strengthen Kazakhstan’s space industry and expand its technological capabilities.

World.title: IOC Recognizes Kazakhstan’s Olympic Team Preparation Model as International Best Practice
World.content:
53082

ASTANA – The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has recognized the National Olympic Committee (NOC) of Kazakhstan’s system for preparing Olympic delegations as a Best Practice and recommended it to other National Olympic Committees.

The IOC highlighted Kazakhstan’s Athlete and Team Official Agreements (ATOA), developed by the NOC to complement the IOC’s standard Conditions of Participation (CoP). The agreements are tailored to Kazakhstan’s national legislation and cover a broad range of legal, organizational and operational matters related to participation in the Olympic and Youth Olympic Games, the NOC said on July 22.

The IOC noted the introduction of four separate agreements for athletes, coaches and medical staff, media representatives, and other team officials. The documents establish standardized provisions governing the code of conduct, compliance with IOC regulations, financial terms, the use of personal social media during the Games, official uniform requirements and dispute resolution procedures.

According to the IOC, the agreements also reflect a multidisciplinary approach, drawing on the experience of previous Kazakh Olympic delegation leaders (Chefs de Mission) and contributions from the NOC’s sports, international relations, media, marketing and legal departments.

The IOC described Kazakhstan’s model as an effective example of integrating international standards and the Olympic Charter into national practice. It recommended it for adoption by other National Olympic Committees, recognizing Kazakhstan’s approach as an international best practice.

World.title: Kazakhstan Forms 82 Overseas Polling Stations for Kurultai Elections in August
World.content:
65009

ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry has announced on July 22 the composition of election commissions established at the country’s diplomatic missions abroad to organize voting in the elections of deputies to the Kurultai, scheduled for Aug. 23.

A total of 82 overseas polling stations have been formed at Kazakh embassies, consulates and permanent missions across Europe, Asia, the Middle East, North and South America, Africa and Oceania to ensure voting access for Kazakh citizens residing or staying abroad.

The ministry said the commissions were established in accordance with the Constitutional Law on Elections, the presidential decree calling the elections, and the Central Election Commission’s calendar plan for election preparations.

The published list includes the chairpersons, deputy chairpersons, secretaries and members of all precinct election commissions operating at Kazakhstan’s foreign missions. The measure is aimed at ensuring the openness, transparency and accessibility of the electoral process for citizens outside the country.

World.title: Kazakhstan Dominates Central Asia’s FDI Stock as Uzbekistan Gains Ground
World.content:
349622

ASTANA – Central Asia’s foreign direct investment (FDI) stock rose 3.6% to $235.5 billion in 2025, with Kazakhstan retaining roughly two thirds of the region’s total, according to the latest World Investment Report released by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD).

Kazakhstan accounted for nearly 66% of Central Asia’s total, solidifying its position as the region’s largest destination for foreign investment. The nation’s FDI stock, which refers to the accumulated value of FDI held in a country, stood at $156.4 billion as of 2025. It went up a little bit from $155.1 billion in 2024. In 2010, the figure was just $82.6 billion.

Uzbekistan, meanwhile, recorded the strongest annual increase from $20.5 billion in 2024 to $26 billion in 2025.

Kazakhstan was a major destination for newly announced large-scale investment projects. One of them relates to a non-ferrous metals project worth more than $12 billion announced by China’s East Hope Group. The report ranks it among the 10 largest greenfield projects announced in developing Asia during the year.

FDI inflows

In terms of FDI inflows, Central Asia received $4.97 billion in 2025, up 12.1% from $4.43 billion in 2024. This is a substantial fall compared to $9.8 billion that the region recorded in 2022.

According to the report, Uzbekistan drove Central Asia’s foreign investment recovery in 2025, attracting nearly $4.4 billion as inflows into Kazakhstan turned negative. Kazakhstan recorded net FDI outflows of $861 million in 2025, compared with net inflows of $227 million a year earlier.

The Kyrgyz Republic posted the region’s fastest percentage increase, with inflows more than doubling to $642 million. Tajikistan’s FDI inflows fell to $86 million, down 70% from $291 million.

According to the report, resource and infrastructure projects in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan featured prominently in the region’s investment activity and project pipeline.

“Investment activity was concentrated in metals and metal products, which together accounted for approximately 45% of total greenfield project activity in the region, followed by energy, transport and storage, chemicals, food processing, and ICT,” reads the report.

Global trends

While global FDI increased by 6% to $1.6 trillion in 2025, this recovery has been uneven and fragile. When excluding financial flows routed through Europe’s largest investment hubs, the increase narrows to 4%.

FDI inflows in developed economies increased by 11% to $723 billion, whereas developing economies received $901 billion in FDI, an increase of 2%.

The largest FDI destination in 2025 was the United States, which received $277 billion. It was also the largest source of FDI last year, followed by Japan and China.

The report indicates that investment activity is becoming more concentrated across regions and sectors.

“Semiconductors, electronics, AI infrastructure, data centres, renewable energy and battery supply chains continued to drive large projects. Project activity was concentrated in China, India, Kazakhstan, Malaysia and the United Arab Emirates, mainly in electronics, digital infrastructure and construction,” it said.

These industries accounted for 44% of global greenfield investment last year, growing from 16% in 2020. Kazakhstan is positioning itself to benefit from the same shift, with major investment plans spanning renewable energy, battery materials, data centers, AI infrastructure and advanced processing of metals and critical minerals, instead of relying solely on extractive industries.

Changing model

Expert Sultan Valikhanov echoes this point in his piece for the EconomyKZ analytical website, cautioning that the rise in global FDI should not be read automatically as a boom in new factories.

“For three decades, the formula was simple: production moved to where labor was cheaper and costs were lower. That allowed dozens of developing countries to join global supply chains and attract factories, logistics hubs and industrial clusters. Capital followed efficiency. The cheaper it was to produce, the greater the chance of attracting an investor,” Valikhanov wrote.

This model is now breaking down. He explained that part of last year’s increase came from intracorporate flows, restructuring and capital routed through international financial centers rather than the expansion of productive capacity.

“What matters, therefore, is not how much capital crossed borders, but where exactly it went,” Valikhanov added.

Stronger domestic capacity

“If most investment is flowing into digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing, the decisive advantage becomes a country’s ability to support such projects through reliable energy, transport links, engineering talent and a digital ecosystem built around production,” Valikhanov wrote.

That is particularly relevant to Kazakhstan. The headline figures tell only part of the story. What is important is whether that capital went to industries that are capable of generating local value, technology transfer and skilled employment.

UNCTAD also emphasized that countries need to make “deliberate national policy choices,” which among others include “realistic entry points” into changing value chains, and coordinating investment, jobs, supplier policies and infrastructure.

“This will also require renewed international cooperation, with partnerships that balance the resilience that investing countries expect with the development that recipient countries need,” said UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno.

Kazakhstan has increasingly treated trade and investment diplomacy as an instrument of industrial policy, not merely foreign relations. High-level diplomatic visits secure capital, technology, logistics links and access to new value chains. This logic shapes Kazakhstan’s ties with long-established strategic partners such as China and its engagement with newer partners.

“Today, investment follows strategic calculation and industrial policy marked by subsidies, economic security and technological advantage. Governments are competing with new investment policy measures, at a record high in 2025,” said Pedro Manuel Moreno.

He noted that the reshaping of global supply chains is creating opportunities for developing economies to become manufacturing bases, critical-mineral processing hubs and gateways to regional markets. In this context, Kazakhstan is trying to position itself in all three areas by developing transcontinental transport routes, expanding domestic processing of critical raw materials and investing in industrial, technological and skills capacity.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Use Digital Tenge Across Government Spending This August
World.content:
93620

ALMATY – Kazakhstan to begin using the digital tenge in public procurement from August after completing the integration of the digital currency platform with the Finance Ministry’s information systems, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on July 22.

The announcement followed a government meeting chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin, where officials reviewed progress on pilot projects testing the central bank digital currency and discussed challenges to its wider implementation.

According to the ministry, the legal status of the digital tenge platform and its operating procedures have now been established. A total of 340 billion digital tenge (US$626 million) has been issued, with 20 pilot projects completed, 10 underway, and 50 more in preparation.

Beginning in August, the digital tenge will be used for public procurement of goods, including medicines, fuel and lubricants, and other material supplies. Pilot projects cover infrastructure construction, budget lending and subsidies, grant financing, government support measures, public procurement, tax administration, as well as procurement by the National Bank and quasi-state entities.

The government has also introduced mandatory use of the digital tenge for eight categories of budget expenditures covering projects worth more than 100 million tenge (US$184,000).

Officials identified end-to-end traceability of public funds as one of the main challenges to expanding the project. According to the government, while digital tenge transactions can already be tracked from budget allocation to the main contractor, many subcontractors are not yet prepared to conclude smart contracts because current legislation does not require their use.

To address the issue, the ministry has prepared amendments to existing legislation that would establish the legal framework necessary for wider adoption of smart contracts and improve transparency throughout the public spending chain.

World.title: Almaty to Host Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 in September
World.content:
147842

ALMATY – The Central Asia Fintech Summit (CAFS) 2026 will take place in Almaty on Sept. 11, bringing together financial institutions, fintech companies, regulators, investors and technology leaders to discuss the future of digital finance in Central Asia.

Organized by the National Payment Corporation of Kazakhstan and the National Bank of Kazakhstan, the summit will take place at Tselinny Center of Contemporary Culture from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.

The event is expected to serve as one of the region’s leading platforms for dialogue on financial technologies, digital assets and the development of modern financial infrastructure.

The summit will bring together representatives of the banking sector, fintech firms, international organizations, technology companies, regulators, investors and industry experts to discuss emerging trends and opportunities shaping the regional financial ecosystem.

Building on the momentum of the 2025 edition, organizers say this year’s summit aims to further strengthen cooperation across the industry. Last year’s event marked a shift from a discussion platform to a mechanism for coordinating the fintech sector, resulting in the launch of digital asset initiatives and the signing of strategic industry agreements, including those related to QR payment infrastructure.

The 2025 summit attracted more than 4,000 participants, featured over 80 speakers, and welcomed delegates from more than 30 countries.

World.title: Kazakhstan Reports Record Ice Cream Production in June
World.content:
131740

ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s ice cream production more than doubled in June compared to the same month last year, reaching nearly 20,100 tons, according to new data released by the Bureau of National Statistics. The surge comes as the country’s dairy industry continues to expand, with ice cream among the fastest-growing product categories in the first half of 2026.

The latest figures complement the bureau’s earlier report showing that Kazakhstan’s overall dairy manufacturing output increased by 11.9% in the first six months of the year, driven primarily by strong growth in cheese, butter and ice cream production.

June’s production was 116% higher than a year earlier and almost doubled compared to May. It also exceeded the previous June average of the past five years by 2.5 times and surpassed the previous monthly record of 10,800 tons, set in July 2016, by 85%.

The sharpest increase was recorded in plombir ice cream, a rich, high-butterfat vanilla ice cream, with production reaching 10,200 tons, 3.6 times higher than in June 2025 and nearly three times more than in May. Cream ice cream production also expanded, rising 75% year-on-year and 57% month-on-month to 7,500 tons.

The value of production also increased sharply. Enterprises engaged in ice cream manufacturing produced goods worth 24.3 billion tenge (US$45.4 million) in June, approximately doubling both year-on-year and month-on-month.

The sector has maintained strong momentum since late 2024. Production volumes have recorded annual growth every month since then, averaging 32% year-on-year throughout 2025 and accelerating to around 60% so far in 2026.

According to the Agriculture Ministry, Kazakhstan also became a net exporter of ice cream for the first time in its history last year, with exports exceeding imports.

World.title: Armenian rights lawyer files ECHR complaint over Ruben Vardanyan’s 20-year jail sentence in Baku
World.content:
ECHR complaint over Vardanyan case

Human rights lawyer Siranush Sahakyan has filed a complaint with the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) over the case of Ruben Vardanyan, the former state minister of the former unrecognised Nagorno-Karabakh Republic. She said she would represent Vardanyan before the court. Sahakyan has represented Armenian detainees at the ECHR for many years.

“The application sets out in detail violations of eight articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, supported by comprehensive legal and factual arguments,” Sahakyan said in a statement shared with the media and posted on social media.

Vardanyan is one of 19 Armenians still held in Azerbaijani prisons. In February 2026, a military court in Baku sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

According to Sahakyan, the defence was only recently able to obtain the court’s written judgment, which was required before an application could be submitted to the ECHR. She said Azerbaijan had withheld the ruling until then, which is why the complaint was filed only on 19 July.

The court found Vardanyan guilty of a number of serious offences, including waging war, financing terrorism and deportation.

Armenian rights groups, however, have described the trial in Baku as “political rather than legal”. Vardanyan himself called the proceedings “a farce” and “a mockery of justice”. During the hearings, he instructed his lawyer not to present arguments in his defence.

“It is impossible to protect rights in a system that fundamentally denies the right to a fair trial. That is why Ruben Vardanyan decided to continue his fight for justice through international legal mechanisms,” Sahakyan said.

Details of Vardanyan case

In her statement, Sahakyan disclosed further details of the case. She said the military court in Baku did not read out the full verdict. Now that Vardanyan’s family has passed the written judgment to his lawyers, it has become clear that he was convicted on 41 counts under 21 articles of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code.

According to Sahakyan, the judgment does not substantiate Vardanyan’s personal criminal responsibility with facts or evidence.

“Instead, the court concluded that the ‘criminal organisation’ – the leadership of the self-proclaimed Republic of Artsakh – had been operating in Nagorno-Karabakh since 1988. It also found that Vardanyan joined this ‘organisation’ in December 2020, although he was living in Moscow at the time.”

She also said the court treated Vardanyan’s appointment to a civilian administrative post as a violent seizure of power. His commercial and charitable activities were classified as illegal entrepreneurship and financing terrorism, while his entry into Nagorno-Karabakh via the Lachin Corridor was deemed an illegal crossing of Azerbaijan‘s state border.

Sahakyan said Vardanyan had not appealed against the verdict because he regarded the trial as staged and pre-planned, and considered all domestic legal remedies ineffective.

Background

On 17 February, a military court in Baku sentenced Russian-Armenian businessman, billionaire and philanthropist Ruben Vardanyan to 20 years in prison. His case was heard separately from those of the former leadership of Nagorno-Karabakh.

A month after the verdict, Vardanyan’s family said he had tried to raise concerns with Azerbaijan’s Human Rights Commissioner, Sabina Aliyeva, during a phone call with relatives, but the call was cut off.

The family has repeatedly appealed to the international community, saying that neither Vardanyan nor the other Armenian detainees in Azerbaijan have access to institutional protection. They argue that the country lacks independent human rights protection mechanisms. They have also noted that the International Committee of the Red Cross, which had facilitated contact between detainees and their families, has ceased operations in Azerbaijan.

On 5 February, two weeks before Vardanyan’s sentence was announced, an Azerbaijani court handed life sentences to several other former Nagorno-Karabakh leaders, including former President Arayik Harutyunyan, former Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, his deputy Davit Manukyan, former parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and former Foreign Minister Davit Babayan. Former presidents Arkady Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan were sentenced to 20 years in prison.

All of the detainees faced a range of serious charges, including terrorism and genocide. Ghukasyan and Sahakyan received lighter sentences because they are over 65, and Azerbaijani law does not allow life imprisonment for people above that age.

Independent media and human rights observers were not allowed to attend the trials. Information about the proceedings was published by Azerbaijani state and pro-government media.

World.title: One minor killed, three injured in shooting in central Tbilisi
World.content:
Shooting in central Tbilisi

Late on July 22, four people, including two minors, were injured in a shooting on Vera, a central street in Tbilisi. All were taken to hospital. One of the minors died shortly after being admitted, Irakli Pirtskhalaishvili, a doctor at the clinic, told reporters.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry confirmed the incident, saying one person had been arrested in connection with it. The suspect has been charged with using a firearm and wounding four people.

He attempted to flee the scene but was detained after a police chase. According to the ministry, the suspect resisted arrest with a weapon and “sustained finger injuries during the arrest.”

The investigation is being conducted under Articles 19 and 109 of Georgia’s Criminal Code (attempted murder), which carry a penalty of up to 20 years in prison or life imprisonment.

Many witnesses to the shooting: what they say

The shooting took place in central Tbilisi, at the intersection of Akaki Shanidze and Akaki Khorava streets. The area was crowded at the time of the incident.

Eyewitness Elene Koridze wrote on social media that three young men sitting in a car “were shot simply because they were laughing.”

“About an hour ago, right outside my home, a man opened fire on three 17- and 18-year-old boys sitting in a car simply because they were laughing. He then also shot a woman who was nearby. He was quickly apprehended.

It was clear this was neither a premeditated attack nor an act of personal revenge. This is not just an isolated serious crime to which the police responded quickly, but a direct reflection of the reality we live in,” Koridze wrote.

Another eyewitness, Tiko Kvaliashvili, said:

“I was walking home when I saw a crowd on Shanidze Street and went over. Two patrol cars arrived, people started shouting, and someone was running. One boy was unconscious in the car, while two others were in shock. I gave them first aid as best I could. One had been shot in the arm, the other in the shoulder. I don’t know why they were shot.”

The son of journalist Eka Kvesitadze also witnessed the incident. She said it happened near their home while her son was out walking the dog.

“Someone had shot several minors. They were lying there covered in blood,” another witness wrote.

Witnesses also told reporters that a nearby parked red Alfa Romeo had around a dozen bullet holes.

As of now, Interior Ministry has not released any additional details.

World.title: Pro-EU protester Onise Okriashvili attacked in Tbilisi after disinformation campaign
World.content:
Georgia protester Onise Okriashvili beaten

Stand-up comedian Onise Okriashvili, an active participant in Georgia’s pro-European protests that have been ongoing for nearly two years, was brutally beaten by three people late on July 22 outside his home in Tbilisi’s Vake district.

Before the attack, Okriashvili had become the target of a disinformation campaign by pro-government media. Based on the context of the attack, this appears to have been the reason behind the assault.

A video of the attack, recorded by eyewitnesses, has spread on social media.

The footage shows three young men brutally beating Onise. “You insulted Nodar Dumbadze (a classic of Georgian literature), how dare you, bastard?” the attackers are heard saying to him.

Onise Okriashvili can be heard calling for help. Several people are nearby, but they do not dare approach him. The desperate screams of a woman trying to stop the attackers can also be heard.

Who is Onise Okriashvili and why did he become a target of propaganda?

Onise Okriashvili is known for his criticism of the ruling Georgian Dream party on social media. He also regularly organises solo protests aimed at drawing public attention — appearing with relevant posters in places where large numbers of people gather, including on public transport.

“Only their children study in Europe” — reads the sign held by Onise Okriashvili during one of his solo protests. Photo from the activist’s social media page

In recent days, the activist has become the target of a disinformation campaign by pro-government TV channels. They have repeatedly aired a fragment from a comedy show Punchline Therapy, in which he uses a vulgar expression while referring to Nodar Dumbadze, a classic of Georgian literature.

The fragment was shown without context, making it appear as if Okriashvili was directly insulting the writer.

On July 19, the comedian recorded a video in which he said:

“I apologise that in this video I am not talking about more important events in the country. Young people my age are dying every day because of drug use; there are political prisoners in the country; emigration is sharply increasing, and these emigrants have been deprived of the right to vote in elections, along with many other problems.

But for the third day now, Georgian Dream’s propaganda machine has been using all its resources to turn people against me. Here is an example of the video they are using to try to discredit me.“

The conversation in the video excerpt goes:

‘Is there someone you cannot stand?’ ‘What if I say Nodar Dumbadze? (vulgar expression) I will only name our government, no one else.’

“During a performance, we speak hypothetically and can say the most absurd thing that comes to mind at that moment.

This video clearly shows that I am, of course, not insulting (Nodar Dumbadze), but speaking only hypothetically, deliberately using the most absurd example that came to mind at that moment. Comedy often works exactly this way — it uses unexpected twists. That is why the audience laughs at that moment.”

“Just today we were discussing filing a lawsuit against the propaganda media for spreading defamatory claims, and today Onise was attacked,” his wife, Mariam Samushia, told journalists.

She said she heard shouting in the street in the evening. Since Onise had become a target of a propaganda campaign in recent days, she called him to warn him. Only later did she realise that her husband had been attacked.

“This is artificially created hatred,” she said.

The Interior Ministry said a criminal case had been opened over the attack on Onise Okriashvili under Article 126 of Georgia’s Criminal Code (violence). According to reports, one of the attackers has been taken to a police station and is being questioned.

News in Georgia

World.title: Chechnya’s recruitment machine: How Kadyrov sustains his forces by enlisting civilians
World.content:
Kadyrov’s Forces in Ukraine

An investigation by Novaya Gazeta Europe shows how the war has reshaped the system of power in Chechnya.

Ramzan Kadyrov has significantly expanded the number of armed units under his control. But his most loyal formations are largely kept away from the front lines.

Instead, combat losses are replenished with ordinary residents of the republic, who are often pressured into signing military contracts.

For the investigation, journalists interviewed 178 Chechen families who lost relatives in the war, as well as current and former servicemen. Their reporting examines how Chechnya’s recruitment system operates and reveals the true scale of its wartime losses.

Kadyrov’s forces

Over the course of the war, five new regiments and five battalions have been established in Chechnya. Formally, they are part of Russia’s Defense Ministry and the National Guard. In practice, however, Kadyrov determines key personnel appointments, where the units are deployed and how extensively they are involved in combat.

According to figures provided by Kadyrov, the number of security personnel in Chechnya has grown from 4,800 in 2003 to 36,243 today. At the start of 2022, before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, those forces numbered roughly 16,000 to 18,000. That means Chechnya’s security apparatus has approximately doubled in size over the course of the three-year war.

The human rights group Memorial argues that the expansion amounts to the strengthening of Kadyrov’s personal army. But a source in Chechnya’s regional office of the Federal Security Service offered a different explanation. According to the source, Kadyrov became trapped by the image of being “Putin’s chief foot soldier.” While he continued to create new units, he also sought to shield his most loyal security personnel from frontline combat.

At first, the authorities attracted recruits with high salaries. They then began actively recruiting people from other parts of Russia. Later, military service was opened to unemployed residents of Chechnya. As the flow of volunteers dwindled, the authorities increasingly turned to coercion.

The safe rear ended in the Kursk region

In 2023, Kadyrov secured the deployment of several Chechen units to the Russian border regions of Bryansk, Kursk and Belgorod. At the time, these areas were considered relatively safe rear positions, allowing Kadyrov’s forces to be pulled back from the most intense sections of the front.

That changed on Aug. 6, 2024, when Ukrainian troops crossed into the Kursk region. The Akhmat-Chechnya Regiment, which had been guarding the border, offered little visible resistance. Its personnel abandoned their positions, and some were surrounded and taken prisoner.

The border regions subsequently became the scene of heavy fighting involving the Akhmat special forces, the West Akhmat Battalion and the Akhmat-Chechnya Regiment. One Akhmat commander claimed that Apti Alaudinov’s unit alone suffered more than 1,500 killed and wounded.

Security forces are shielded, civilians sent to the front

After the fighting in the Kursk region, Kadyrov moved to reduce the involvement of key National Guard units in the war. Much of the burden was shifted instead to formations under Russia’s Defense Ministry.

Sources interviewed by the publication say the decision was driven by the need to preserve the foundations of Kadyrov’s rule. His grip on power depends on the loyalty of the republic’s security forces. A prolonged war depletes that resource faster than the Chechen leadership can replace it.

A telling example is the National Guard’s Baysangur Benoevsky Battalion. It is overseen by Adam Kadyrov, the 18-year-old son and presumed heir of the Chechen leader. The battalion has been equipped with modern weapons, its own training ground and a well-funded infrastructure. Its personnel signed contracts that предусматривают service in the war. Yet the unit has remained almost entirely in Chechnya, where it focuses on training.

Another National Guard unit, the Sheikh Mansur Battalion, was deployed to the front in December 2023 and has been engaged in combat ever since.

According to the investigation, the Baysangur Battalion is effectively financed with federal funds allocated for the war while serving as the Kadyrov family’s personal security reserve.

Coerced recruitment

Since the autumn of 2024, the Chechen authorities have carried out a large-scale campaign of forced recruitment. Kadyrov publicly proposed sending what he called “troubled youth” to the front. District police departments were then assigned monthly recruitment quotas of between 25 and 50 people.

Those detained are taken to collection centers in Sernovodsk and at the Khankala military base. According to testimonies from recruits and their relatives, they are held under guard, given inadequate food and receive little to no military training. Some are sent without proper uniforms or equipment, receiving weapons only after they reach the front.

People can be sent to the front for reasons as minor as a street fight, a traffic violation, driving without insurance, tinted car windows or unpaid utility bills. Others are detained for subscribing to opposition channels or for political posts found on their phones. In some cases, relatives are offered the chance to pay for a detainee’s release or to find other “volunteers” to take their place.

According to the journalists’ estimates, 67 such raids were carried out across Chechnya between October 2024 and May 2025.

Hidden casualties

The Chechen authorities prohibit the publication of information about those killed in the war. Families are often instructed to bury relatives at night and to forgo the traditional multi-day mourning rituals. As a result, publicly available casualty lists capture only a fraction of the true death toll.

Officially, around 500 residents of Chechnya have been confirmed killed. But a source in the republic’s government told the investigators that more than 2,300 deaths have been verified internally. Another roughly 1,000 people are listed as missing in action.

Of the 183 fatalities documented by the journalists, 113 were sent to the war after October 2024. Of those, 97 had signed military contracts under coercion. The average time between deployment and death was about two months. Only 84 of the 178 families interviewed were able to recover and bury the bodies of their relatives.

The investigation identifies a fundamental shift in Kadyrov’s approach. At the start of the war, he deployed members of the security forces while portraying those forcibly recruited as volunteers. Now, his most loyal units are kept inside Chechnya, while civilians are openly treated as expendable manpower.

The authors argue that this marks a troubling precedent. Repressive practices first tested in Chechnya have often, over time, spread to the rest of Russia.

exchange

World.title: Aliyev confirms secret Russia–Germany talks in Baku during Berlin visit, urges Europe to invest in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s Berlin briefing

At a joint press conference with Friedrich Merz in Berlin on 21 July, Ilham Aliyev appeared to be addressing three different audiences at once.

To Berlin, he signalled that Azerbaijan does not intend to serve as a venue for other countries’ secret diplomacy. To Brussels, he argued that if Europe wants more Azerbaijani gas, it should also help finance pipelines and interconnectors. And to Moscow and Kyiv, Aliyev sought to demonstrate that Baku remains committed to its multi-vector foreign policy while insisting on setting its own rules.

A strategic agenda signed later that day formally enshrined this political course.

Secret meeting in Baku: what is known and what remains speculation

According to Aliyev, after The Times published its report, the Azerbaijani authorities checked records held by the State Border Service and confirmed that Ronald Pofalla and Matthias Platzeck arrived in Baku from Berlin on 12 July and left on 14 July. During the same period, Viktor Zubkov and Valery Fadeyev flew to Baku from Moscow.

Aliyev said Azerbaijan had received no prior notification from either Germany or Russia and that “Azerbaijan’s territory was used without the knowledge of the authorities”. He stressed that Baku had no confirmed information about the substance of the meeting, but said the travel records suggested that such a meeting could have taken place. He added that if its purpose had been to help end Russia’s war against Ukraine, Azerbaijan could only welcome such efforts.

Merz, for his part, denied any involvement by the German government, saying he had no knowledge of such a meeting.

Investigations by German media describe the contacts as an informal continuation of the Petersburg Dialogue. According to ARD/RBB and Die Zeit, Baku has hosted unofficial meetings since 2024 between former German politicians and figures close to Vladimir Putin.

RBB reported that German security agencies view the meetings as a possible Russian influence operation. Roderich Kiesewetter, a member of the CDU, described them as “shadow diplomacy” that undermines Germany’s position on Ukraine.

At the same time, some participants and their supporters argue that channels of dialogue should remain open even during periods of heightened tensions.

Ukrainian sources have raised a different concern: if the discussions were about the war in Ukraine, why was Ukraine itself not represented at the table? That question remains unanswered, and any conclusions at this stage remain speculative.

Russia’s response

Moscow’s initial reaction was predictable and came in the form of a warning. Alexander Tolmachyov, a member of Russia’s State Duma, told Lenta.ru that Baku was “following Armenia’s path”, arguing that closer ties with Europe had brought neither Ukraine nor Armenia success.

That prompted a sharp response in an article published by Minval.az. The author argued that Azerbaijan had never accepted Moscow’s vision of a “big brother”, had chosen not to join the CSTO, and had consistently pursued a multi-vector foreign policy. In the author’s view, the strategic partnership with Germany does not represent “turning away from Russia” but rather reflects a pragmatic approach. Notably, Baku has framed the issue not in defensive terms but as its sovereign right to make its own decisions.

Other assessments have been more nuanced. German critics view the meetings in Baku as evidence of weaknesses in Berlin’s Russia policy and an attempt to revive old German-Russian political ties.

A different perspective emerges in analyses by the Kyiv Post and the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. They argue that while Baku continues to support Ukraine’s territorial integrity and expand cooperation with Kyiv, it has not completely severed channels of communication with Moscow, seeking instead to preserve room for diplomatic manoeuvre.

Taken together, the Berlin briefing suggested not so much a decisive “pivot to the West” as a policy of careful balancing. Azerbaijan’s energy interests are increasingly tied to Europe, its security calculations continue to take Russia into account, and its stated position remains grounded in support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity.

Call for investment in gas infrastructure

The second major theme of the Berlin briefing attracted less controversy but carried greater strategic significance. Aliyev announced that Azerbaijan had begun supplying natural gas to Germany this year. Under a ten-year contract, initial deliveries amount to around 1.5 billion cubic metres annually. However, he said any increase in volumes would depend on two factors: additional purchase commitments and expanded infrastructure.

According to Aliyev, both the TANAP and TAP pipelines are already operating at full capacity, leaving no spare transit capacity. Expanding infrastructure within Europe and building new interconnectors will therefore require additional investment. He singled out the European Investment Bank’s decision to stop financing oil and gas projects under the EU’s green transition policy as one of the key obstacles.

The ten-year gas supply agreement between SEFE and SOCAR reinforces this trend. In June, Germany’s ambassador to Azerbaijan, Ralf Horlemann, said contracts signed by German companies provide for annual imports of around 2 billion cubic metres of Azerbaijani gas.

The political message was clear: Baku is urging Europe to help finance the expansion of gas infrastructure. Merz likewise stressed that Germany has a strong interest in diversifying its gas imports.

The scope for increasing gas deliveries to Europe via the Southern Gas Corridor now depends less on political declarations than on whether European countries are willing to invest in new infrastructure. The contradiction is evident: Europe needs additional gas supplies to strengthen its energy security, yet remains reluctant to finance gas projects as part of its green transition agenda.

Declaration on a Strategic Partnership

The Joint Declaration on the Strategic Agenda of the Bilateral Partnership between the Republic of Azerbaijan and the Federal Republic of Germany, signed on 21 July, is a wide-ranging document drafted in technical language.

It outlines cooperation across a broad spectrum of areas, including high-level political dialogue and diplomatic consultations; the German-Azerbaijani High-Level Working Group on Trade and Investment; energy cooperation, including natural gas supplies; renewable energy; low-carbon hydrogen; energy efficiency; transport connectivity and infrastructure; security and defence; humanitarian demining; as well as culture, education, science and innovation.

The declaration also reaffirms Germany’s support for the normalisation of relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia and for peace initiatives launched after the Washington summit on 8 August 2025. It further highlights the “strategic importance” of the partnership between Azerbaijan and the European Union.

What does it mean?

First, the agreement formally elevates relations between Azerbaijan and Germany to the level of a strategic partnership.

Second, Baku is signalling that its cooperation with Germany extends well beyond natural gas. The agenda also includes renewable energy, transport and logistics, industrial modernisation, science and innovation.

Third, Berlin appears to be viewing the South Caucasus not only through the lens of values and norms, but increasingly in terms of energy security and transport connectivity.

In other words, the declaration is more than a symbolic political statement. It provides a framework for expanding German-Azerbaijani cooperation and institutionalising the European dimension of Azerbaijan’s foreign policy.

Ilham Aliyev’s Berlin briefing

World.title: Georgia jails opposition TV host for 14 days over Facebook posts
World.content:
Arrests over social media posts in Georgia

On 22 July 2026, the Tbilisi City Court sentenced journalist and Formula TV host Vakho Sanaia to 14 days of administrative detention over posts he published on Facebook. The ruling was handed down by Judge Zviad Tsekvava.

The case against Sanaia was launched over Facebook posts about Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and MP Vladimer Bozhadze. Bozhadze has represented the European Socialists party since 2025, although he entered parliament on the ruling Georgian Dream party list following the 2024 parliamentary elections.

The Hate Speech Department, established within the Ministry of Internal Affairs, referred the case to Tbilisi City Court for legal review.

Following an investigation by the department, Sanaia was fined 6,000 lari on 10 July.

In the post that led to the fine, Sanaia wrote: “I hope no one called [Vladimer Bozhadze] d**k, because the law prohibits calling Lado d**k. I would also like to urge everyone not to call Lado a d**k.”

After being fined, Sanaia published another post of a similar nature on social media: “I wrote a post saying, ‘Don’t call Papuashvili and Bozhadze d**k,’ and I was fined 6,000 lari. Am I missing something? Give them a call.”

On 18 July, Sanaia said the court had contacted him over the post and informed him that a hearing had been scheduled in his case.

Sanaia did not attend the court hearing.

“I’m laughing,” he wrote on social media after news emerged that he had been sentenced to administrative detention.

Brief overview of the department

Administrative cases over opinions expressed in the public sphere are initiated on the basis of reports compiled by the Hate Speech Department, which was established within the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

The new department has been operating since 1 June.

Its mandate is to monitor and identify public statements that violate human dignity, contain insults or elements of hate speech, where they may constitute an administrative offence.

According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, between the department’s launch and 2 July, it identified 170 alleged offences, 150 of which were referred to court.

Of those 150 cases, rulings had been issued in 33 by that date. Thirty-one people were fined, while two received verbal warnings. Most of those fined were activists. Vakho Sanaia became the first journalist to be fined on the basis of a report compiled by the department.

АArrests over social media posts in Georgia

World.title: Russia destroyed 40,000 Armenian roses shipped via Belarus
World.content:
Russia destroys Armenian roses

Officials from Russia‘s agricultural watchdog Rosselkhoznadzor in Smolensk Region discovered a shipment of freshly cut roses from Armenia that was being transported via Belarus.

According to the Belarusian outlet Euroradio, the shipment was deemed illegal because Russia has banned the import of nearly all Armenian goods since the spring.

Armenian roses imported via Belarus / 32.fsvps.gov.ru

Moscow says the import ban was imposed in response to what it described as violations of phytosanitary requirements. However, the restrictions were introduced after Armenia declared EU integration as a foreign policy goal, leading officials in Yerevan and the EU to view the move as politically motivated.

Russia has previously imposed similar trade restrictions on Georgia and Moldova to exert economic pressure amid political disagreements.

According to the accompanying documents, the lorry travelling from Belarus’s Minsk Region to Moscow was carrying non-alcoholic carbonated energy drinks. However, an inspection found 39,200 roses instead.

The flowers were being transported without the required phytosanitary certificates or shipping documents.

Rosselkhoznadzor said some of the boxes still bore labels identifying Armenia as the country of origin.

The roses were destroyed, while the carrier was held administratively liable.

Russia suspends flower imports from Iran over suspected re-exports from Armenia

Shortly after the reports emerged that Armenian roses transported via Belarus had been destroyed, Russia’s agricultural watchdog Rosselkhoznadzor suspended the certification of flowers for export to Russia from Iran, also over suspicions that they had been re-exported from Armenia.

The agency said flower shipments from Iran in 2026 had significantly exceeded the volume recorded during the same period last year.

Rosselkhoznadzor also said that although Iran was listed as the exporting country, the appearance of the flowers and their packaging were identical to products previously supplied from Armenia.

Background

Since early spring 2026, Russia has gradually introduced restrictions on Armenian products.

Initially, the measures targeted Jermuk mineral water, followed by a range of alcoholic beverages.

On 30 May, Russia banned imports from Armenia of tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, herbs and strawberries.

This was followed by a temporary ban imposed by the Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (Rosselkhoznadzor) on the import of flowers and ornamental plants from Armenia.

Rosselkhoznadzor has also reported problems with imports of certain livestock products, as well as fish and fish products.

Armenia also received a letter from Russia warning of the possible termination of an agreement on supplies of natural gas, petroleum products and rough diamonds.

The restrictions imposed by Russia are significant for Armenia, as the Russian market has been the main destination for Armenian agricultural exports for decades.

The Armenian authorities are currently working, with active support from the European Union, to rapidly open alternative export markets for Armenian products.

World.title: Armenia begins recruiting and training border guards for Azerbaijan border
World.content:
Armenia launches border guard recruitment

The Armenian government plans to gradually transfer responsibility for guarding the entire Armenia-Azerbaijan border from the Defense Ministry to the Border Guard Troops of the National Security Service (NSS).

To make that possible, the agency needs additional personnel. The government therefore plans to expand the NSS by introducing the “I Have the Honor“ programme, which the Defense Ministry already runs successfully.

Under the programme, university students sign a contract to undergo military training while completing their studies. After graduation, they perform their military service at the location and under the conditions specified in the contract.

Under the new proposal, participants will first serve as conscripts in the rank of private in Defense Ministry units. They will then transfer to the NSS as commissioned officers.

“The new mechanism will help strengthen the National Security Service, particularly the Border Guard Troops, by recruiting personnel with higher education,” the explanatory note to the draft says.

Under an intergovernmental agreement signed in 1992, the Russian Federal Security Service’s Border Guard Service has been responsible for guarding Armenia’s borders with Turkey and Iran. In recent years, however, Armenia has steadily moved to place the protection of its borders entirely under its own control. In 2024, Russian border guards withdrew from Zvartnots International Airport and from border areas along the frontier with Azerbaijan. On January 1, 2025, Russian border guards also left the border crossing on the Armenia-Iran frontier. Then, on March 1, Armenia’s National Security Service assumed sole responsibility for guarding the Margara border crossing with Turkey. Since the beginning of 2026, only Armenian border guards have been serving at the Akhurik border crossing on the Armenia-Turkey border.

Deferring military service during university in exchange for serving as an officer

The “I Have the Honor” programme allows students to defer compulsory military service while at university. In return, they commit to serving later as commissioned officers.

“Students attend university free of charge, with the state covering tuition fees in full at the rate set by the university for the relevant programme.”

After graduating from university and completing the required military training, participants receive the rank of lieutenant and begin contract service.

Officers receive their assignments through a lottery system.

Those trained as platoon commanders serve for two years and three months.

Those trained for military medical service serve for four years after graduation, followed by one year of clinical residency.

What other changes does the draft propose?

The legislative package also includes amendments to several laws governing military service, the National Security Service’s Border Guard Troops, and the country’s national security agencies.

In particular, the draft would clearly define the circumstances in which NSS officers may use firearms, special equipment and physical force.

Before using force, officers would have to issue a warning and allow enough time for a person to comply with a lawful order, unless any delay posed an immediate danger. The draft also requires officers to use force proportionately to the level of resistance or threat. They would also have to provide first aid to anyone injured.

If parliament passes the legislative package, border guards will also be able to use video and audio recording devices while carrying out their duties.

The draft would also raise the retirement age for senior NSS officers from 52 to 55.

Armenia launches border guard recruitment

World.title: Billions in new funding for AUKUS shipyards in Adelaide
World.content:
The shipyards that will construct Australia's fleet of AUKUS nuclear-powered submarines have been handed a $4.6 billion funding boost.

The additional investment will help further develop the new Submarine Construction Yard at Adelaide's Osborne shipyards.

The announcement, to be made on Friday, comes on the sidelines of the ALP's 50th National Conference in Adelaide which appears set to avoid a public debate over the AUKUS pact.

Billions of dollars in state and federal funding are going into the shipyards to prepare for the submarine construction project, with the first AUKUS-class submarine to be delivered in the early 2040s.

This funding boost comes on top of $3.9 billion already announced for the commonwealth Australian Naval Infrastructure shipyards earlier this year.

Two AUKUS submarine optimal pathways Scrutiny of AUKUS's delivery reveals two "optimal pathways" for Australia's submarines.

Australian Naval Infrastructure is a commonwealth-owned company.

Under AUKUS, five nuclear-powered submarines will be constructed at Osborne, on top of the three Virginia-class submarines being acquired from the United States.

Construction on Australia's fleet of Hunter Class frigates is already underway, but the new submarine shipyards are expected to be 10 times the size of the existing precinct.

The development includes the construction of a 420-metre-long fabrication hall, along with outfitting, consolidating and commissioning precincts within the yard.

The government is seeking to highlight the jobs that will be created during construction, with 1,100 people already employed on the site and thousands more expected in South Australia.

Peter Malinauskas has highlighted the scale of the project. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the funding was another step on the path towards making the AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine program a reality.

"This investment is another important step in building the sovereign capability Australia will need to build, operate, maintain and sustain our future submarine fleet," he said.

"The work underway right now at Osborne demonstrates that AUKUS is on track and happening now, all while creating opportunities for Australian industry and workers for decades to come."

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said it was an enormous undertaking.

"It is difficult to comprehend the scale of the billions of dollars of investment being delivered at Osborne to enable us to build the most complex machines on the planet," he said.

Construction underway across the country

This funding announcement brings the total volume invested into the Osborne shipyards under AUKUS to $8.5 billion in taxpayer funds.

But that funding is still dwarfed by other AUKUS projects, including the $12 billion announced for the Henderson shipyards in Western Australia last year.

Henderson will maintain the Virginia Class submarines Australia will operate from the 2030s, along with AUKUS submarines.

This new multi-billion-dollar funding announcement comes as Labor's national conference takes place in Adelaide.

Australia is expected to operate the US Navy's Virginia-class submarines from the 2030s. (Supplied: US Department of Defense)

While AUKUS was publicly debated at Labor's last national conference three years ago, it appears unlikely to flare up at this year's conference.

Despite some concerns over the pact within parts of Labor's rank-and-file membership, and Labor MP Ed Husic calling for the pact to be renegotiated, the conference appears to be set to avoid another public discussion of AUKUS.

That has caused dismay among some of the pact's most vocal opponents, like former Labor minister Peter Garrett, who is leading a "public inquiry" into AUKUS at present.

"This week's Labor conference in Adelaide — one of the key locations for AUKUS, as it happens — looks unlikely to accommodate any meaningful debate on the issue," he said in a piece for Guardian Australia.

"This is a great pity."

World.title: Netball agents frustrated as pay talks roll into Glasgow 2026
World.content:
Has netball learned much since 2023? You be the judge.

The messy and drawn-out pay negotiations that dominated headlines during that World Cup year are once again overshadowing a major tournament for the sport.

The Diamonds are aiming to defend gold at the Commonwealth Games, and that mission starts on Saturday night in their opening match against Tonga at 8pm AEST. But the world number one team hit the court in Glasgow with uncertain futures.

The current Super Netball collective player agreement (CPA) expires on September 30, meaning all 88 players will be off contract. It is a chaotic way of doing things and leads to a mad scramble for everyone involved, with so many trying to secure opportunity at the same time.

Netball Australia surrenders, as players win long and bitter pay war Netball Australia has finally agreed to a modest revenue share partnership with its players, but how much have its brutal tactics throughout the pay negotiations damaged the game?

The 2027 signing window was supposed to open the Monday after the grand final on July 4. That has been delayed a month so the athletes can focus on their international duties while the terms of the next deal are worked through.

There are several sticking points that the national sporting organisation and the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA) cannot agree on. More on that later.

It is important to note that ANPA provided a detailed submission late last year to try and get the ball rolling. Netball Australia wanted to wait and sort out its new broadcast agreement with Nine, which underwrites the majority of the costs of the CPA first. That was done in April.

Although from the sport's point of view, discussions are more respectful and constructive this time, with greater transparency of information shared amongst parties, the players are incredibly frustrated. And so are their agents, who argue they are unable to make meaningful progress on behalf of their talent.

There is no prohibition to hold non-binding conversations with your own club or another right now, yet a request to allow non-binding written offers while CPA talks take place was denied. The agents believe this would've freed up the system and given players more certainty.

Kathryn Deiulioi is the founder of Behind Your Brand, which manages several Diamonds athletes, including the Australian captain. (Image Supplied)

Kathryn Deiulio, the founder of Behind Your Brand, said it was her understanding that the Diamonds players did not ask the sport to push back the contracting window and wanted discussions to continue. There are concerns this kind of assumption could create a divide amongst the group, positioning some as more important than others.

"This misunderstanding creates the impression that they didn't consider the impact it could have on the remaining 60-70 players not playing at the Games," Deiulio told ABC Sport.

"It is our role to continue contract negotiations on their behalf, and it would have created an additional layer of complexity, given the time difference and the need to carefully manage communication with players so as not to distract them from their performance.

"However, ultimately, that is part of our role as agents and something we are equipped to manage … These are professional athletes who dedicate their lives to their sport, and they deserve the same level of security around employment expected in any other profession."

Australia won gold at the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham. (Getty: Sue McKay)

Jace Bode is the chief executive of W Sports & Media, which works across a range of elite codes, such as cricket, Aussie Rules, football, golf and tennis.

"The fact that 80-plus athletes have once again been put in this position is incredibly disappointing and challenging to manage from our perspective," Bode told ABC Sport.

"We have the best netball competition in the world, and it is frustrating to watch these athletes continue to navigate uncertainty around their careers when it has so much potential."

This CPA will only be a 12-month deal, allowing Netball Australia to try and bring in more revenue from 2027 onwards with the free-to-air broadcast agreement and present a stronger offer. But both agents worry that without a longer CPA in place we may be right back here next year, ahead of a World Cup on home soil.

The Diamonds players have been in camp since Friday July 10. (Supplied: Netball Australia)

According to the new dates, contracts will open for clubs' own players from August 4-16. Non-binding written offers are permitted for all players during these 12 days. Then, from August 17-28, contracting officially opens for those looking to switch allegiances.

The agents argue this process favours those who intend to remain at their existing club, while placing players who may be looking elsewhere at a significant disadvantage. The time frame is also not ideal for those weighing up their options overseas, with the English Superleague contracting window already in full swing.

Complicating things further, in other sports it is normally the responsibility of the governing body to handle CPA talks with the players' association, but here the clubs appear to have taken greater control of the wheel.

All eight Super Netball franchises are likely to have competing ideas slowing progress further, and it is unclear if their vested interests will be prioritised over what is best for the sport as a whole.

Shimona Nelson represents Jamaica at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games. (Getty: Mark Kolbe)

The delay has wide-reaching implications beyond the Australian team at the Games.

In-form Melbourne Mavericks star Shimona Nelson had already flagged with Netball Jamaica that she would be unavailable for selection for Glasgow ahead of the Super Netball season. The goal shooter needs to get her tonsils removed and deal with a knee issue.

Although the Sunshine Girls did try and get her to change her mind, an appearance at the major tournament would be risky. Should she injure herself, with only one-year contracts being offered, where would that leave her?

It makes sense that Nelson has put herself first, considering the history of her career. After the Collingwood team disbanded, Nelson had to forge her way back into the league as a No.11 player with the Mavericks, working hard to return to a full-time contract the next season.

It is unfair that athletes are being forced to make these tricky decisions based on what is happening in Super Netball, and what is right for each of them is extremely individual.

Shimona Jok keeping an open mind as 11th player signing confirms she's eligible for Diamonds Super Netball import Shimona Jok was in the headlines after the Mavericks found a loophole to sign her as their 11th player. But now her eligibility for the Diamonds has been confirmed, would she ever go there?

There has been a rumour that Nelson isn't playing because she instead wants to represent the Diamonds at the next World Cup.

Nelson indeed plans to get her citizenship in September, purely to cement her status in a country she has lived in for almost 10 years and now classes as home.

At this point, there have been no discussions between the Australian camp or Shimona's about the possibility of her playing for the Diamonds.

So, what are some of the sticking points of the CPA talks?

Currently on the table is a 25 per cent pay increase for those on the minimum wage and a three per cent pay increase for everyone else.

This all sounds rosy until you do the numbers. Australia's consumer price index sits at four per cent. Once these changes are factored into the salary cap, with increased superannuation contributions and the rising cost of living, the take-home pay for many of the athletes could actually be worse off than they were this year. It may lead to a pay cut in real terms.

Former Thunderbird and Diamond Kathryn Harby-Williams is the chief executive of the players' association. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Despite this, the sport will continue to restrict player opportunities to make extra cash in sponsorship deals. The cap for commercial arrangements with an existing team sponsor or partner is going to be raised to $50,000 but the agents want the cap removed entirely.

There are no monetary limits on a player's commercial agreements with third parties, but agents find the amount of compliance their talent must go through to get approval is unreasonable and leads to sponsors turning to athletes from other codes.

"When athletes are able to work with brands and authentically leverage their own platforms, they bring different eyeballs to the sport … This should be viewed as a positive, not a threat," Bode and Deiulio said.

"If netball does not evolve in this increasingly competitive female sports landscape, these limitations will have a broader impact on its growth and visibility."

World.title: Death toll climbs after flooding in India, Afghanistan and Pakistan
World.content:
At least 82 people have died in 72 hours after heavy rain and flash flooding began sweeping through India, Pakistan and Afghanistan.

More than 650,000 people have been affected across 11 districts in the Indian state of Assam, according to the state's disaster management authority.

Local authorities said at least 10 people had died in the past 24 hours, taking the death toll in India to 36.

At least 46 people have been killed and more than 100 people injured across Afghanistan and Pakistan, according to disaster management authorities in both countries.

The extent of damage in some parts of Afghanistan is undetermined. (AP Photo: Wahidullah Kakar)

The Nuristan governor's office confirmed one of the district mayors, Sayed Ahmad Arhabi, had died in the floods.

Infrastructure damage

The Afghanistan National Disaster Management Authority said the water had caused an undetermined number of buildings to collapse.

The provincial capital city of Parun, in India, was among the areas affected, authorities said.
