World.title: Brisbane’s best cafes & bakeries (on the north side) in 2026
World.content:
Eating outFood Brisbane’s best cafes & bakeries (on the north side) in 2026 Our city’s cafes aren’t what they used to be. They’re better. From internationally known CBD coffee spots to expansive suburban cafes, here’s what you need to tick off. Matt Shea July 23, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What a difference a decade makes – particularly with a pandemic tossed in the middle. Brisbane’s cafe scene used to be dominated by full-service venues – places with a broad menu and a traditional ordering system. But COVID changed the game. These days it’s more about doing one or two things and doing them well, whether it’s coffee, sandwiches, baked goods or matcha. Don’t get us wrong: there are still great cafes in the traditional sense, but we’re living in the age of hyper-specialised venues, fancy bakeries and chef-run sandwich shops. But that just makes the AM dining and drinking scene all the more interesting. It also makes it harder to parse what’s worth your attention. Because in 2026 the tiniest coffee window could easily be making the best coffee.



So instead of rounding up the 60 best cafes in Brisbane, we’ve split it in two. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Next week, it will be everything south of the river. But this week, here are the 30 essential cafes, coffee spots, bakeries and sandwich shops in Brisbane’s north. Coffee Anthology and Fika Adam Wang’s Coffee Anthology is the yardstick by which all other

specialty coffee in this city is judged. Outside the Charlotte Street venue. Markus Ravik



Last year, it was ranked the eighth-best coffee shop in the world. Why? Because Wang presents the best roasters from around the country across espresso, filter and batch brew, with few compromises on technique or equipment. Since moving to Charlotte Street in 2022 it’s become part of the Intersection precinct, which also includes Fika, a slick full-service cafe that serves an elevated

Asian-inflected brunch. Good to know: Wang’s superb tilt at a roastery cafe, The Maillard Project, is located a few doors down the road. 155 Charlotte Street, Brisbane, intersectionfd.com.au Kin You know Kin. It’s the one with the coffee window beneath the heritage-

listed Australian Estates Woolstore building that draws Teneriffe’s bright

young things every morning, waiting patiently for their takeaway

Almanac coffee.



Kin serves elevated breakfasts in a beautiful dining room beneath a heritage-listed woolstore. But you need to sit down in Kin to truly understand its virtues: it’s in the brief but brilliant menu (dippy eggs with 24-month aged Valserena parmigiano reggiano, say, or a pad kra pao jaffle with makrut lime mayonnaise), the beautiful, homey dining room with its warm timber furnishings, and owners Tim and Allison MacIntyre’s hospitality, which is precise but genuine. A modern Brisbane classic. Good to know: Kin’s also a go-to for some of the best matcha in town. 24 Macquarie Street, Teneriffe, bykinbne.com Bellissimo



Australia’s most highly awarded coffee roaster hasn’t closed for a single

day since it opened in this Wandoo Street warehouse in January 2011. Outside Bellissimo Fortitude Valley. And more punters flock than ever before: for the exceptional specialty coffee, sure, but also a brunch menu that is perhaps better than it has any right to be. Bellissimo’s other outlets, in Coorparoo and Bulimba, are by now more well-rounded venues, but Wandoo Street remains the brand’s spiritual home. Good to know: Bellissimo’s breakfast burger is an unheralded contender for Brisbane’s best. 30 Wandoo Street, Fortitude Valley, bellissimocoffee.com.au





John Mills Himself All of Marcus Allison’s venues are worth your time: Anytime Coffee,

Bessa and Bunker Coffee. John Mills Himself can be found down an alleyway in the Brisbane CBD Michelle Smith But it’s John Mills Himself that makes this list on account of its unique digs (which, considering Bunker, is saying something) in an old print shop right in the guts of the city. That hidden setting, with its exposed brick, vintage lights and mosaic tile floor, will get the seekers through the door; the specialty coffee sourced from different roasters around the country does the rest. Good to know: The address is Charlotte Street but it’s easier to find via

Elizabeth – look for the laneway next to Thai on Time.



40 Charlotte Street, Brisbane, instagram.com/johnmillshimself Sprout Artisan Bakery One of Brisbane’s best bakeries is all grown up with this beautiful light-filled cafe on Skyring Terrace. Grab a seat inside. Morgan Roberts Also new is a short, sharp brunch menu that elegantly touches up the classics. What hasn’t changed is baker and co-owner Lutz Richter’s precisely folded and shaped seasonal fruit Danishes, berry croissant baskets, double chocolate croissant buns, cardamon custard scrolls and so much more. Espresso and specialty coffee comes via New Zealand’s Coffee Supreme.



Good to know: Yes, Richter and co-owner Rebecca Foley still maintain a presence at the Saturday Fresh Market in Rocklea. Shop 4/60 Skyring Terrace, Newstead, sproutartisanbakery.com.au Idle Agnes Bakery’s successor has everything that made it such a pandemic-era hit: the fire-licked sourdough loaves, Basque cheesecakes, caneles, kouign-amanns and so on – but also an all-day menu more imaginative than most around town, with daily salads and sandwiches added to the mix from 10am. Idle in New Farm. Markus Ravik



Coffee is by Sydney’s Single O and, of course, this is an Anyday venue so you know it looks a million dollars. Good to know: Part of the new(ish) Little Lane precinct, Idle’s neighbours include RUMA Rooftop, Green Cup and Johnny Gio Pizza. 84 Merthyr Road, New Farm, anyday.com.au/idle-venue-page Kosta’s Takeaway Benji Terkalas brought his viral, pandemic-era Sydney sandwich shop north in March, opening a tiny terracotta-tiled counter operation at Gasworks Plaza.



Schnitty sandwich. Morgan Roberts Onboard for its debut menu was star chef Adam Wolfers, whose influence shines in two sandwiches in particular: a chicken shawarma, and a breakfast yiros built with bifteki, egg and cheese. Otherwise, the breakfast and lunch menu covers sandwiches, toasties, focaccias, wraps and a pair of salads, with everything – other than the bread – made in-house. Coffee is by Canberra-based superstar

roaster Ona. Good to know: Yes, Kosta’s Instagrammable Schnitty sandwich is present and correct. 76 Skyring Terrace, Newstead, kostastakeaway.com Emme



Tommy Tze Lian’s restaurant that opened early has evolved into more of a breakfast cafe that finishes late. Emme on James Street. It’s in the morning that it absolutely heaves with customers, split between its handsome, stone-finished interior and a breezy dining island out front. But the care and precision of its woodfired dinner is reflected in breakfast dishes that include potatoes and eggs with cumin, fried garlic and chilli oil, and wagyu pastrami tartine with Russian sauce, pickles and a poached egg. A contender for

Brisbane’s best all-day dining spot right now. Good to know: Emme’s all-day dining means it serves it serves coffee to

the James Street massive until 3.30pm. Shop B03, 22 James Street, Fortitude Valley, emmejamesst.com



Baker D. Chirico Almost every weekend since its 2024 Brisbane debut, Melbourne-born

Baker D. Chirico has had queues out the door. Inside Baker D. Chirico’s Newstead outlet. Tammy Law Locals and interlopers come for the sourdough (made using a 25-year-old starter), bombolini and maritozzi, of course. But there’s also a greater focus here on savoury sandwiches, rolls and croissants. The shop itself is a striking evolution of the Carlton original’s “breadbasket” design, with a curved timber ceiling and reams of white terrazzo on the floors. Good to know: As of last week, Baker D. Chirico has (finally) started opening on Tuesdays.



18 Longland Street, Newstead, instagram.com/bakerdchirico Riser Bread Tom Cooney, Kieran Ryan and Duncan McKay opened Riser in 2022 in

the old Queenslander-style shopfront once occupied by the iconic

Bruno’s Tables, and more recently 85 Miskin Street. Riser is tucked away on a back street in bucolic Toowong. Morgan Roberts On weekends, it’s the scene of orderly chaos as customers compete for precisely baked Danishes, croissants, scrolls and sausage rolls, and a short selection of

fresh-made sandwiches that are among the best in town. For drinks, there’s Coffee Supreme coffee, hand-whisked matcha, craft sodas and fresh squeezed orange juice.



Good to know: It’s set up for grab-and-go but Riser’s upstairs courtyard

is one of the prettiest in town. 85 Miskin Street, Toowong, riserbread.com Bistro Tino Bistro Tino opened earlier this year in the old WWII-era Nissen hut premises previously occupied by King Arthur Cafe. Bistro Tino has opened in the premises previously occupied by King Arthur Cafe. Morgan Roberts



The Mosconi team has created a low-key stunner with beautiful parquetry, and mission brown and clothed cream colour palette. The food is just as good: think Italian sausage served with silverbeet, butter beans and baguette; or a potato and zucchini frittata served with blue swimmer crab and creme fraiche. For drinks, there’s Single O espresso, Somage teas and Hunted + Gathered organic hot chocolate. Good to know: Bistro Tino will begin opening for dinner in September. 164C Arthur Street, Fortitude Valley, instagram.com/bistro_tino Industry Beans



Opening in 2019, Industry Beans Newstead remains one of the city’s best

looking cafes, making the most of its light-filled warehouse space to

create the “breakfast restaurant” by which all others are measured. Indsutry Beans. The coffee menu is innovative and extensive, and the brunch menu has

improved to hit a sweet balance between approachable and elevated. It’s

not the most cutting-edge spot around but it remains a Northside brunch

date go-to for a reason. Good to know: This place sells stacks of beans and brewing equipment. 18 Proe Street, Newstead, industrybeans.com



Nodo Donuts Kate Williams’ Nodo was a game changer when it opened in Newstead in

2015 serving its baked-not-fried gluten-free doughnuts (they were

arguably more cake than doughnut, but the quality was exceptional, the

range of flavours imaginative). Nodo’s cake-like doughnuts remains as popular as ever. Must Do Brisbane Later, an expansion and a gluten-free brunch menu followed, as did other venues in the CBD and on the south side. It’s perhaps not as bleeding edge as it once was but those doughies remain undeniable. Good to know: Nodo has a stack of gluten-free flours and cake mixes

available in-store and online.



1 Ella Street, Newstead, nododonuts.com The Green Green by name, green by nature – a seat in this open-air stunner, among

its stacks of foliage, is a James Street prize on Saturday and Sunday

mornings. Moreish mezze in a sun-dappled courtyard at The Green. The Green The Middle Eastern menu is a cracker too: there’s Turkish eggs with muhammara, labne, hazelnut dukkha and house bread, crispy spiced garlic sujuk sausage, and Levant-spiced charcoal chicken. Coffee is by St. Ali.



Good to know: The Green goes late on Fridays and Saturdays. 1/27 James Street, Fortitude Valley, thegreen.com.au Yolk Yianni Pisarris took a “secret” menu item from his Morning After cafe in

West End and created a minor sensation when he opened Yolk at Gasworks in 2019. Yolk CBD. Dean Swindell



Its short menu was built around one thing: the perfect bacon and egg roll. Pisarris prefers a soft milk bun with streaky bacon, American cheese and a gooey fried egg. To that you can add your choice of sauce – including hollandaise, cayenne pepper hollandaise, chimichurri, and truffle mayo – and perhaps a hash brown (Pisarris reckons you should). Elsewhere on the menu there’s a steak and egg roll, a mushroom and egg roll, a chicken burger and a cheeseburger. Specialty coffee is by Five Senses. Good to know: Yolk opened a second store in the CBD (pictured here) earlier this year. 76 Skyring Terrace, Newstead, loveyolk.com.au Felix for Goodness Hiding in plain sight on Burnett Lane in the CBD, this sustainably minded exposed brick and timber cafe remains as vital as ever.



Felix for Goodness in Brisbane City. The all-day brunch menu features a potato and chorizo cutlet, a spiced jackfruit toastie and vanilla pancakes. Where to enjoy it all? A morning slot here at the hight open window overlooking the laneway outside is rite-of-passage stuff. Good to know: The Felix team recently opened Riffe for Goodness in the

storied spot once occupied by Sourced Grocer. 50 Burnett Lane, Brisbane, felixforgoodness.com Sarni



Best sandwich shop in town? Sarni is an absolute contender. A smoked brisket sandwich at Sarni. Markus Ravik The brainchild of Marty Coard, Mat Drummond, Noam Lissner and Hugo

Hirst, Sarni emerged in an unfussy, bright blue space on Racecourse Road in 2024. The menu? A tight set of sandwiches, all of which are served on either a slow-fermented bun or focaccia (both house-made), but that otherwise rotate regularly. Typical proteins are pork, and an Angus brisket that’s brined for seven days, then smoked. Coffee is Bellissimo served espresso and in Vietnamese iced coffees. Good to know: Marty Coard, Mat Drummond and Noam Lissner also own Ach, a cracking Middle Eastern restaurant in Hamilton. 143 Racecourse Rod, Ascot, instagram.com/sarni.bne



Eat at Billy’s Eat at Billy’s sandwiches were an immediate hit when it opened in early

2023 – particularly its take on a reuben, which throws together 150 grams of wood-smoked wagyu brisket pastrami, red cheddar, pickles, and a generous squirt of signature sauce. Eat at Billy’s sandwiches sell out quickly. The masterstroke, though, is the soft, thick-cut white bread used on all the sandwiches – it soaks up any excess sauciness and makes them a cinch to eat. EaB often sell out super early, meaning you need to hustle to catch a sanger – but they’re so good you’ll hardly care. Good to know: Yes, Eat at Billy’s is the sister business is the exceptional Meat at Billy’s, located just next door.



155 Baroona Road, Paddington, eatatbillys.com.au So What Stereo Walking into this obscurely located Valley spot feels like stumbling into the ultimate retro rumpus room, full of found furniture, mid-century layered pendant lights and vintage JBL speakers. So What Stereo is a retro-styled spot that’s cooking legit Thai brunch. Markus Ravik Owner Kawid “Meek” Brikshavana’s Thai brunch menu is just as vivid: expect Thai-style scramble with coal-grilled tiger prawns and nam prik num; Thai boat

noodles; and khao kai kon served with coal-grilled scotch fillet. For drinks, there’s Single O espresso and filter coffee, and chilled drinks such as iced coconut matcha.



Good to know: Thursday through Saturday, the cafe operates at night as

Kasem Sook Social, serving Thai street-style food and natural wines. 4/15 Little Street, Fortitude Valley, instagram.com/so.what.stereo Beurre Pastries Beurre opened mid-2023 and straightaway had inner-west locals lining up

for owner-patissier William Leung’s imaginative spins on classic pastries. Beurre Pastries in Milton. Morgan Roberts.



You might order a smoky cauliflower and bonito Danish, a black sesame and yuzu morning bun, or a caramel brownie pain Suisse. Coffee is Bear Bones. The setting is a slick glass-enclosed spot with stone gardens, the day’s pastries displayed on an eye-catching granite counter. Good to know: Go early if you can – Leung often begins to sell out of

product well before closing time. 33 Park Road, Milton, instagram.com/beurrepastriesbne Salud Salud finds chef Vince Estacio (formerly Naim) leaning into the Latin American cuisine on which he cut his teeth in his native San Francisco more than a decade ago.



Salud cafe & restaurant in Auchenflower. Expect dishes such as a wet burrito smothered in salsa verde sauce and melted cheese, chorizo patatas bravas, and a Latin-inflected shakshuka. The digs, in old Queenslander-style digs on Haig Road, account for the rest of the charm. Coffee is by Campos. Good to know: Salud has one of the best dining backyards in the city

(perfect for functions). 109 Haig Road, Auchenflower, saludbne.com.au Goodfolk Cafe



Great suburban cafes aren’t meant to have a second life but Goodfolk is

arguably better than (the very good) Neighbourhood Coffee Roasters that preceded it in the brilliant old Rainworth General Store space. Goodfolk Cafe in Bardon. Josh Tate Owner Adam Murphy trusts his punters to roll with an imaginative menu that includes Turkish eggs, green eggs topped with lamb rosemary sausage, and dukkah crusted Lebanese lamb meatballs. Neighbourhood lives on by supplying the coffee, and it’s backed by a bunch of teas and house-made juices. Good to know: Goodfolk features a winsome backyard with a produce garden. 58 Rainworth Road, Bardon, goodfolkcafe.com.au



Passport Specialty Coffee This might be the very best. Passport Specialty Coffee in Northgate. The location in a Northgate warehouse is low-key but refined and almost retreat-like, decked out in timber and aggregate concrete floors, with the team pumping out the brews from an enormous coffee bar anchored by a La Marzocco Strada espresso machine. There’s also batch, filter and cold brew available, and blends and equipment for sale on a retail shelf. Good to know: Arguably the best coffee you can get close to the airport,

if you’re chasing a pre- or post-flight brew.



49 Toombul Road, Northgate, passportcoffee.com.au Salt Coffee Roasters Look for the crowd of post-run, pre-shopping Newstead locals on the corner of Doggett Street and Commercial Road and you’ve found Salt Coffee Roasters, Zac Lazarac’s long-term passion project (he used to be a stockbroker) that was finally made manifest in 2019. Tomato flatbread at Salt Coffee Roasters. What started as refined, polished venue built around its custom San Remo coffee machine is a bit more freewheeling these days, but the coffee is first-class and the concise brunch menu on-point, with baked items supplied by Idle.



Good to know: Combine with a visit to newly opened Eclair at the Bay,

which is just across the road. 50 Commercial Road, Newstead, instagram.com/salt.au Bella & Tortie Suzi Unwin’s cherished little bakery that disappeared from Grange in late 2022, before later being reborn in a much more pared back form in Stafford in 2023. Bella & Tortie Markus Ravik



The equation? An unassuming space, stacks of flaky pies and sausage rolls, focaccia sandwiches, and a menu of the best sweets in the business that rotates weekly. An absolute treasure on the north side. Good to know: Open just Friday through Sunday, check B&T’s Instagram for this week’s sweets. Farmhouse There’s nothing subtle about this enormous country-themed shed out at Kedron, but there’s little not to love either, Amanda and John Scott opening Farmhouse in part as a tribute to the Farmer Joe’s produce store, which closed in the same spot in 2009. The OG Breakfast at Farmhouse.



Expect generously sized, produce-driven breakfasts in a rustic space that overflows with verdant greenery. Good to know: Make use of the online bookings because this place

absolutely murders on weekends. 9 Somerset Road, Kedron, farmhousekedron.com.au The Hideout Eddie Cho’s The Hideout is relatively new to the coffee scene but has built a dedicated following on the back of an unfussy, engagement-savvy approach to speciality brews.



The Hideout on Edward Street. He runs three blends at his Edward Street cafe – all produced by Melbourne’s Axil Coffee Roasters – available via espresso and batch brew. There’s also a food menu that’s much better than it needs to be. The handsome white and red cafe itself, with its welcoming alfresco design, accounts for the rest of its charm. Good to know: The Hideout has two other locations, on Adelaide Street in the CBD and St Paul’s Terrace in the Valley. 100 Edward Street, Brisbane, thehideoutspecialtycoffee.com Death Before Decaf



Serving espresso coffee 24-7, 365 days a year is the ultimate excuse to phone it in, but this New Farm institution steadfastly refuses to do so. Death Before Decaf serves coffee 24 hours a day. AFR It’s not uncommon to find taxi drivers and roadworkers gathered around its neon-lit frontage in the depths of a Friday or Saturday night. The shop’s blends, AAA and Roadie – custom-made by local roasters – are bracing for that reason, but the coffee’s always exactingly poured, making this a cherished beacon for serious coffee drinkers. Good to know: The shop itself is a charming spot. Inspired by tattoo and

skate culture, it stocks beans and coffee pods, and hardcore or metal is

always playing. 760-766 Brunswick Street, New Farm, deathbeforedecaf.com.au



Eclair at the Bay Michelin-trained Pavel Stolarsky’s pastry skills are on full display at this

beautiful little shopfront on Commercial Road, which, as you might expect, specialises in immaculately presented eclairs, but also protuberant profiteroles, textural craquelins, and immaculately styled tarts. Eclair at the Bay's white chocolate ganache tart with raspberry coulis. Markus Ravik For drinks, it’s simple: black coffee, tea and fresh-pressed juices. Otherwise, there’s a shelf full of merch, imported candy, books and the like. A very welcome Byron Bay-import. Good to know: Stolarsky and partner Mary Martin also do a buzzing trade in event cakes, including show-stopping croquembouche.



58 Commercial Road, Newstead, eclairatthebay.com Kimino This Ashgrove cafe is all about detail, Kyoto-born owner Mine Hirayama, a pour-over obsessive. Kimino in Ashgrove. Hirayama usually runs three four roasters at anyone time, usually sourced from Japan. There’s also house-baked sweets such as sable cookies and raisin butter sandos, and this beguiling, light- filled cafe’s ceremonial grade matcha is regularly rated as some of the best in town.



Good to know: Kimino is worth visiting for its curated selection of fancy Japanese ceramics alone. 71 Wardell Street, Ashgrove, instagram.com/kimino__bne Honourable Mentions Scout – One of Brisbane’s most beguiling cafes still serves bagels you should care about. Foster & Black – This chain boasts a slick roastery and cafe HQ in the Valley.



Time & Temp – Precision baked pastries and filter coffee in the old Brewbakers spot in Albion. Blue Bear Coffeehouse – this unassuming corner cafe on James Street serves breakfasts locals in the know swear by. Rise Bakery – find first-class French-style pastries at this Newstead and Portside spot. Riffe for Goodness – the Felix for Goodness crew take on Teneriffe in the old Sourced Grocer premises. Dicki’s – a fabulous plant-based cafe that’s hugely popular with New Farm locals.



Dopo Eatery – the old Tognini’s in Milton gets a light and bright refresh. The Single Guys – it might not be pushing any boundaries, but this Kenmore classic is just as charming as ever. Method to the Madness – By now a Kenmore favourite because of its ambitious brunch menu. This and That – It’s all about location at this New Farm cafe in a quaint old Queenslander. Naim – This Paddington cafe’s Middle Eastern-inspired brunches remain a local favourite.



Joe’s Famous Deli – One of the movers and shakers in Brisbane’s fancy sandwich craze. Queen Amann – A slick King Street bakery dedicated to kouign-amann. Wolff Coffee Roasters – Beautifully presented roastery in a handsome Hendra warehouse. Fonzie Abbott – An Albion classic overlooking bucolic Crosby Park. Pancha – Ascot and Hamilton locals flock here for hearty breakfasts and Campos coffee.



Jocelyn’s Provisions – The storied bakeshop remains a James Street and Albion favourite. Brolly Coffee – The Botanica team is behind this beautiful Red Hill coffee shop. James Street Bakery – The engine of James Street Market serves a cracking selection of sourdough. Doughcraft – One of the CBD’s best bakeries transforms into an Italian restaurant at night. Priorities – A brilliant little coffee shack on a grassy strip in Alderley.



Hussk – This cracking Grange cafe boasts some Michelin-trained cred in the kitchen. Sippy Tom – An inviting bolthole slotted beneath the Winchcombe Carson Woolstores. Mr Valentine – Allpress espresso and Doughcraft pastries in a buzzy Valley spot. Supernice – This hidden Bowen Hills gem serves some of the best sandwiches in the area. Blackout Paddington – There are few Paddington coffee spots more popular with locals.



Fave Specialty Coffee – A McLachlan Street gem with precision coffee and a surprisingly refined food menu. The Tiller Coffee – Semi-Pro espresso out of a bright orange shipping container in Alderley. Neighbourhood Coffee Roasters – A beautiful warehouse cafe and roastery in the Albion Fine Trades precinct. Danny’s Bread – Some of the best loaves in Brisbane’s north can be found in this Commercial Road hole in the wall.

World.title: Google hit with $1.5 billion fine over app store, search breaches
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesRegulation Google hit with $1.5 billion fine over app store, search breaches Foo Yun Chee July 23, 2026 — 9:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Alphabet’s Google was fined a total of €890 million (A$1.45 billion) on Thursday for flouting European Union rules aimed at reining in the power of Big Tech, the European Commission said. However, the US tech giant is likely to avoid fresh fines as EU regulators lauded good progress in its ongoing efforts to comply with the landmark legislation. The fines underscored Europe’s determination to prevent Big Tech companies from thwarting rivals, defying US criticism and retaliatory tariff threats. One of the two fines was for Google’s favouring of its own services in shopping, hotels, transport and sports in search results. Getty Images One fine of €460 million ($750 million) was handed out to Google by the European Commission under the Digital Markets Act for favouring its own services in shopping, hotels, transport and sports results in search results.



A second fine of €430 million ($700 million) targeted Google’s restrictions on its app store Google Play that prevented app developers from steering users free of charge to cheaper offers on rival app stores or websites. The fines are the first for the US tech giant under the DMA but the fifth and sixth overall for anti-competitive practices, making for total penalties of €10.38 billion ($17 billion) over nearly two decades. Related Article Opinion

Regulation The $3 billion bomb: Apple and co are under attack Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “Our duty and obligation is to comply with the laws, that our laws are fully respected,” EU antitrust chief Teresa Ribera told reporters when asked about US pushback. “The DMA is to make sure we have a fair and level playing field. With these decisions we want to make sure there is competition,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told reporters.



Google, which has 60 days to comply with the Commission’s orders to treat rivals in a fair and non-discriminatory manner and to allow app developers to steer users away from its app store, criticised the EU findings and said it might take the Commission to court. “To comply, we are having to strip away real-time Search features Europeans love - like instant pricing and direct

availability for hotels, flights, and restaurants - and dismantle safety protections on Google Play,” Google President of Global Affairs Kent Walker said in a statement. “This isn’t fair competition; it’s product degradation driven by a small group of self-serving complainants, with European businesses and consumers taking the hit. Regulation should improve products, not make them worse,” he said. More fines unlikely given ‘constructive dialogue’ The Commission, which acts as the EU competition enforcer, pointed to a “constructive dialogue” with Google and significant progress made to comply with the DMA, indicating that daily penalties for non-compliance are likely off the table.



“Google has proposed and started testing changes to how it presents its own services on Google Search for free services such as shopping, hotels and flights,” the Commission said, calling it substantial progress. “The Commission also notes that Google has proposed and started testing changes to how it presents shopping ads and content related services, such as sports,” it said, adding it would assess the changes and continue talks with Google. Related Article Regulation Apple and Meta hit with €700 million fines in Europe under new digital rules The EU watchdog also said Google may apply the principles of Thursday’s decision to its AI-generated summaries known as AI Overviews and AI Mode and that talks would continue to this end. Google’s changes to its steering terms on Google Play received a tentative thumbs up from the Commission.



“These constitute good progress towards compliance and will also be assessed in light of the cease and desist order of today’s decision,” it said. Europe’s crackdown on Big Tech has angered US President Donald Trump’s administration, which has threatened to retaliate with tariffs for what he said are moves targeting US companies while US lawmakers have also piled on the pressure. The fines are the third under the DMA after penalties handed out to Apple and Meta Platforms in April last year. Reuters

World.title: Appliances with a high ceiling
World.content:
Being ensconced in Midsomer, UK, and struggling to find meaning in a pressure cooker (C8) indicates that Jo Rainbow isn’t exactly home on the range, but the explainers have come thick and fast. Representing the positive is Jane Page of Cromer: “I loved my pressure cooker. It made the best pea and ham soup using the ham bone left over from Christmas as well as delicious porcupine meat balls. My mouth waters when I think of the golden syrup dumplings my mum used to make. Long live the pressure cooker!”

Margaret Collins of Terrigal adds: “Keep that pressure cooker! I still cook succulent stews and soups within 20 minutes using my mother’s old cooktop pressure cooker. Way better than many modern gizmos such as air fryers. No fats and no lost nutrition. Also saves on energy.”

Representing the negative, we have Stein Boddington of St Clair: “Apart from quickly cooking food at higher temperatures, the real purpose of a pressure cooker is to apply a thin, irregular coating of chicken stew to the ceiling of old rectories, after the little rubber thing pops out. My mother successfully did this in Gunning in 1955, and that rectory is still standing.”

Ted Richards of Batemans Bay says his aunt was the first member of the family to have one. “She experimented by trying to stew apples. All through the stewing process a fine jet of steam rose from the cooker, and when the stewing was over there were no apples in the cooker. They had all condensed on the ceiling.”

“I, too, like Paul Taylor (C8) have noticed the reversal of the BYD logo lettering and recall this brand being launched as ‘Build Your Dreams’,” says Gino DeBono of Collaroy. “Perhaps CYE stands for ‘Choice Yielding Electric’.”

World.title: ‘Is this the end?’: The contract call that changed plagued new Wallaby’s fate
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘Is this the end?’: The contract call that changed plagued new Wallaby’s fate Nick Wright July 23, 2026 — 8:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I always knew he’d be diligent enough to get himself back.” That was what former Wallabies star Sam Cordingley declared when asked about Isaac Henry – the Reds star who received a shock call-up to the Australian squad on Thursday having overcome a series of career-threatening injuries. It was the outcome that was always destined for Henry, Cordingley believed, as long as he refused to allow his worrying health to seal his fate. Isaac Henry contemplated whether his career was over. Now he is in the cusp of a Wallabies’ debut. AFP Four serious surgeries in as many years curtailed Henry’s career, and left him pondering whether he would realise his potential.



The resilient centre suffered foot, quad, knee and hamstring injuries from his 2021 Queensland Reds debut, and at one stage was sidelined for 19 months within a two-year period. He spent 15 months out of action as he fought to cast aside a ruptured patella tendon sustained in March 2024. Related Article City life Rugby star on the family ties that bind him to Brisbane Henry’s career revival began under coach Les Kiss’ tutelage at Ballymore, and Kiss as Wallabies honcho has now ushered the 27-year-old into his first Test squad. Now he will duel with Reds teammate Hunter Paisami for an inside centre berth in the two-Test series against Japan. “Everyone’s known what his potential has been, he just didn’t have the continuity to prove it. Those injuries, they were pretty significant – and they were back-to-back – and I do know during his time he was contemplating ‘is this the end?’” Cordingley told this masthead. “He was obviously quite upset on the back of the last injury, but he’s had really good support. He’s kept his head up during the time, he’s never been someone who’s complained and has never had a woe-is-me attitude.



“Every time he’s had a setback, it’s onto the next thing he needs to resolve. It was a long road for him, I imagine, and now that he’s seen where the effort has got him to, it would be really pleasing for him and his family.” Season 2026 was the most fruitful of Henry’s career, earning six Reds caps. He has not played since round 14, which came after four weeks out nursing further niggling injuries, but was called into Wallabies camp ahead of the Nations Championship clash with Italy as cover. Loading His resurgence is one Cordingley, now the Reds’ general manager of football operations, believed would eventually happen at a crossroads in his career, as the luckless No.12 came off contract during his patella recovery. “From a contracting point of view, he was three years into his contract at the time – I think it was coming into the third year when he ruptured that patella tendon – and we recontracted him through that period, so we backed him in based on his diligence around it,” Cordingley said.



“I can’t remember thinking at the time, from a contracting perspective, that this was the end – we wanted to see him. We’ve always had that eagerness to see him get back, so I didn’t really contemplate it was the end for him.” Related Article Wallabies As Kiss’s first Wallabies signing is revealed, a boom rookie is next on the radar The fortitude Henry has shown throughout his professional playing days was honed during his junior days, at one stage playing through a broken rib and lower back stress fracture to captain Brisbane Boys College. Cordingley remembers a young tearaway who proved to be “a pretty elite goal kicker” – converting at more than 90 per cent off the tee – who possessed a diligent work ethic that would ultimately hold him the stead needed to overcome his years in the casualty ward. He stressed Henry should not be considered a fill-in option, adamant a lengthy international career beckoned if he remained fit.



“I know he’s a pretty avid golfer – sometimes with those long-terms rehabs, it’s getting out of rugby that can help you by having other things that spike your interest, and he does that pretty well,” Cordingley said. “We’ve always known he had the capacity to play Test rugby. I think what you’ve seen in his ability to carry, the defensive efforts he makes, he’s got a short and long kicking game, but I’d just really say it’s his ethic, and he’s a player who doesn’t make a lot of mistakes. Isaac Henry has earned a call-up to Les Kiss’ first Wallabies squad. Getty Images “He has a very consistent bandwidth in between the good and bad, which I think is really important for professional players, and certainly is at the Test level.” Henry’s selection comes at the expense of reigning John Eales Medal winner Len Ikitau, who is recovering from a minor ankle issue. He has also nudged ahead of Benetton-bound Josh Flook, with Kiss confirming Henry’s ability to cover wing and both centres was a compelling factor. World.title: Setka to be sacked: Threats, abuse behind push to remove former CFMEU boss
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Setka to be sacked: Threats, abuse behind push to remove former CFMEU boss Nick McKenzie July 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

John Setka is set to be expelled from the union he led for 12 years and a powerful Victorian organiser has been summarily removed from the CFMEU in a dramatic effort by the union’s new administrator to reassert control of the rogue Victorian branch. The move to formally tear up Setka’s CFMEU membership for repeatedly threatening and intimidating administrator Michael Crosby and his staff comes after the disgraced former union chief was photographed dining at an upmarket steak and oyster restaurant with a building company boss notorious for ripping off union members and subcontractors. Lunch companions Frank Nadinic (left), John Setka (centre) and John Perkovic (right). Nathan Perri Also at the Esca Grill Seafood and Steak restaurant lunch with company boss Frank Nadinic— who the CFMEU once labelled “cruel Frank” for rorting workers — was Setka’s former union lieutenant John Perkovic. Perkovic is under active federal police investigation for taking up to $3 million in suspected bribes from other building company bosses also accused of exploiting workers.



Five industry and union insiders said the sight of Setka rubbing shoulders with Nadinic - an exploitative building firm boss whose building firm Setka attacked publicly in 2015 for conduct that denied dozens of union members their entitlements — was illustrative of the demise of the CFMEU under Setka’s reign into a union that privileged company and gangland bosses above ordinary workers. This masthead could not confirm allegations from those sources that Setka and Perkovic were assisting Nadinic in handling a building industry dispute, as all three men were not able to be contacted. John Setka outside his lunch venue. The Age In his LinkedIn profile, Nadinic describes himself as an “experienced senior consultant with a demonstrated history of working in the construction and development industry” and a “strong consulting professional with a First class honours focused in Life from School of hard knocks”. Perkovic was sacked from the union last October after this masthead revealed he had received undisclosed benefits worth up to $3 million from company bosses he oversaw as a union official.



Over the last two years, this masthead’s Building Bad series has revealed how multiple companies with track records of mistreating workers or offering them insecure gigs in labour hire roles were given preferential treatment by the CFMEU. Editor's pick Exclusive

Building Bad Top Victorian CFMEU official sacked over alleged mistreatment of union organiser It has also revealed how Setka and Perkovic’s underworld ally, union fixer Mick Gatto, has been paid millions of dollars by companies that have gone bust owing workers or paid the underworld veteran to keep the union from enforcing hard union-won pay and conditions EBAs. On Wednesday evening, Crosby wrote to Setka saying he intended to initiate formal proceedings to rip up Setka’s CFMEU membership “for a period of 5 years” for allegedly engaging in “misconduct” by threatening, abusing and denigrating administration staff by calling them dogs in expletive-ridden tirades on email and in other forums. As recently as Sunday, Setka threatened Crosby with violence in an interview he gave to this masthead.



“If he wants to come after me, he better f---ing watch himself,” Setka said on Sunday. “Because if I run into him in the street, it’s not going to be good for him ... He’s not a f---ing koala bear. He’s not, f---ing, a protected species.” Editor's pick Updated

Victorian Parliament ‘I don’t just ditch my mates’: New minister defends CFMEU links Police have also moved to obtain a personal intervention order for Crosby against Setka following the remarks. Setka, who did not return calls on Thursday, has until August 7 to make his case to Crosby as to why he should not be expelled as a member of the CFMEU. His expulsion would complete an extraordinary fall from power of a man who once wielded significant influence over the Victorian Labor Party and who continues to have allies in select union and political circles, including Allan government minister Luba Grigorovitch.



The move against Setka by Crosby comes after the administrator declared on Monday the culture in the union’s previously all-powerful Victorian arm remained broken and warned that the pariah branch would stay in administration indefinitely while its sacked former bosses still exert control. In the interview, Crosby also called on government and the wider industry to do far more to combat the construction industry organised crime and corruption that Victoria Police has separately warned it is powerless to tackle. Loading On Thursday, Crosby also moved to sap the ongoing influence of ex-CFMEU vice president Joe Myles, who this masthead revealed on Monday was still influencing the activities of union officials on Labor’s Big Build. Crosby removed union organiser Adam Olsen from the CFMEU amid concerns Olsen, who is a close friend of Myles, was still acting on Myles’ orders. Olsen and Myles could not be contacted for comment.



Myles was previously the top CFMEU official on the Big Build and has been accused - including in a report tabled in the Queensland royal commission into the union - of placing bikie gang members as union delegates on state government rail and road projects. World.title: NZ Warriors lose tryscoring star Lavinia Tauhalaliku to NRLW suspension
World.content:
NRLW: Parramatta Eels v NZ Warriors

Kickoff 2pm Sunday, 26 July

Eric Tweedale Stadium, Sydney

Live blog updates on RNZ

NZ Warriors tryscoring star Lavinia Tauhalaliku has been stood down for two games, after violating the NRLW code of conduct.

The flying wing has been in sensational form over the first three rounds of the Aussie women's league competition and leads all tryscorers with six, after bagging four against North Queensland Cowboys last weekend.

She also had a double in the season-opening win over Canterbury Bulldogs.

The NRLW has issued her with a breach notice, after she was involved in an off-field altercation over the summer, although no police charges resulted.

The timing of her ban could not be better for Tauhalaliku, who was unable to travel across the Tasman and has been omitted from the team to take on Parramatta Eels on Sunday, due to visa complications.

Born in Nuku'alofa, she has had to re-apply for clearance to enter Australia and that has not yet been approved.

Even before the suspension, Warriors coach Ron Griffiths expected her to miss the Eels fixture, as well as next week's 'Magic Round' clash with Gold Coast Titans in Wagga Wagga.

World.title: New Zealanders warned not to transit through Middle East as Trump threatens further strikes
World.content:
The government is again warning New Zealanders not to transit through the Middle East as Donald Trump threatens further military strikes on Iran.

The US President on Wednesday said that the United States would bomb Iranian civil infrastructure every time Tehran fires at ships in the Hormuz Strait.

A Safe Travel advisory issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFAT) said it advises against all non-essential transit travel through the United Arab Emirates and Qatar.

"The security situation in the Middle East remains highly volatile and travellers could be stranded with little warning and few options.

"Given this, we advise New Zealanders not to transit the Middle East, including through Dubai or Doha, unless their travel is absolutely essential and there are no other flight routes available through Asia or North America."

The agency said those who decided travelling through the region was necessary should keep transit times to a minimum and be prepared for flight cancellations, delays, and airspace closures.

It also advised New Zealanders in Iran to leave as soon as possible, if it was safe to do so.

A limited number of flights are still operating from Khomeini International Airport in Tehran but airspace closures could occur at any time, it said.

Land routes out of Iran via Turkey and Armenia are still viable and have been successfully used by other New Zealanders to leave the country.

Anyone who could not leave Iran should follow the advice of local authorities and move to or remain in a safe place and ensure they have essential supplies such as food, water, torches, batteries or power banks and any medications.

The advisory said there are a number of steps people should take if they are at risk of drone or missile attacks:

Know how advance warnings are communicated in the area

Follow all local authority instructions

Identify the nearest shelter or safest locations

If no shelter is available, move to a basement or interior room away from windows

Avoid any potential target locations, including military sites, airports and oil and energy infrastructure

Keep in contact with family and friends where possible

World.title: Body found in search for missing Dargaville man Saxzin Steedman
World.content:
A body has been found in a river in Northland's Dargaville amid a search for missing man Saxzin Steedman.

Steedman, 22, had been missing for three weeks, after last being seen leaving Cranley St on June 30 about 4pm.

Detective Senior Sergent Shane Pilmer, Northland CIB said police teams found a body in the Wairoa River at 12.15pm on Thursday.

While formal identification was still underway, police believed the body was that of the missing 22-year-old.

"Family members have been informed and are being supported by police," Pilmer said.

The formal identification process was underway, and the man's death had been referred to the Coroner.

World.title: Global oil prices climb closer to US$100 a barrel
World.content:
Global oil prices have climbed closer towards US$100 (NZ$172) a barrel on Thursday afternoon, with the conflict between Iran and the US showing no sign of de-escalating.

Earlier in the day, a tanker was reportedly struck by an unknown projectile off Saudi Arabia's coast.

It follows US President Donald Trump threatening to bomb Iranian infrastructure in response to any attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

The price of Brent crude has risen around 2 percent this afternoon to a six-week high of around US$96 a barrel.

West Texas Intermediate is sitting at around US$88 a barrel.

With the announcement of a ceasefire last month, oil prices, which had peaked at US$126 a barrel in April, dropped to around US$72 a barrel.

Prices at the pump in New Zealand have not yet reacted to the recent resurgence in global oil prices, with the average price of a litre of 91 sitting at around NZ$2.89 on the Gaspy fuel monitoring site on Thursday afternoon.

World.title: Fuel boss expects price to rise 15-20 cents a litre in coming weeks
World.content:
A fuel boss says he expects prices to climb 15 - 20 cents per litre in coming weeks, after new developments in the US - Iran conflict.

Earlier today, a tanker was reportedly struck by an unknown projectile off Saudi Arabia's coast.

It followed US President Donald Trump threatening to bomb Iranian infrastructure in response to any attacks on ships travelling through the Strait of Hormuz.

Petrol prices may rise again as Middle East conflict escalates Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Waitomo Group chief executive Simon Parham told Checkpoint he expected those developments, as well as Ukranian drone strikes on Russian refineries, would push prices up.

"I'd forecast that we'd be going close to $3, just a little bit under. But on diesel, about $2.50. So that's where I'd sort of see it pan out in the next one to two weeks."

But Parnham did not expect prices to get as high as previous peaks in March and April.

"The reason for that is that there has been a rebalancing in the system, with crude coming from countries such as the United States, Brazil, and Guyana across to refineries."

China had also relaxed its restrictions on petrol and diesel exports and were selling more to international markets, Parham said.

He said oil markets no longer seemed to be reacting to every word that President Trump said.

"I think the market... started to shrug their shoulders and say this is the new normal... the days of him talking the market up or down seem to have gone."

People in New Zealand had started to buy more petrol after demand plummeted in April and May, Parnham said.

World.title: The House: MPs return after two-week break
World.content:
When MPs return to Parliament after a two-week break, the first day or so in the debating chamber can involve a surprising amount of catch-up on the endless business awaiting attention, and on rejuvenated arguments and debates, as well as on not losing ground in the inch-by-inch battles over procedural interpretation. Some of the catch-up is official business, some is tactical and some is political.

Select Committees don't experience the same level of catch-up. They typically lose so many sitting days to extended sittings in the House that many keep working across the sitting breaks, at least to some degree.

Refreshed MPs add new debates to business backlog The House Download MP3 5m

Parliament's 'mail box'

Each sitting day the Clerk of the House informs MPs of what you might describe as mail. New bills, reports from committees, papers from entities (things like Annual Reports or Statements of Intent), and newly arrived petitions. Most days there are a few, but after a two week break, the weight of new reading is staggering.

On Tuesday the Clerk announced 13 petitions, 64 papers, 15 select committee reports, and two new bills. Just reading the titles of that two-lozenge-worthy list took six and a half minutes. Thank goodness most are now electronic and can be found on Parliament's website. Papers can be found here, petitions are here, committee reports are here, and bills are here.

Labour MP Camilla Belich tried to add an extra item to the mailbox, when she asked the House to agree to introduce a new member's bill - the Crimes (Consent Reform) Amendment Bill. The bill would establish "affirmative consent as New Zealand's approach to consent to sexual activity". She wanted it debated on member's day. Permission would need to be unanimous, and was never likely to be given. The move was a political response to National's promise to introduce consent law post-election. Belich was saying something like 'if you care, why wait?'

Noting events

When MPs return there are also often events that need mentioning in the House. This week there were four.

The recent deaths of Bill Birch (a senior National Party MPs from the 1970-80s), and Sam Neill were both given brief attention. The recent triumph of Ryan Fox at the British Golf Open was also noted. Arguably, if only one of those events had occurred it might have resulted in some speeches, rather than a motion.

A recent policy decision was also given an airing when the Speaker agreed to the requested urgent debate into the Government's decision to give financial assistance to New Zealand's remnant cement company.

The procedural recap segment

Something else that often happens after a break is a series of reminders of where things stand in any ongoing procedural tussles. These reminders might come from the Speaker or the Opposition.

This is the parliamentary version of the 'previously on...' segment at the beginning of a TV episode.

This week, for example, Shadow Leader of the House Kieran McAnulty made a gentle point early in the week's first Committee of the Whole House. Labour supports the bill being considered, but the Government has offered substantial amendments to it half way through the parliamentary process. McAnulty wanted to remind everyone that the Speaker had spoken about this kind of thing recently - regarding the importance of giving fair notice.

"We are faced with, at this stage, an Amendment Paper from the Minister that is just as large as the bill. I'd like some reassurance from him that ...the Finance and Expenditure Committee has considered all aspects of this and that the inclusion of this amendment bill is not contrary to the guidance that the Speaker gave the House only last sitting week."

New stakes in the ground

With a new sitting block there are also often new issues to raise, new issues raised by media across the break, maybe newly scandalous events to pick up on, or political feuds to continue or begin. For example, this week there have been various (sometimes oblique) responses to comments by Shane Jones and Stuart Nash.

There was also a new squabble over a privilege issue. During Tuesday's debate on the Arms Bill, Labour's Ginny Andersen accused the Minister in charge of the Bill (ACT's new deputy leader Nicole McKee), of having broken parliament's rules by sharing privileged information with a gun lobby group. McKee was outraged by the claim and demanded a retraction, and while Andersen professed herself happy to provide evidence, matters of privilege shouldn't be raised or debated in the House, nor can they be retracted in the House. They have to be raised directly with the Speaker.

New energy

At the end of the previous sitting block MPs were visibly drained after long days of urgency. Their speeches did not sparkle. Humour was a rarity.

After a week or two with family in their home electorates, MPs have more zest, better humour, and sharper snark. So for example, Labour MP Camila Belich typically debates the careful nuance and detail of law. But on Tuesday, considering New Zealand First's English Language Bill she was refreshingly acerbic. The bill is, at its core, just eight words long, and boldly asserts that English is officially allowed in New Zealand.

Bellich called it "statutory recognition of a fundamental truth. What is the Government going to legislate for next? That it should get dark at night, that the sun should rise in the morning, that the sky is blue, and that flowers should bloom?"

All of that on just the first day back.

World.title: Arthur Easton murder: Lawyers give closing arguments against former police officers
World.content:
A "conscious and deliberate" act to help police secure a conviction, or a legitimate decision to exclude evidence that was deemed unreliable?

Those are the key questions that a judge will consider as he determines whether two former officers attempted to pervert the course of justice in their handling of a 40-year-old murder.

Alan Hall spent 17 years in prison for the 1985 murder of Arthur Easton.

He was later exonerated by the Supreme Court, which found a significant miscarriage of justice had occurred.

Now the former officers, who have name suppression, are facing charges over their role in Hall's conviction.

Lawyers made their closing arguments in the High Court at Auckland on Thursday.

On 13 October 1985, Arthur Easton and his teenage sons, Brendan and Kim, were at home when one heard an intruder in their home.

Closing arguments made in Alan Hall case Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Crown prosecutor John Billington KC recounted what happened next.

"There was a fight and in the course of that fight Mr Easton was fatally wounded and Brendan Easton was seriously wounded. The offender escaped by leaving the home through a hedge into a walkway and made his way down Alma Crescent to Shirley Crescent and close to Clevedon Road."

Later that night, a man called Ronald Turner phoned the Papakura Police Station to reported seeing a hooded Māori man running across Clevedon Road around the time of the attack.

His description tallied with what the Easton brothers had told police in their 111 call - that they were attacked by a six-foot-tall Māori man wielding a bayonet.

Although the brothers would later cast doubt on their recollection, two further witnesses also described seeing a man of a similar description.

"Mr Hall, by reason of his ownership of a bayonet and a hat found at the scene was interviewed on 11 December, 1985. He gave a number of explanations as to why the bayonet and hat were not in his possession on the night of the murder. He was also questioned in relation to his ownership of a blue sweatshirt which was similar to that seen by Mr Turner," Billington said.

"Now obviously, Mr Hall did not match the description given by Mr Turner. Mr Hall is a Pākehā, somewhere close to five-foot-eight in height, frail build and clearly not Māori."

Billington questioned why police only presented some of Ronald Turner's evidence to the jury at Alan Hall's trial, excluding his description of the offender's ethnicity.

And why did the former officers not provide his original statement to Hall's defence team when they requested all relevant evidence?

"By modifying the Crown case, the defendants denied the defence lawyers, the trial judge, the jury, the Court of Appeal access to the prior statements.

"They each carried out an act which was intended to and had the obvious effect of preventing the courts from doing justice."

John Billington said it was difficult to accept that their conduct was anything but "conscious and deliberate".

But defence lawyer David Jones, KC, said police had "very real concerns" about Turner's recollection of the man he saw.

"What someone says in a statement to a police is not evidence. It is a statement they have made which could or could not be used as evidence in the case," he said.

"That has to go through a filtering process. And that is exactly what happened here."

Furthermore, Jones said, it was ultimately for the Crown to decide on what evidence was admissible in court.

"What we have is a recreation of events by the Crown which is castling a sinister light on an investigation which is carried out in an entirely normal and logical and legal way.

Jones urged Justice Gault not to rely on the findings of the Supreme Court when it quashed Alan Hall's conviction in 2022 because, he argued, the Crown had "capitulated" during the appeal.

Acting for the second defendant, Paul Wicks, KC, said there was no statutory framework guaranteeing pre-trial disclosure in the mid-1980s, as there is today.

"The Crown in this case has endeavoured to weave a few loose threads into a tapestry of guilt working backwards from the Supreme Court judgement," he said.

"It has failed, in my submission, to establish to the required standard that [the former officer] acted with any intention to pervert the course of justice and ultimately the only correct and safe verdict is one of not guilty."

World.title: Bomber Caddy to face Hawks after heart scare
World.content:
Essendon interim coach Dean Solomon says Nate Caddy will play in Saturday's match against Hawthorn following his recovery from a heart scare.

Caddy was taken to hospital during last Sunday's three-point win over GWS due to an elevated heart rate.

Bombers star cleared for return Nate Caddy is expected to fully train and play next weekend despite experiencing an elevated heart rate during Essendon's win over GWS.

The 21-year-old was released from hospital after being given the all-clear.

The club's medical staff has since given its approval for Caddy to face the Hawks.

"He'll be good to go," Solomon said.

"They said there's no risk with what happened and he's fully good to go. I trust our medical staff, and Nate's in a good headspace as well.

"He spent a lot of time with the docs and medical staff, gone through it all and has a good understanding that there's no risk at play here, and he's really confident.

"So we've just got to trust our medical staff."

Essendon has lost Xavier Duursma (hamstring) for the rest of the season, while Kyle Langford will miss the Hawthorn match due to suspension.

McKay sits out Blues training

Star Carlton forward Harry McKay failed to participate during the Blues' main training session on Thursday.

McKay suffered a minor tear to his meniscus, as well as bone bruising to his knee, during Saturday night's 21-point defeat to Collingwood.

The 28-year-old was ruled out early in the match after his knee knocked into teammate Sam Walsh.

Harry McKay was forced from the field against the Magpies last weekend. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

But speculation around McKay ran rampant, with Fox Footy commentator David King questioning the one-time Coleman medallist's injury.

The Blues were privately seething with McKay's character being criticised, before the severity of the injury was confirmed on Sunday.

Interim Blues coach Josh Fraser said he "didn't spend a lot of time thinking about" the commentary surrounding McKay.

"Whenever there's an injury, your mindset goes to the care and support for the player," Fraser said.

"We act on the information we're given from our medical team, the commentary around all of that, I probably push it to the side.

"I can only judge him on the way he's presented and he's presented his usual self.

"Great energy around the group, trying as hard as he can to play and leading internally around the club."

Carlton's wildcard hopes will go on the line on Saturday when it host out-of-form Gold Coast at Docklands.

World.title: Aussie captain relishes 'special' chance 'to take time to be a dad'
World.content:
Water polo is a brutal sport.

Relentless swimming. Incessant wrestling. Elbows and fists flying around as if the combatants were half-submerged within a flooded UFC cage.

To put it mildly, it is not a place for the faint of heart.

So it is somewhat incongruous, then, to see Australian Sharks captain Nathan Power sitting on the side of the Griffith University pool on the Gold Coast with his son, Sebastian in his arms, feeding him a bottle.

Power, 33, will lead the Australian men's water polo team at the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup event in Sydney this week, with the Sharks taking on reigning world champions Spain on Thursday.

He is also on six months of parental leave from his role as a manager with KPMG, giving him valuable time to be a dad as well as skippering his nation.

Nathan Power will skipper the team in his home town of Sydney. (Supplied: Water Polo Australia)

"It's been fun to get to do this," Power told ABC Sport, with Sebastian still in his arms.

"To get an opportunity to take time to be a dad, it's really special."

It's created some changes within the team environment too.

"This is the first time in my time with the men's team that there's been a baby on tour — and there's actually two at the moment, Blake Edwards has his son Jude here as well," Power said.

"It makes for a bit of a shift; even at breakfast time now, the boys all roll in and it's a case of, who's gunna take hold of the baby and who wants to look after a baby.

"It's amazing to see how a large group of men have all very quickly clicked into dad mode to help out where they can."

Australian Sharks Water Polo coach Tim Hamill (left) says the addition of kids to camp has been great. (Supplied: Zac Hudson)

Head coach Tim Hamill, who has led the Sharks since taking the reins post-Tokyo in 2021, also made note of the positive changes to the dynamic young children can have.

"It's a first for us," the former international player told ABC Sport.

"One of our values as a team is around family, so we talk to that in having those families here.

The 'precious' bond driving the Stingers to success Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, were the most successful Australian team at the Paris Olympics, winning a stunning silver medal. This is the secret to their success.

"We're really fortunate to have a nice balance of the group, we've got the spectrum covered in terms of interests and ideas and for the first time, in this preparation, we've got two of our players who have children, which we've never had before.

"So that changed the dynamic of the group.

"A lot of people have spoken about Paris and how do we get those results [that we got] and I'm conscious to talk culture because it's that overused word in sport at the moment.

"But for me, culture as a word is derived from that care, there's real care in this team.

"We know that our culture needs to be the best in the world, we know that our team care needs to be the best in the world, otherwise we can't compete, so we invest time in all of that, and that's conversations with those 18s all the way through to 30 plus year olds and now fathers."

The topic of keeping mothers in sport has been a hot one in the Australian space for a while now.

In December, the Australian Olympic Committee created the Olympians Future Fund, with a key pillar of that designed to help support female Olympians return to high-performance sport after giving birth, making them eligible to receive $10,000.

Although Power's situation is different, he noted that the support that he has received from KPMG and Water Polo Australia was just as valuable to him in order to allow both he and his partner Maddy to continue their careers.

Water polo is not exactly a gentle sport, as Power shows while wrestling Spain on their way to the world championship title last year. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

"That's kind of the thing that can maybe get lost at times, but really it's support for the family," he said.

"With the support that I get through my work at KPMG, that then enables Maddy to get back into work; the support I get from Water Polo Australia, that enables us as a family to be here.

"We both get to keep on pursuing what we want to pursue, but also get to spend some really meaningful time with Sebastian too.

"It's been awesome to come home from training and the first thing I see is a silly smile from the window, him looking out at me.

"It's a new, fun way to come home from training when you're a bit cooked and tired and maybe a bit grumpy."

Power beamed with joy when recounting how much Sebastian was enjoying finding his feet in the water during his lessons, adding that fatherhood has "massively" changed his perspective.

Nathan Power has competing priorities now. (Supplied: Water Polo Australia)

"I think, obviously parenthood becomes that key identity that you have and you see yourself as," he said.

"It's also something which for me, at 33, I guess we can probably confidently say I'm closer to the end than the start of my career, so it means you also get to take some moments and really appreciate that this isn't normal to get to do this and to share this experience with your family.

"It gets you to appreciate these experiences you have with the team too, because they can be very fleeting."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The World Cup Final is the first time Australia has hosted a major water polo championships since the 2007 World Championships in Melbourne, and the first time Sydney has hosted a combined event since the 2000 Olympics.

Power said the opportunity to compete in front of friends and family will never be undervalued by the squad.

"The importance of it and the rarity of it is not lost on us," Power said.

"I've had teammates who've started their career and gone through their career and finished their career and didn't get that opportunity to be able to play in an event at home like that.

"Obviously, as we move towards Brisbane, this is one of those good examples of something which can hopefully lead to more of these events occurring as well."

World.title: Nina Kennedy knows now is the time to soak it all in — if she remembers to
World.content:
For most of us, falling for 5 metres is terrifying. For Nina Kennedy, provided there's no bar following her down, the fall is the fun part.

But last year introduced her to a fresh fear: the fear that it might all be over.

The reigning Olympic and world champion in pole vault tore her hamstring early in April last year.

Despite the long recovery from surgery, Kennedy was initially named in the Australian squad for the World Athletics Championships in September, but a strained muscle just a couple of days later dragged her back to reality.

How we got to Glasgow 2026 The bumpy road to Glasgow 2026 has produced a Commonwealth Games that will look a little different than the ones that came before.

She had to watch as American rival Katie Moon won outright the title they shared two years earlier.

Yesterday, she was named Australia's flag-bearer for the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony, which felt like a long shot when she was in the depths of rehab less than a year ago.

"Whenever you have a major surgery and you're out for the whole season, there's definitely that doubt of, 'Will this get fully better and will I return to my best and better?'" she said after flying out of a pre-Games athletics training camp early to accept her flag-waving honour.

"You have those thoughts, but you put in the work you do the rehab, you listen to your team, speak to your sport psychologist and never stop dreaming.

"I'm so proud of myself. Of course there were doubts, but I'm lucky enough to do this as a job and I'm pretty damn good at it. I work my arse off every day. So I'm not surprised but I am really proud of myself.

Kennedy has warmed back into the 2026 season after a torn hamstring last year. (Getty Images: Marco Mantovani)

"As athletes we try and get the best out of ourselves, so my mind always goes to, 'What if I don't get to defend my Commonwealth title? What if I don't make it back to the Olympics? What if this hamstring goes again and my career's over and I haven't really soaked up the last few years like I should have?'"

Kennedy has been representing Australia on the world stage for more than a decade, but the past five years since turning to the sport full time have seen her conquer the world and set the Australian women's pole vault record 10 times, including just two weeks ago in Monaco.

The 29-year-old admitted the Brisbane 2032 Olympics would probably be a bridge too far for her, so it was time to look around and enjoy what was happening while she was still on the field.

"Sport can be so fleeting so I've really learned to enjoy every step and this is such a special honour. I'm really going to try and soak this in and make some good memories," she said.

Unfortunately, she knows herself too well and is pretty sure she will not nail it when she leads her teammates into Glasgow's Hydro for the opening ceremony tomorrow morning (AEST).

"I'll be thinking, 'Soak this in, soak this in, soak it in,' and then I won't soak it in," she said.

"That's what will happen."
