Tech.title: Samsung’s Foldables Got Pricier. The RAM Shortage Is Part of the Bill
Tech.content:
Samsung’s latest foldables bring upgrades over last year’s models — including a new wider-screen device — but they also carry the industry’s favorite trend: higher prices.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Z Flip 8 each cost $100 more than last year’s Z Fold 7 and Z Flip 7, while the brand-new, confusingly named Galaxy Z Fold 8, lands between them in price. Foldables have always sat at the top of the smartphone price ladder, and none of Samsung’s new ones are bucking that trend. Raising prices on some of the most expensive phones you can buy only pushes them further into niche territory.

Samsung said the higher prices reflect increased memory and component costs, which have affected phones, PCs and other products across the tech industry. The company also pointed to improvements over last year’s devices, including the new Titanium Flex displays, larger batteries and better 50-megapixel ultra-wide cameras on the Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra.

That pricing pressure isn’t unique to Samsung. Nearly every 2026 phone has either cost more than its predecessor or arrived with so few upgrades that the price stayed flat, and Samsung’s foldables are also facing similarly pricier competition from Motorola’s Razr lineup.

The bigger picture is the RAM shortage, fueled in large part by the AI boom, which has driven memory prices sharply higher and left manufacturers with a choice: raise prices or cut specs. The explosive demand for AI data centers and models has pushed chipmakers to prioritize high-bandwidth memory for AI workloads, leaving less capacity for standard DRAM and NAND used in phones and PCs. Tariffs and other costs may be adding to the squeeze, but AI-driven memory demand is the main culprit behind the broader run-up in phone prices.



Outer screens of the folded-up Galaxy Z Fold 8 (left) and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra (right). Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Prices of Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Galaxy Z Flip 8

The Galaxy Z Fold 8, Samsung’s newest foldable, is the company’s new entry-level book-style foldable. In addition to its wider, shorter format that unfolds to reveal an inner 4:3-screen, the device lacks a handful of features of its more premium sibling. The Z Fold 8 starts at $1,900 for 256GB of storage, goes up to $2,100 for 512GB, and reaches $2,500 for 1TB.

256GB 512GB 1TB Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 $1,900 $2,100 $2,500

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, in comparison, is a taller book-style foldable with slightly more premium features — namely, a 10-megapixel telephoto camera and a large 5,000-mAh battery. It starts at $2,100 for 256GB of storage, then goes up to $2,300 for 512GB and tops out at a staggering $2,700.

256GB 512GB 1TB Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra $2,100 $2,300 $2,700

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 is the newest clamshell foldable from Samsung and has minor improvements over its predecessor: it’s lighter, has a slightly thinner design, and, like Samsung’s other foldables released alongside it, runs on Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip. It starts at $1,200 for 256GB and rises to $1,400 for 512GB.

256GB 512GB Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 $1,200 $1,400

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 in pink, cream and graphite colors. A mint color is also available as an online exclusive. Joseph Maldonado/CNET

Colors for Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Galaxy Z Flip 8

The new wider-format Galaxy Z Fold 8 debuts with colors in lavender, graphite and cream, with a pistachio hue exclusive to Samsung’s online store.

The slightly more premium Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s colors are violet shadow and graphite cream, with a green shadow hue as an online-only exclusive to Samsung’s store.



The clamshell Galaxy Z Flip 8 colors are pink, graphite and cream, with mint as an exclusive to Samsung’s online store.

Tech.title: Original Xbox Games Are Coming to PC Starting With 4 Fan Favorites
Tech.content:
Four classic Xbox games are heading to PC as part of a new program from Microsoft. These older titles, which are currently available on Xbox Game Pass, will now be playable on desktops, laptops and handhelds such as the ROG Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X.

On Wednesday, the Xbox Backward Compatibility preview went live, allowing owners of four titles first released for the original Xbox – Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge and Fuzion Frenzy – to play them on their Windows PC and handhelds. Microsoft says it will roll out more features for these games in the future, including Xbox Achievements.

Microsoft

The four games may be more than 20 years old, but Microsoft did add some options to improve the gaming experience. Players can change the graphics settings, including up to 4x resolution upscaling, VSync support, display mode options, anisotropic filtering, enhanced anti-aliasing and more customizations to improve the look of these older titles.

Each game is available for $10 on the Xbox Store, and once owned on Xbox, it can be played on PC or handhelds via Xbox Play Anywhere or streamed with Xbox Cloud Gaming. The titles are also available on Xbox Game Pass.

To play these games on a desktop, laptop or handheld, it must meet certain hardware specs:

Minimum system requirements:

GPU: Nvidia GTX 950 or AMD Radeon RX 550 or Intel UHD 770 or Intel Arc A310

Nvidia GTX 950 or AMD Radeon RX 550 or Intel UHD 770 or Intel Arc A310 CPU : Min 4 Cores Intel Core i3-8100 or AMD Ryzen 3 1200 or AMD Ryzen Z2 A Processor

: Min 4 Cores Intel Core i3-8100 or AMD Ryzen 3 1200 or AMD Ryzen Z2 A Processor RAM: 8GB

8GB OS: Windows 11

Windows 11 Drivers and Versions: Latest Version as of January 2026

Recommended specifications:

GPU : Radeon RX 68005 or Nvidia GTX 1070 Ti or Intel Arc A770

: Radeon RX 68005 or Nvidia GTX 1070 Ti or Intel Arc A770 CPU : 6 cores and 12 threads Intel Core i5-10400 or AMD Ryzen 5 3600 or AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme

: 6 cores and 12 threads Intel Core i5-10400 or AMD Ryzen 5 3600 or AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme DirectX Version : DirectX12 API, Hardware Feature Level 11

: DirectX12 API, Hardware Feature Level 11 GPU VRAM: 8GB

8GB OS : Windows 11

: Windows 11 Drivers and Versions: Latest Version as of January 2026

Microsoft says the Xbox Backward Compatibility program is a form of game preservation, which has become a concern for gamers. With Sony announcing it will phase out physical discs and Nintendo’s Game-Key Cards that don’t contain the actual games, many worry that game ownership will become entirely dependent on publishers rather than having a physical medium to hold onto. There is a growing number of delisted games that are no longer available to those who purchased them, and with the future of gaming looking increasingly uncertain because of the current memory shortage, many fear their digital game collections could simply disappear from their accounts.
